listings.description:
Modern information technologies demand ever-increasing computational power and data storage capabilities. However, these advances come with significant energy costs, as a substantial fraction of the electricity consumed by today's computing hardware is ultimately dissipated as heat. While heat is often regarded as a limitation, non-uniform temperature distributions can give rise to unique physical phenomena that can be harnessed for novel computing concepts. For example, temperature gradients can be used to manipulate magnetic data bits, drive domain-wall motion, and enable stochastic and unconventional computing approaches.

This PhD project will explore the non-equilibrium behaviour of magnetic materials and nanomagnetic devices. Working within an interdisciplinary research environment, the successful candidate will develop and investigate novel reconfigurable magnetic metamaterials using fast, efficient, and optically controlled nanoscale heating techniques.

The project aims to uncover how thermal gradients and non-equilibrium conditions can be exploited for information processing applications, including controlled magnetic switching, magnetic domain manipulation, and unconventional computing architectures (for examples see https://dx.doi.org/10.1039/C9NR01628G, https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevApplied.18.024014 or https://doi.org/10.1103/9mlg-ckxl

The scope of this PhD project allows to either take an experimental approach (including nanofabrication of devices and table-top measurements of optical, magnetic and electrical properties), a focus on numerical multi-physics simulations, or a combination of both, depending of the candidates interests.

As a research student within the Department of Physics you will be exposed to diverse material research such as magnetism, spintronics, and novel 2D and topological materials for energy-efficient applications, as well as interdisciplinary links to neuromorphic computing architectures. You will benefit from our recent £4.2m building refurbishment and the University's investment in updating our physics, chemistry and engineering laboratories.

Research within the Department of Physics is further supported by access to an experienced team of researchers and state-of-the-art facilities of the Loughborough's Material Characterisation Centre (LMCC), which contains over £6m of world-class characterisation equipment.

At Loughborough University you will join a diverse, supportive and academically stimulating community

listings.title: Breaking Ground: Investigating Soil Aeration as a Natural Flood Management Strategy
listings.summary: Flooding is one of the fastest-growing environmental risks worldwide, intensified by climate change and evolving land use. Communities across the UK are already facing the consequences. But what if managing soil differently could help reduce flood risk?
listings.description:
Flooding is one of the fastest-growing environmental risks worldwide, intensified by climate change and evolving land use. Communities across the UK are already facing the consequences. But what if managing soil differently could help reduce flood risk?

Natural Flood Management (NFM) offers a promising, nature-based solution by working with landscapes to slow, store, and absorb water. Among the techniques gaining attention is soil aeration, a practical intervention used by land managers to reduce compaction, improve infiltration, and enhance water storage. Despite its growing adoption, there remains surprisingly little robust, real-world evidence of how effective it truly is. This Master’s by Research project puts you at the forefront of that question.

Based in Calderdale, West Yorkshire, you will work within a live, practitioner-led field experiment using a Before–After–Control–Impact (BACI) design—considered one of the strongest approaches for evaluating environmental change. With baseline data already collected and aeration due to be implemented, you’ll be uniquely positioned to measure real impacts as they happen.

- Real world impact: Your findings will directly inform flood resilience strategies used by practitioners and policymakers.

- Hands on fieldwork: Get out into the landscape to measure infiltration, soil compaction, and moisture dynamics using professional techniques.

- Collaborative experience: Work alongside land managers and NFM practitioners, gaining insight into how science shapes decisions on the ground.

- Strong employability focus: Develop skills in field methods, data analysis, and applied environmental research that are highly valued in consultancy, government, and NGOs.

Calder Rivers Trust have established a Before–After–Control–Impact (BACI) experiment in Calderdale, West Yorkshire. Baseline data have already been collected across treatment and control sites, including measurements of soil structure, infiltration, compaction and soil moisture. Aeration is scheduled for September 2026 across half of the study area, with the remaining sites retained as controls. This provides a valuable opportunity to analyse a well-designed field experiment assessing soil aeration impacts under real-world conditions.

The Loke Centre for Trophoblast Research (CTR) provides a dynamic environment for PhD training in placental biology and reproductive science. Founded in 2007, it brings together over 30 Principal Investigators with a shared interest in the scientific study of the placenta, early development and maternal-fetal interactions during pregnancy.

Our PIs are recognized international experts in their fields based across Cambridge in the Departments of Physiology, Development, and Neuroscience, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Pathology, Genetics, and allied institutes, including the Institute of Metabolic Science, Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, Cambridge Institute of Therapeutic Immunology and Infectious Disease, the LMB, Babraham, and Wellcome Sanger Institute. A Loke CTR Studentship will be held within the relevant department or Institute, where an internal Departmental Postgraduate Educational Committee is responsible for administering your degree.

Our PhD students have access to unique training opportunities to prepare them for successful careers in research. Students will present their research by giving seminars at our annual Away Days and international conferences, and attend a variety of seminars given by distinguished scientists with the Loke CTR and affiliated Department or Institute.

There are also opportunities to participate and present in interdisciplinary seminars hosted by Cambridge Reproduction of which the Loke CTR is a founding member. Students will gain training in our Placental Biology Course and receive support from them to attend international meetings. Loke CTR PhD students will also become members of the Postgraduate School of the Life Sciences, which organises and promotes many further training opportunities.

We are pleased to consider applications for fully funded, full-time study over four years or part-time over five years. Studentships are open for applications in October of the year prior to the start of your studies.

listings.title: Waters rising again: The loss and reconnection of floodplains
listings.summary: This funded PhD studentship is an exciting opportunity to conduct new interdisciplinary research on floodplains. It will combine approaches from the natural and social sciences to investigate the factors that influence the loss and, more recently, reconnection of floodplains. The research findings will inform new…
listings.description:
This funded PhD studentship is an exciting opportunity to conduct new interdisciplinary research on floodplains. It will combine approaches from the natural and social sciences to investigate the factors that influence the loss and, more recently, reconnection of floodplains. The research findings will inform new policy and best practice for nature-based solutions and the ecological restoration of rivers and floodplains. The studentship covers fees and stipend for a home (UK) student to study a PhD with funding provided by the Leverhulme Trust through the Connected Waters Leverhulme Doctoral Programme.

Floodplains are naturally dynamic components of river systems that support diverse and productive ecological communities. However, human activities have caused many floodplains to become partially or completely disconnected from their rivers, resulting in numerous impacts to nature and society. Though, waters are beginning to rise again. Floodplains are being reconnected through initiatives like ecological restoration and nature-based solutions for flooding.

In this study, a PhD researcher will investigate the factors that influence the loss and, more recently, reconnection of floodplains. The project aims to determine how social, economic, political and environmental factors interact to drive hydrological, topographic and ecological changes that influence floodplain inundation frequency and extent.

The PhD researcher will have considerable flexibility in the design and implementation of the project, adjusting the focus based on their interests and the latest research findings. For example, the project could take a historical perspective and combine archival information (e.g. maps, documents, artwork) and environmental analyses (e.g. hydrological, GIS). Alternatively, the researcher could apply a theoretical framework appropriate for the social-hydro-ecological system and employ social science approaches and qualitative methods (e.g. interviews). In either case, we would encourage a forward-looking element to the research that places the new knowledge in the context of changing domestic and/or international policy.

The research project will likely involve fieldwork within the UK, and potentially internationally, to conduct surveys, interviews and/or questionnaires. There is the potential to collect new environmental data (e.g. water levels, vegetation cover), if the applicant is interested.

listings.title: Characterisation of High Shear Mixers for Process Intensification
listings.summary: High shear mixers such as rotor-stators, ultrasonicators, high pressure jets, are used for dispersion processes during the manufacture of numerous high value products.
listings.description:
High shear mixers such as rotor-stators, ultrasonicators, high pressure jets, are used for dispersion processes during the manufacture of numerous high value products.

These may be in the form of liquid-liquid dispersions (emulsions), a dispersion of fine powder (nanoparticle, nanoclay, graphite dispersions) or three phase systems, for ex. Pickering emulsions. varying from pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, food, personal care products to paints, lubricants, cosmetics. The generation of a fine dispersion, i.e. small particle or droplet sizes are essential in achieving the high performance products and the high levels of local energy dissipation rate make such devices suitable for dispersion processes.

The product quality depends on both the breakup performance of these devices and the homogeneity achieved within the bulk as breakage would typically occur locally. It is also common to have significant changes in the dispersion rheology during the dispersion process: a highly non-Newtonian behaviour may develop during emulsification or the delamination of layered structures or the pre-dispersion rheology, i.e. prior to deagglomeration may be complex. This would have severe effects on the overall bulk flow and hence homogeneity. Scale up is another challenge.

This project will aim to study the flow and power characteristics of high shear mixers. The study will build on the previous work of the supervisor and make use of bench scale high shear process devices- a selection of rotor-stator designs and an ultrasonicator- in both batch and re-circulation mode. The objectives will be to establish the flow and power characteristics of such devices in liquids of a range of rheological properties and how the flow established may have an effect on dispersion processes, demonstrating this with case studies of emulsification and deagglomeration.

The knowledge developed will provide guidelines for industrial practice applicable to a wide range of products. You will have the opportunity to make use of a range of devices and analytical techniques. The knowledge and skills developed should enhance your employability in a wide range of industries.

It is anticipated that there will be the opportunity to present and discuss findings during international conferences and also network with other researchers in the field. For further information, contact Dr Nerime Gül Özcan-Taşkın.

listings.summary: Coatings are used for a wide range of applications with formulations developed or adapted according to the needs specific to the surfaces they are used on- smoothness, brightness, scratch resistance are among these. Challenges of global dimension experienced in the recent years have accentuated the need to develop new…
listings.description:
Coatings are used for a wide range of applications with formulations developed or adapted according to the needs specific to the surfaces they are used on- smoothness, brightness, scratch resistance are among these. Challenges of global dimension experienced in the recent years have accentuated the need to develop new formulation coatings with antimicrobial properties that can be used areas of dense populations, such as hospitals, schools, in public transport to inhibit or minimise the risks of spreading diseases in the community.

It has also been shown that coatings that include nanoparticles in their formulation have far more superior performance provided that a fine dispersion can be obtained through size reduction, i.e. through the deagglomeration of a hierarchy of particle clusters that typically

form when fine powders are added into a liquid. Large sizes also hinder control over the final distribution in the dried coating after solvent evaporation.

This multi-disciplinary project, which will be performed in collaboration between Chemical and Materials Engineering Departments, has the overall objectives of developing a high performance coating formulation and associated processing route to achieve fine dispersions enabling control over the final coating architecture and optical properties.

The project therefore has two main strands: product and process development. There will be the opportunity to both learn about analytical techniques to determine the properties of new coatings, characterise their performance and develop related energy intensive processes to implement across a range of scales of operation.

listings.title: Connectivity-driven Reef Resilience: Fish Community Structure and Functional Redundancy Across Indo-Pacific Seascapes
listings.summary: This project seeks to determine how connectivity between mangroves, seagrass, and coral reefs shapes reef fish community structure, functional redundancy, and productivity across the Indo‑Pacific, and to assess whether these connectivity‑driven patterns are influenced by marine protected area (MPA) presence. In…
listings.description:
This project seeks to determine how connectivity between mangroves, seagrass, and coral reefs shapes reef fish community structure, functional redundancy, and productivity across the Indo‑Pacific, and to assess whether these connectivity‑driven patterns are influenced by marine protected area (MPA) presence. In particular, the research will tackle three main objectives; a) determine whether and how proximity to mangrove and seagrass ecosystems affects coral reef fish communities in terms of biomass, productivity, and function; b) quantify fish co-occurrence patterns and community turnover from mangrove, seagrass, and coral reef habitats as a function of benthic structure and unseen taxa; and c) discover whether and how connectivity-driven patterns in biomass and function relate to reef fish community turnover and productivity, and is this influenced by MPAs?

The PhD candidate will have an opportunity to work with leading world experts in an interdisciplinary environment, embedded into a Horizon Europe project that not only evaluates many aspects of connectivity, but also works with local communities to implement change based on the research.

The successful PhD candidate will work with experts in the field of conservation science, ecology, social science, remote sensing, and quantitative ecology. The University of Leeds-based team leads in conservation science and quantitative ecology.

Tropical marine ecosystems are rapidly changing under climate change, driving large-scale shifts in habitat quality, species distributions and marine food-web structure. Coral reefs form the primary habitat of hundreds of economically valuable fish species, with many of those relying on adjacent “green” habitats (seagrass, mangroves). Interconnectivity between adjacent coral, mangroves and seagrass meadows underpins the ontogenetic migration of important fish species from nursery grounds in green habitats to feeding and spawning grounds in coral reef habitat, enabling lifecycle completion across a coastal ecosystem mosaic. Previous studies have examined connectivity and functional redundancy in isolation, without considering adjacent green habitats. This project will address this knowledge gap through comparing fish community assemblage, functional diversity and demographic structure.

listings.title: Development of natural-ageing-resistant, heat-treatable lean aluminium alloys for automotive applications
listings.summary: Applications are invited for one full-time EPSRC Industrial CASE (ICASE) PhD studentship for the project “Development of natural-ageing-resistant, heat-treatable lean aluminium alloys for automotive applications”
listings.description:
Applications are invited for one full-time EPSRC Industrial CASE (ICASE) PhD studentship for the project “Development of natural-ageing-resistant, heat-treatable lean aluminium alloys for automotive applications”

The Brunel Centre for Advanced Solidification Technology (BCAST) is a specialist research centre in metallurgy with a focus on the processing of metallic materials for lightweighting applications. See BCAST for more information. The project is sponsored by Constellium, a leading global manufacturer of high-quality, technically advanced aluminium products and systems.

Successful applicants will receive an annual stipend (bursary) starting from approximately £23,000 plus payment of their full-time home tuition fees for a period of up to 48 months (4 years).

Lean automotive aluminium with a lower concentration of alloying elements offers moderate strength and relatively high productivity compared to its highly alloyed counterparts. However, automotive aluminium alloys are susceptible to natural ageing at room temperature, resulting in the formation of clusters from a supersaturated solid solution produced after fast quenching from solution heat treatment. This leads to increased hardness, which affects both formability and the subsequent precipitation hardening process. In addition, promoting a circular economy in the aluminium industry by increasing recyclability and using more recycled aluminium is essential for saving resources, reducing waste and creating a more sustainable future.

This project will focus on understanding the effects of vacancy-trapping element addition and quench rate sensitivity of lean Al-Mg-Si-based alloys with varying level of recycled content on the natural ageing response at room temperature and precipitation hardening behaviour during artificial ageing treatment, with the aim of developing lean recyclable Al-Si-Mg-based alloys that are resistant to natural ageing, tolerant of slower quenching rates, and capable of offering high productivity and moderate mechanical properties for automotive applications.

The project will be part of the activities of the Constellium University Technology Centre (UTC) established with BCAST. The successful candidate will have the opportunity to interact with researchers in BCAST and with Constellium’s industrial research engineers. Over the years, supply chains have become more complex, more interdependent and more vulnerable, making resilience an indispensable business capability. The need for resilience capabilities has reached high levels of urgency in the wake of recent and current conflicts around the world, unprecedented rupture in geopolitics, climate emergency, pandemics, technological changes, systemic competition etc. The economic, social and environmental impacts of these are so consequential that resilient supply chains are now viewed as national security matter.

Supply chains are complex adaptive networks that can change and reorganise to adapt to prevailing challenges. As these complex networks operate and interact with both exogenous and endogenous entities whilst adapting to threats, there is emergence of situations, circumstances, events, further threats and vulnerabilities that may not be known a-priori, and these can be seen as novelties.

Whilst a range of literature have explored strategies to address known threats and vulnerabilities, novel threats and vulnerabilities are under-explored particularly in supply networks. Novel threats and vulnerabilities affect all kinds of supply networks including food supply networks which have significant exposure. With the food sector being the UK’s biggest industrial sector, developing resilience capabilities in this sector is of high importance.

listings.title: MPhil/PhD Studentship in The Great British Battery: Efficient, Grid-Scale Subsurface Storage of Nuclear Heat for UK Net-Zero Energy

The transition to a low-carbon energy system requires innovative solutions that can balance fluctuations in renewable energy supply while maximising the efficiency of future energy infrastructure. This PhD project will investigate high-enthalpy subsurface heat storage, a novel concept that could enable excess thermal energy to be stored underground and recovered when energy demand is high or renewable generation is low.

The research will undertake the first comprehensive assessment of subsurface heat storage potential at three strategically important UK sites, each representing distinct geological and engineering conditions. Using a combination of advanced geological characterisation, machine learning-enabled subsurface modelling, and dynamic heat transport simulation, the project will evaluate the technical feasibility and long-term performance of geological heat storage systems.

Located at the interface of geoscience, energy systems and computational modelling, the project offers an exciting opportunity to contribute to a rapidly emerging field with significant relevance to the future energy transition. The research will help advance scientific understanding of how the subsurface can be used to improve energy flexibility, reduce waste, and support the integration of low-carbon power generation technologies.

The purpose of this project is to determine whether geological reservoirs can provide safe and effective long-term storage for excess nuclear-derived heat, helping improve the flexibility and efficiency of future low-carbon energy systems.

Are you passionate about bridging computer vision and clinical biomechanics to revolutionise healthcare? Clinical gait analysis is an established standard for evaluating medical conditions such as cerebral palsy and age-related pathologies. However, it is severely bottlenecked by its reliance on traditional marker-based optical motion capture. This methodology requires expensive hardware, extended patient preparation, and can cause significant discomfort.

This doctoral project will engineer and validate a markerless motion capture pipeline directly resolving these clinical limitations. You will leverage Human Mesh Recovery to extract highly accurate multiplanar joint kinematics and kinetics without physical laboratory markers. By comparing the HMR pipeline against gold-standard 3D marker-based systems across healthy controls, individuals with age-related gait decline, and patients with cerebral palsy, you will establish clinical accuracy and sensitivity to pathological deviations.

Working closely with clinical scientists and the wider orthopaedic surgery team, you will scale proven methodologies into pipelines and clinical workflows. This is a unique opportunity to translate cutting-edge computational biomechanics directly into point-of-care public health practice.

The primary purpose of this doctoral programme is to transition validated artificial intelligence motion capture methodologies from functional screening into active clinical workflows. By addressing the limitations of traditional marker-based systems, this project aims to drastically reduce patient preparation

The LGM project: in vitro modelling of the Lipid metabolism in the Glioblastoma tumour Microenvironment: the proposed PhD project focusses on the most aggressive and difficult-to-treat brain cancer in adults, glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). How can creative practice help us understand and improve reproductive health futures? This interdisciplinary PhD project sits at the intersection of arts and health, exploring how speculative fictioning can be used to investigate reproductive health experiences and imagine more equitable futures with communities experiencing reproductive health inequities.

The project focuses on reproductive imaginaries; the ideas, values and expectations that shape how people understand reproduction including pregnancy decision-making, parenthood, family-making, health and care. While reproductive health is often discussed through medical, policy or technological frameworks, less attention has been paid to how communities themselves creatively imagine alternative futures.

Working with communities experiencing reproductive health inequities, the successful candidate will use speculative fictioning as a participatory arts method to explore lived experiences of reproductive health. Participants will co-create stories, artworks to create future scenarios that challenge dominant assumptions and generate new possibilities for reproductive justice.

The project offers an exciting opportunity for candidates interested in arts and health, creative research methods, visual culture, social justice and community engagement. It aligns strongly with the University of Derby's academic themes of Creative and Cultural Industries and Public Services.

The University of Derby has an opportunity for a full-time postgraduate research studentship in the Data Science area of research in the College of Science and Engineering.

The successful applicant will receive a maintenance stipend (based on the minimum stipend defined by UKRI, currently £21,805 for the academic year 2026/27) and home MPhil/PhD tuition fees (£5,238 - subject to amendment) only up to the target submission date.

Please note: If your application is successful and you are assessed as international for fees purposes, you will need to pay the difference between the home fees and the international fees.

The successful applicant will be expected to complete their MPhil/PhD within 3 years on the MPhil/PhD route, contribute to the College REF submission and get involved in the wider research activities of the College.

This PhD project explores how trustworthy agentic AI can improve cyber security assessment and resilience in cyber-physical systems, including connected infrastructure, industrial environments and IoT-enabled services. As organisations increasingly rely on interconnected IT, OT, IoT and cloud technologies, assessing cyber risk consistently and transparently becomes more difficult, particularly where systems are safety-sensitive or operationally constrained.

The project will develop AI-assisted methods that interpret security requirements, translate them into executable assessment workflows and support evidence-based analysis across heterogeneous environments. Using an existing hybrid experimental testbed that combines real devices and virtual infrastructure, the research will evaluate these methods under realistic cyber-physical scenarios. The project is well suited to candidates interested in cyber security, AI, IoT, critical infrastructure or resilient digital systems.

This project aims to investigate how agentic AI can be used responsibly to support cyber security assessment in complex cyber-physical environments while maintaining trust, explainability and evidence-based decision-making.

The successful applicant will receive a maintenance stipend (based on the minimum stipend defined by UKRI, currently £21,805 for the academic year 2026/27) and home MPhil/PhD tuition fees (£5,238 - subject to amendment) only up to the target submission date.

Please note: If your application is successful and you are assessed as international for fees purposes, you will need to pay the difference between the home fees and the international fees.

Crime is not randomly distributed. Offences cluster in particular places and at particular times, but these patterns may contain information about the processes that generate crime that conventional hotspot analyses cannot reveal.

This interdisciplinary PhD will develop new mathematical and computational methods for investigating the spatial and temporal structure of crime. The project will develop spatial and temporal correlation methods and apply them to large-scale and potentially near-real-time crime data, with the aim of extracting information about underlying crime-generating processes.

You will investigate how these ideas can be adapted to spatial and spatio-temporal event data and apply them to large-scale UK police-recorded crime datasets. Starting with spatial correlation and anti-correlation, the project will examine the characteristic distances over which crime events are statistically related before extending the theory to temporal and spatio-temporal patterns.

A particularly exciting aspect of the project will be investigating whether observed crime patterns can reveal properties of the underlying processes generating them, potentially providing new ways to understand repeat offending, crime-generating mechanisms and latent offender populations.

The project combines data science, complex systems, statistical modelling and policing, with opportunities to work with academic and policing collaborators.

The purpose of this PhD is to develop a new correlation-based framework for understanding how crime events are related across space and time, and to establish what these relationships can reveal

In Europe, an estimated 1 in 5 children fall victim to some form of sexual violence (Council of Europe, 2020). However, the true extent of child sexual abuse (CSA) remains largely unknown as it is underreported with as little as 12% of all cases of abuse being reported to the authorities (Lahtinen et al., 2018). In cases where there is known risk or allegations of sexual harm in the community, the responsibility for assessing risk and making defensible decisions about protecting children often belongs to frontline child protection professionals e.g. social workers, youth and family workers (Blagden et al, 2026; Stokes & Schmidt, 2012). However, such decision-making is complicated and hampered by incomplete information and a lack of tools to help CSA practitioners make such decisions. This exciting PhD studentship will break new ground by addressing a crucial gap in the CSA prevention landscape, and will contribute to new knowledge and practice in effectively assessing men at-risk of committing CSA in the community. The PhD will explore the current approaches to balancing risk and protective factors in those at-risk of committing CSA in the community, explore the needs, confidence and judgements of practitioners when making child protection decisions and finally contribute to robust evaluation of the Risk and Desistance Hexagon.

Children and young people are increasingly expected to play an active role in shaping the services and support they receive. Within Special Educational Needs and Disability (SEND), participation is a core principle of policy and practice, yet evidence suggests young people are often consulted without having meaningful influence on the decisions that affect their lives. The challenge is no longer simply ensuring that young people are heard, but understanding how their views contribute to real change.

This PhD will explore how young disabled people influence local authority SEND decision-making and service improvement. Drawing on the work of the University's Inclusion and Special Educational Needs and Disability (ISEND) Research Cluster, and regional and national local authority youth voice links, the project will investigate how disability youth participation moves from voice to influence within local authority systems.

Using qualitative and participatory research approaches, the successful candidate will explore how disabled young people, local authority professionals and policymakers participate in and shape decision-making processes, examining how participation contributes to SEND service improvement within the public sector. The project offers an exciting opportunity to contribute to a growing area of research with direct relevance to policy, practice and social justice.

The purpose of this project is to understand how young disabled people influence decision-making and service improvement within local authority SEND systems.

listings.title: Understanding legume nitrogen dynamics and their implications for greenhouse gas mitigation in regenerative agriculture
listings.summary: Understanding legume nitrogen dynamics and their implications for greenhouse gas mitigation in regenerative agriculture PhD
listings.description:
Understanding legume nitrogen dynamics and their implications for greenhouse gas mitigation in regenerative agriculture PhD

We invite applications from ambitious life-science graduates for a fully funded PhD at Cranfield University, supported by the EPSRC Doctoral Landscape Award. The award covers Home fees (£5,238 p.a.) and provides a £24,500 annual tax-free stipend for three years. Based in the Cranfield Environment Centre, the student will investigate how legumes shape nitrogen cycling, crop performance and greenhouse-gas emissions in regenerative arable rotations, developing science to support sustainable, lower-input farming and UK Net Zero goals.

UK agriculture produces around 70% of national nitrous oxide emissions, a greenhouse gas with 273 times the global warming potential of carbon dioxide over 100 years. Much arises from inefficient nitrogen fertiliser use. Legumes can reduce this reliance by fixing atmospheric nitrogen, removing synthetic nitrogen fertiliser requirements for themselves and potentially reducing requirements for following crops. Yet we cannot reliably predict when, where or how much legume-derived nitrogen becomes available. This limits farmers’ ability to adjust subsequent fertiliser applications and realise the full economic and environmental value of legumes.

This PhD will uncover how legumes regulate soil nitrogen cycling across arable rotations. The student will quantify effects on subsequent cereal yield, nitrogen-use efficiency, greenhouse-gas emissions and fertiliser-replacement potential under contrasting arable management systems. Field, laboratory and controlled-environment experiments will determine when and where legume-derived nitrogen becomes available within bulk soil and the rhizosphere. Conventional soil mineral nitrogen testing will be compared with detailed measurements of mineralisation, biological nitrogen fixation, crop nitrogen uptake and microbial processes. The research will test whether this deeper nitrogen accounting can deliver worthwhile financial and environmental gains over current practice.

This EPSRC-funded studentship will be based in the Cranfield Environment Centre, whose research spans soil and air quality, climate change, crop monitoring, resilience and ecosystem services. The project also offers close collaboration with the James Hutton Institute, an internationally recognised centre for sustainable-cropping research. listings.summary: We are inviting applications for an eight-week paid research internship (€250/week) investigating age- and sex-specific biomechanics of distance runners.
listings.description:
We are inviting applications for an eight-week paid research internship (€250/week) investigating age- and sex-specific biomechanics of distance runners.

The internship provides an exciting opportunity to work with a comprehensive biomechanical dataset of distance runners and develop practical experience in working with 3D motion capture data, kinematic profiling, and advanced movement variability analysis.

The project will focus on understanding how movement variability in distance runners differs between athletes of different ages and sexes.

Outcomes are expected to contribute to high-quality research outputs (e.g., peer-reviewed journal publications and/or presentations at the International Society of Biomechanics in Sports (ISBS) conference).

During the internship, you will have access to Cardiff Metropolitan University’s biomechanics facilities, including its state-of-the-art laboratories and equipment, and work under the supervision of experienced sport biomechanics researchers (note that attendance at Cyncoed Campus is required throughout the internship). Moreover, this internship will provide hands-on experience in:

We are seeking an enthusiastic student with an interest in sport biomechanics, distance running science, and/or human movement research. The internship is open to current MSc or PhD students in a relevant field, and applicants from all countries and universities.

Previous experience of working with motion-capture data (VICON), 3D kinematic analysis (Visual3D), programming (e.g., MATLAB, Python), and/or movement variability analysis (e.g., continuous relative phase, vector coding) would be advantageous but not required. However, applicants with a strong interest in developing these and other skills are encouraged to apply.

The internship will be supervised by Dr Jasper Verheul and Sophie Burton, and is supported by the ISBS Student Internship grant.

To apply, please submit a brief CV and statement of interest (max of one A4 each), outlining your relevant experience and why you would like to undertake this internship. Applications or any questions related to the internship can be submitted via email to Dr Jasper Verheul (jpverheul@cardiffmet.ac.uk) by Friday 13th November 2026.

Applicants will be contacted within three weeks of the application deadline, and interviews are expected to take place in December 2026.

listings.title: Advancing temperature-differentiated carbon isotope analysis
listings.summary: Carbon isotope analysis is a crucial tool for tracing biogeochemical processes, yet effective differentiation of organic and inorganic carbon components often requires targeted pre-treatment, such as acidification or bleaching, to isolate specific carbon pools prior to analysis. While total organic carbon (TOC) is…
listings.description:
Carbon isotope analysis is a crucial tool for tracing biogeochemical processes, yet effective differentiation of organic and inorganic carbon components often requires targeted pre-treatment, such as acidification or bleaching, to isolate specific carbon pools prior to analysis. While total organic carbon (TOC) is typically analysed using an elemental analyser coupled to an isotope ratio mass spectrometer (IRMS), this approach aggregates all organic carbon within a sample, limiting its capacity to distinguish between labile and refractory carbon fractions. By isolating carbon based on temperature-dependent decomposition, it is possible to obtain distinct isotopic signatures for more recently assimilated, labile carbon versus older, more stable carbon pools. Furthermore, this method provides insights into the relative contributions of different organic carbon sources within a sample, and the linkages between thermal stability and organic matter composition.

Our project seeks to validate an innovative approach to temperature-dependent carbon isotope differentiation using the Elementar soli TOC cube and isoprime precisION IRMS. By varying combustion temperatures and analysing the resulting CO₂ isotope signatures, we aim to achieve high-resolution differentiation of both organic and inorganic carbon fractions within the same sample. Additionally, this approach will allow for the isotopic characterisation of specific organic carbon pools, providing enhanced precision in the analysis of complex environmental matrices.

Methodological development will focus on optimising analytical procedures and combustion parameters, as well as testing across diverse sample matrices to ensure reproducibility and accuracy. The outcomes of this work are expected to advance our ability to resolve carbon sources and transformations in heterogeneous environmental samples, offering new opportunities for carbon cycle research in soils, sediments, and other carbon-rich systems. The system will offer efficient isotopic analysis of different carbon sources on a single sample aliquot.

The project will be based at Loughborough University and the British Geological Survey (BGS), utilising the existing soli TOC cube and isoprime precisION IRMS instrumentation in the BGS Stable Isotope Facility. listings.title: Macroevolution of seastars
listings.summary: This project will advance our understanding of biodiversity patterns in the sea, with a focus in deep-sea echinoderms, using a multidisciplinary approach to investigate drivers of biodiversity and predict changes in response to changing environmental conditions.
listings.description:
This project will advance our understanding of biodiversity patterns in the sea, with a focus in deep-sea echinoderms, using a multidisciplinary approach to investigate drivers of biodiversity and predict changes in response to changing environmental conditions.

We currently face a triple planetary crisis with pollution, climate change and biodiversity loss. Understanding evolutionary histories can provide important information on how species are related, how they have adapted to past changes, and to identify unique lineages, helping us predict biodiversity changes with climate change and prioritise areas for conservation.

In recent decades, technological advances have allowed increased exploration of the deep sea, and DNA sequencing techniques have become more cost-efficient and capable of generating large datasets that can resolve deep-phylogenetic relationships.

Members of the class Asteroidea are important component of benthic ecosystems, inhabiting from intertidal to abyssal depths, have a global distribution and are functionally diverse, with different feeding strategies, locomotion and reproduction.

This project will aim to investigate the evolutionary history of a group of deep-sea seastars. To achieve this goal, the student will use both recently collected samples and historical material from the Natural History Museum and the Discovery Collections. The student will generate phylogenomic data using innovative molecular techniques.

Additionally, the student will expand an existing distributional database by identifying/analysing new material and material housed in other scientific collections incorporating high-resolution imaging. The student will identify new species to science and will conduct formal species descriptions. Distributional data and traits will be mapped on to the phylogenomic tree to examine patterns of trait evolution and correlations with ecological and/or functional transitions.

The student will gain experience in different molecular techniques including generation of short barcode sequences through Sanger sequencing, to whole genome sequencing techniques using Next Generation Sequencing, PCR.

The student will also receive training in bioinformatics, processing of sequence reads, phylogenetic reconstruction, comparative phylogenetics and biogeographic analyses, and large data handling using R and Python.

listings.title: AI-Enhanced EMC Digital Twin for Automotive WBG Converters
listings.summary: The global shift toward electric mobility requires automotive power electronics with elevated power density, thermal performance, and efficiency. Adopting Wide-Bandgap (WBG) semiconductors, like Silicon Carbide (SiC) and Gallium Nitride (GaN), enables extreme switching frequencies and reduced losses. However, the fast…
listings.description:
The global shift toward electric mobility requires automotive power electronics with elevated power density, thermal performance, and efficiency. Adopting Wide-Bandgap (WBG) semiconductors, like Silicon Carbide (SiC) and Gallium Nitride (GaN), enables extreme switching frequencies and reduced losses. However, the fast switching transients produce severe high-frequency electromagnetic interference (EMI). Ensuring compliance with automotive standards (such as CISPR 25) traditionally requires extensive physical pre compliance testing late in the product cycle, resulting in costly iterations.

This PhD project addresses this bottleneck by developing a predictive, multi-domain Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) Digital Twin framework. The research combines electromagnetic modelling, machine learning, and hardware validation to deliver rapid virtual pre-compliance evaluation for automotive power converters.

This 3.5-year PhD studentship aims to develop an AI-driven Digital Twin capable of predicting high-frequency conducted and radiated emissions against CISPR standards, bridging 3D virtual simulations with real-world physical compliance testing.

The student will undertake a structured programme of virtual modelling, AI development, and experimental validation. Initial activity will involve designing baseline and degraded EMI layout prototypes for WBG converters and extracting layout parasitics using 3D electromagnetic solvers. Using these datasets, dual AI surrogates will be developed: a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model for low-frequency conducted emissions, and a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) that embeds Maxwell’s equations to predict spatial radiated fields. These surrogates will be integrated into a unified digital twin. Finally, the virtual framework will be validated and calibrated against prototype hardware.

Experimental diagnostics will utilise Coventry University’s pre-compliance laboratories to calibrate the AI models. By improving the reliability of virtual EMC screening, this project will help reduce the cost, risk, and time required to develop next-generation automotive power electronics.

listings.title: Fast multi-wavelength variability of accreting compact objects
listings.summary: As matter falls onto compact objects like black holes and neutron stars, due to the presence of turbulence, matter emits a huge amount of strongly variable radiation. The development of fast-readout optical and infrared cameras has made it possible to study X-ray binaries on timescales down to sub-second, and to…
listings.description:
As matter falls onto compact objects like black holes and neutron stars, due to the presence of turbulence, matter emits a huge amount of strongly variable radiation. The development of fast-readout optical and infrared cameras has made it possible to study X-ray binaries on timescales down to sub-second, and to compare their variability directly with the X-rays. This has opened a new window on the accretion–ejection process. For instance in recent years, it has allowed strong constraints to be placed on the properties of the jet and inner accretion flow around both black holes and neutron stars.

The successful candidate will work with strictly simultaneous multiwavelength observations of black hole and neutron star X-ray binaries, obtained with XMM-Newton, NICER and Insight-HXMT in the X-rays, HAWK-I at the VLT in the infrared, and HiPERCAM at the GTC and ULTRACAM at the NTT in the optical. Using time-series analysis techniques in both the time and Fourier domains, the student will extract key physical information on the accretion flow and jet in these systems. Modelling of the observed variability will then be used to place tight constraints on fundamental parameters such as the jet speed, the inner disc truncation radius and the magnetic field strength.

The successful candidate will receive comprehensive research training including technical, personal and professional skills. All researchers at Coventry University (from PhD to Professor) are part of the Doctoral and Researcher College, which provides support with high-quality training and career development activities.

As a C-CDT member you’ll benefit from structured AI training (from core research methods to ethics and innovation), interdisciplinary peer networks, specialist supervision, shared GPU/cloud resources, workshops, seminars and industry-focused challenge projects.

This additional training and community, complements your home research centre programme, accelerates your technical and professional development, and connects you with a broad AI research ecosystem tackling impactful problems across sectors.

listings.title: Additive-Manufacturing-Enabled Electrical Machine Design Using Multi-Physics Optimization
listings.summary: This PhD project forms part of an A*STAR Singapore Research Attachment Programme (SRAP), in collaboration with Coventry University (UK) and the A*STAR's Advanced Remanufacturing and Technology Centre (ARTC), Singapore. The project includes between 1-2 years mobility to Singapore.
listings.description:
This PhD project forms part of an A*STAR Singapore Research Attachment Programme (SRAP), in collaboration with Coventry University (UK) and the A*STAR's Advanced Remanufacturing and Technology Centre (ARTC), Singapore. The project includes between 1-2 years mobility to Singapore.

Through SRAP, Coventry-based PhD researchers undertake one to two years of research training in Singapore under the joint supervision of researchers from both Coventry and ARTC. The programme offers PhD researchers an exceptional opportunity to gain international research experience while contributing to ambitious, multidisciplinary research addressing global technological and sustainability challenges.

This collaborative PhD programme enables researchers to work at the interface of academic research, advanced engineering and industrial innovation. Researchers will engage with expertise and facilities across both institutions, build international research networks, and develop experience in translating advanced research into practical solutions for future mobility and remanufacturing systems.

The programme is particularly suited to ambitious researchers seeking to shape next-generation electric mobility systems and circular manufacturing technologies, while gaining valuable research experience across the UK and Singapore.

This PhD project will investigate the use of additive manufacturing (AM) to develop high-performance electrical machines with enhanced power density, efficiency and thermal performance. The research will establish a design methodology that exploits the geometric and material flexibility offered by AM while addressing the electromagnetic, thermal, mechanical and manufacturing constraints associated with practical machine development.

Candidate machine architectures, including radial- and axial-flux configurations, will first be assessed to establish suitable baseline designs. These designs will then be investigated using coupled electromagnetic, thermal and mechanical modelling and subsequently refined through multi-objective optimisation. Attention will be given to the interaction between machine geometry, AM material properties, cooling requirements, mechanical integrity and manufacturing constraints. Experimentally measured properties of AM materials will be incorporated into the design process to improve the accuracy and practical relevance of the models.

Conventional battery management systems are typically designed and calibrated using battery characteristics measured at the beginning of life. However, batteries continuously evolve during operation due to ageing, temperature variations and changing usage conditions. Capacity, resistance, electrochemical characteristics and degradation mechanisms can change significantly over lifetime. As a result, fixed BMS models and control strategies may become increasingly inaccurate and suboptimal as the battery ages, limiting performance, lifetime and safety.

This PhD project will develop a closed-loop adaptive battery management framework that continuously learns the evolving condition of the battery and adapts its estimation and control strategies to maximise useful lifetime.

The proposed framework will integrate battery sensing, state and parameter estimation, ageing diagnosis, model adaptation and optimal control within a closed loop. Operational battery data will be used to identify changes in battery behaviour and update models and parameters throughout life. Reliable prediction of battery lifetime normally requires months or years of ageing tests, creating a major bottleneck in battery development, qualification and management. Conventional accelerated ageing approaches expose cells to elevated temperatures, high currents or extreme states of charge to shorten testing time. However, aggressive acceleration can alter the underlying degradation modes and mechanisms, meaning that ageing observed under accelerated conditions may not accurately represent degradation during normal operation.

This PhD project will develop a new closed-loop design-of-experiments (DoE) framework for accelerated battery ageing and early-life prognostics. The central research question is: how can battery degradation be accelerated while preserving the degradation modes and mechanisms observed under normal ageing conditions?

The project will combine battery experiments, advanced diagnostics, degradation modelling, optimal experimental design and machine learning. This particular PhD research project will develop an advanced physics-informed artificial intelligence (AI) framework for battery prognostics, enabling accurate prediction of battery degradation trajectory, and remaining useful life (RUL) under dynamic operating conditions. The research will integrate electrochemical and degradation physics with machine learning and data-driven modelling to understand and predict battery ageing trajectories. A key objective will be to develop models capable of predicting future degradation trajectories together with quantified confidence levels, providing reliable uncertainty estimates for decision-making rather than relying solely on point predictions.

The project will further investigate second-life battery applications, forecasting the RUL of batteries when they are repurposed for different operating profiles and applications. This will involve considering variations in duty cycles, temperature, charging strategies, load profiles, and application requirements.

Orthopaedic staples are widely used to fix bones and joints in foot and ankle surgery, for example in arthrodesis (joint fusion) and osteotomy procedures. Yet how many staples to use, which material to choose, and where and at what orientation to place them is still decided largely by surgical convention rather than by quantified biomechanical evidence. Sub-optimal choices can lead to loss of compression, implant loosening, delayed healing or revision surgery. This fully funded PhD offers the opportunity to bring advanced computational mechanics to bear on a real clinical problem, working closely with a practising orthopaedic surgeon.

Swansea University is pleased to offer a fully funded PhD studentship as part of the Faraday Institution PhD Training Programme, focused on developing next-generation microporous membranes for low-cost, long-duration iron–sulfur (Fe–S) redox flow batteries.

Membrane separators are critical to the efficiency and lifetime of redox flow batteries; however, existing commercial membranes suffer from severe active-species crossover, leading to capacity decay and reduced operational efficiency. This project will investigate how the molecular structure, microporosity and chemical functionality of polymers of intrinsic microporosity (PIMs) govern ion transport and selectivity in Fe–S battery chemistries. The successful candidate will design and synthesise functional PIMs with tailored sub-nanometre pores, develop solution-processable membranes, and establish quantitative structure–ion transport–battery performance relationships through advanced membrane characterisation and electrochemical testing.

The project will be hosted by Dr Rui Tan at Swansea University, in close collaboration with Leaf-Tech Ltd, an industrial partner working on the development and scale-up of advanced materials and technologies for energy applications.

Dr Rui Tan’s research group focuses on functional microporous polymers, selective ion-transport membranes and electrochemical energy storage, with particular expertise in molecularly engineered membranes and their application in redox flow and other emerging battery systems. Leaf-Tech Ltd will support the scale-up and manufacturing of PIM materials and membranes, alongside technical input and industrial mentorship to evaluate their manufacturability, scalability and commercial potential for next-generation flow batteries.

The successful candidate will undertake an industrial placement with Leaf-Tech Ltd during the PhD, gaining direct experience in polymer and membrane scale-up, manufacturing, process optimisation and industrial R&D challenges associated with translating advanced membrane materials from laboratory discovery towards practical long-duration energy-storage technologies.

listings.title: Degenerations, fibrations, and mirror symmetry
listings.summary: The Department of Mathematical Sciences at Loughborough University seeks a qualified candidate for a PhD position in algebraic geometry. Algebraic geometry is a vibrant, growing field that has deep links to many other parts of pure mathematics. The proposed project is motivated by recent ideas in mirror symmetry,…
listings.description:
The Department of Mathematical Sciences at Loughborough University seeks a qualified candidate for a PhD position in algebraic geometry. Algebraic geometry is a vibrant, growing field that has deep links to many other parts of pure mathematics. The proposed project is motivated by recent ideas in mirror symmetry, which lies on the interface of algebraic geometry and mathematical physics; the successful candidate will have the potential to contribute to significant new developments in this field.

The successful candidate will work on a project to investigate the properties of Calabi-Yau and Hyperkahler manifolds. Such manifolds are of central importance in many branches of geometry, but many of their properties are still poorly understood.

The project will focus on studying degeneration and fibration structures on these manifolds. Degenerations involve deforming an object until it breaks up into a number of pieces; image bending a piece of stiff plastic until it snaps. Fibrations involve slicing an object into lower-dimensional slices (called “fibres”); envisage the way in which a 3-dimensional pad of paper is made up of many (essentially) 2-dimensional sheets.

Mirror symmetry is a mysterious duality which states that many types of geometric objects (such as Calabi-Yau manifolds) come in pairs, which have related properties. A 2016 conjecture states that degeneration and fibration structures should correspond to one another under this duality: if an object admits a degeneration, then its mirror object should admit a fibration, and vice versa. The aim of this project is to investigate this correspondence.

The successful applicant will join the Centre for Geometry and Applications, which currently includes 11 permanent academic staff, 1 research associate, and 4 PhD students. The Centre has a vibrant research culture, with activities including weekly research seminars, weekly meetings between students and supervisors, and excellent links with groups in neighbouring institutions.

listings.description:
How do we make sense of the continuous stream of events that make up everyday life, and how do those experiences become memories? This PhD will investigate how people understand and remember real-world events, and how these processes change in dementia. The project will combine fundamental research on human memory with studies of how people living with dementia understand, engage with and respond to ongoing experiences.

If your first language is not English you will need to demonstrate that you meet the University’s English language requirements. Our website provides detailed information on the English language tests we accept, as well as the countries that are exempt from the English language requirements.

Please clearly state that you are applying for the School of Psychology Studentship under the supervision of Professor Chris Bird.In the title of your research proposal, please include the name of the studentship for which you are applying.

Our everyday experience is continuous, complex and constantly changing. Nevertheless, we are remarkably good at organising this stream of information into meaningful events: conversations, activities, journeys and other episodes that can later be remembered. Understanding how we achieve this is a fundamental question for memory research. It is also particularly important for understanding dementia, where changes in memory may affect not only the ability to remember the past, but also how people understand and engage with events as they unfold.

The first concerns how we make sense of the present and remember the past. The student will investigate the cognitive processes that allow people to understand complex, continuous experiences and transform them into memories. Rather than relying only on traditional laboratory memory tasks, the research is likely to use more naturalistic materials such as videos, narratives and everyday activities.

The second concerns how people living with dementia understand and engage with the present. Much research on dementia focuses on what people can no longer remember. An important complementary question is what information remains available while an experience is taking place, and what helps people to remain cognitively and socially engaged.

listings.title: ​Magnitude and Controls of Tropical Wetland Methane Emissions Using Novel Satellite Data
listings.summary: Atmospheric methane (CH4) is the second most important anthropogenic greenhouse gas after carbon dioxide and is a major contributor to global warming. Global CH4 concentrations have been increasing, following a stabilisation between 1999 and 2006. However, the causes of the renewed growth remain poorly understood,…
listings.description:
Atmospheric methane (CH4) is the second most important anthropogenic greenhouse gas after carbon dioxide and is a major contributor to global warming. Global CH4 concentrations have been increasing, following a stabilisation between 1999 and 2006. However, the causes of the renewed growth remain poorly understood, predominantly due to uncertainties in the drivers of the sources and sinks of CH4.

Wetlands are one of the largest natural sources of CH4 globally and are one of the biggest uncertainties in the CH4 budget (Saunois et al., 2025). Wetland emissions are predominantly driven by temperature and persistent inundation, resulting in large emissions from tropical wetlands. Current global wetland maps are inconsistent, particularly in densely vegetated regions, leading to uncertainties in the global CH4 budget.

Record breaking increases in atmospheric CH4 were observed in 2020 and 2021 and studies have shown that enhanced emissions from tropical wetlands were a large contributing factor (Feng et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024). Understanding how wetland extent and their associated CH4 emissions respond to climate change is important for constraining the CH4 budget and informing mitigation strategies.

This PhD project aims to exploit cutting-edge satellite observations to improve our understanding of tropical wetland extent and quantify its relationship with CH4 emissions. The project will take advantage of the unique capabilities of the European Space Agency’s Biomass mission, launched April 2025, alongside atmospheric CH4 observations from Sentinel-5 and Sentinel-5P.

ESA Biomass is a radar satellite which is capable of penetrating through vegetation canopies, enabling detection of wetland extent beneath the tropical forests for the first time (ESA, 2025). This provides a new opportunity to map previously unresolved wetland systems in regions such as the Amazon and the Congo basin. At the same time, Sentinel-5 and Sentinel-5P provide high resolution global observations of atmospheric CH4, allowing surface processes to be linked with atmospheric concentrations.

By combining these different Earth Observation techniques, this project aims to investigate the following research questions:

To what extent do recent changes in tropical wetland extent contribute to the increase in atmospheric CH4 concentrations?

listings.summary: Radiotherapy is a critical treatment for improving outcomes in patients with brain tumours. listings.description:
Radiotherapy is a critical treatment for improving outcomes in patients with brain tumours. Radiotherapy can result in side effects, including changes in neurocognitive function, e.g. difficulties with memory and information processing. Such problems impact negatively on quality of life. Neurocognition is complex and involves multiple interconnected regions of the brain. The impact of radiotherapy dose on these networks has not been well described. Identification of areas within the brain that are particularly at risk of neurocognitive damage from radiotherapy could allow these areas to be spared from high radiotherapy doses in future patients.

The APPROACH (Analysis of Proton vs Photon Radiotherapy in Oligodendroglioma and Assessment of Cognitive Health) trial randomises patients with oligodendroglioma, a good prognosis brain tumour, between two different types of radiotherapy (standard photon radiotherapy and Proton Beam Therapy). The trial evaluates neurocognitive function before radiotherapy, one month after radiotherapy and then annually. This project will focus on the baseline and one-month neurocognitive outcomes for the whole group.

Voxel based analysis (VBA) is a spatial data mining technique which is relatively novel in the field of radiotherapy. VBA uses radiotherapy dose distributions, which describe the radiation dose deposition in each part of the brain for every included patient. By mapping the dose distribution of multiple patients to a template anatomy, the relationship between local doses and outcomes can be explored. This project will allow identification of brain sub-regions that are susceptible to neurocognitive dysfunction in relation to radiotherapy dose.

This exciting and novel project will include a systematic review of VBA use in irradiated brain tumour patients, an analysis of pre-treatment and one-month neurocognitive outcomes in APPROACH trial participants and the set up and performance of VBA based on one-month post-radiotherapy neurocognitive outcomes for patients treated in the APPROACH trial.

We are seeking a highly motivated candidate to undertake a PhD program titled "3D Temperature Field Reconstruction from Local Temperature Monitoring in Directed Energy Deposition." This exciting research opportunity focuses on advancing large-scale additive manufacturing using metal wire as feedstock and electric arc as the heat source. The project aims to develop an innovative and efficient method for reconstructing full 3D temperature fields from partial temperature measurements, utilising monitoring techniques deployable in industrial settings. This work will provide critical thermal insights for diagnosing and controlling defects and lay the foundation for a thermal physics-based approach to process qualification.

Additive manufacturing (AM) is a rapidly evolving technology that continues to drive innovation and find diverse applications across industries such as aerospace, energy, and automotive. Among its various techniques, wire-arc directed energy deposition (WA-DED) stands out as a highly promising approach for fabricating large-scale structural components. This process involves feeding a metal filler wire—either coaxially or off-axis—into an electric arc to generate a molten pool that solidifies on a substrate, enabling the layer-by-layer construction of complex 3D objects. The temperature field created by the interaction between the electric arc and the material is a critical factor influencing the microstructure, residual stress, and distortion of the deposited parts, all of which significantly impact their mechanical properties and overall performance. Consequently, accurately determining and effectively controlling the temperature field are essential to achieving a high-quality WA-DED process.

However, accurately determining thermal variables during AM processes remains a significant challenge due to limitations in both measurement and modelling techniques. Current in-process measurement methods are restricted to surface-only monitoring devices (e.g., cameras and pyrometers), which fail to capture subsurface and internal temperature distributions. Semi-destructive approaches, such as embedding thermocouples by drilling holes, can provide internal data but often disrupt the process, alter the thermal fields, and risk damaging the part during fabrication. This project is related to the assessment of a minimally invasive treatment for back pain called ‘nucleus augmentation’. The treatment involved the injection of a hydrogel into a damaged spinal disc to restore its biomechanics. The aim of the study is to examine how the performance of novel hydrogels developed at Leeds can be optimised for nucleus augmentation.

Specifically, the project will focus on the functional performance under adverse loading conditions causing repeated high shear loading and herniation. The three core objectives are (1) to develop a suite of in-vitro test methods to apply physiologically relevant shear loading to the disc. This will involve using our unique multiaxis spine simulator and developing protocols that generate the most adverse loading on the hydrogel-augmented tissue; (2) to evaluate how the hydrogel composition affects the performance, using the new testing methods developed; (3) to develop inclusion/exclusion criteria for the clinical use of the hydrogels. This will involve utilising advanced MRI sequences for characterising soft tissue structure/composition, and developing new methods (including AI-based approaches) to correlate tissue characteristics to the functional performance following nucleus augmentation.

Low back pain is the single largest cause of disability, affecting over 300 million people worldwide. Degeneration of the intervertebral discs (the articulating soft tissues between vertebrae) is strongly linked to low back pain. Nucleus augmentation is an emerging new treatment for disc degeneration that involves injecting a hydrogel into the disc to restore biomechanical function. This cross-disciplinary PhD project will investigate how the performance of a novel hydrogel developed at Leeds can be optimised for nucleus augmentation to both withstand mechanical loading while preventing disc herniation.

The PhD will involve a range of experimental methods including in-vitro testing using donated human tissue. There will be opportunities to use a range of specialist measurement and characterisation equipment, and to develop computational methods (including AI-related algorithms) to process and analyse the data.

Understanding how surgical placement influences implant biomechanics is critical to improving long-term outcomes.

The research will combine computational modelling, experimental simulation, and analysis of retrieved implants to identify the mechanisms driving implant wear and failure. Working closely with clinicians and industry partners, the successful candidate will contribute to research with direct translational impact on orthopaedic surgery, implant design, and patient care.

The aim of the project is to develop and validate (through experimental simulation) a musculoskeletal modelling framework for reverse shoulder replacement that can predict the effects of implant positioning on shoulder biomechanics, implant performance, and potential failure mechanisms.

Reverse shoulder replacement is increasingly used to restore function and reduce pain in patients with severe shoulder disease and rotator cuff deficiency. Despite generally successful outcomes, some implants fail prematurely because of instability, loosening, or excessive wear, often linked to the surgical positioning of implant components. Limited understanding exists of how implant placement influences shoulder biomechanics and long-term performance. Improved predictive tools are needed to support surgical decision-making and optimise outcomes. This project addresses this by combining computational modelling, experimental biomechanics, and analysis of retrieved implants to better understand failure mechanisms and develop evidence-based strategies for more durable shoulder replacements.

listings.description:
Cells experience continuous mechanical forces that regulate their behaviour and function. Understanding how cells respond to these forces is essential for investigating disease mechanisms and developing new therapies. This PhD will advance CellQ-Twin, a soft robotic cell stretching platform, to reproduce physiological and pathological mechanical environments in vitro, enabling disease modelling and therapeutic discovery.

- Develop a next-generation platform capable of delivering programmable multiaxial and rhythmic mechanical loading alongside controlled environmental stimuli.

- Integrate optically transparent printed conductors within elastomeric substrates to enable real-time strain monitoring during live-cell experiments.

- Investigate cellular responses to physiological and pathological loading using advanced imaging, molecular biology and functional assays, focusing on cardiovascular, musculoskeletal and cranial suture mechanobiology.

- Advance translation and commercialisation by improving scalability, usability and compatibility with existing laboratory infrastructure.

Working with interdisciplinary academic and industrial partners, the student will develop expertise in soft robotics, advanced manufacturing and mechanobiology. The project aims to deliver an accessible and versatile research platform that improves disease modelling, supports therapeutic development and reduces reliance on animal experiments.

Mechanical forces play a fundamental role in regulating cellular behaviour, tissue development and disease progression. However, existing cell stretching systems are often expensive and limited in their ability to reproduce complex physiological loading conditions. There is a need for accessible, versatile platforms that enable precise control and monitoring of mechanical stimuli during live-cell experiments. CellQ-Twin addresses this gap by combining programmable soft robotic actuation with integrated strain sensing. This project will enable researchers to investigate cellular responses to physiological and pathological mechanical environments, advancing disease modelling, therapeutic discovery and the development of alternatives to animal experimentation.

listings.description:
This PhD project will investigate the erosion-corrosion behaviour of tungsten carbide produced using a novel sintering-based additive manufacturing process. The research will combine advanced manufacturing, erosion-corrosion testing, electrochemical monitoring, and materials characterisation, providing multidisciplinary training with strong industrial relevance.

- Establish the erosion-corrosion performance of conventionally manufactured tungsten carbide in particle-laden corrosive environments.

- Evaluate the degradation resistance of the newly manufactured materials and identify governing wear and corrosion mechanisms.

- Use relationships between the manufacturing process and degradation processes to enhance manufacturing performance and deliver more durable tungsten carbide components for demanding industrial applications.

During the PhD, the successful candidate will establish benchmark erosion-corrosion performance data for conventionally manufactured tungsten carbide, and begin development of the additive manufacturing process. The focus will then shift to the production and characterisation of novel tungsten carbide materials, alongside detailed erosion-corrosion testing and mechanistic investigations to understand degradation behaviour. Finally, insights into the relationships between manufacturing conditions, microstructure, and performance will be used to enhance the process and maximise material durability.

Conventional manufacturing routes can limit design flexibility and increase production costs, however, powder-based additive manufacturing methods remain challenging for refractory metal composites. As components are increasingly required to operate in aggressive environments involving solid particle erosion and electrochemical corrosion, there is a growing need for innovative manufacturing approaches that deliver enhanced performance and durability. This project addresses this challenge by developing a novel sintering-based additive manufacturing process and establishing how manufacturing influences the degradation and reliability of tungsten carbide in demanding environments.
