listings.summary: Battery electrode manufacturing relies on effective mixing of active materials, conductive additives, binders and solvents to produce homogeneous slurries with suitable properties for coating. However, scaling mixing processes from laboratory to industrial production remains challenging and often relies on…
listings.description:
Battery electrode manufacturing relies on effective mixing of active materials, conductive additives, binders and solvents to produce homogeneous slurries with suitable properties for coating. However, scaling mixing processes from laboratory to industrial production remains challenging and often relies on trial-and-error, increasing development time, material waste and cost.

This PhD project will develop a physics-based computational framework for battery slurry mixing and scale-up, combining Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Discrete Element Method (DEM) with experimental validation. The research will investigate the complex particle-fluid interactions occurring during mixing and establish relationships between material properties, mixer design, operating conditions and slurry quality.

- Investigate the effects of material properties, mixer geometry and operating parameters on slurry homogeneity, mixing efficiency and energy consumption.

The project will ultimately deliver predictive modelling tools to support faster process development, reduce experimental trial-and-error, and enable more efficient scale-up of battery manufacturing.

The project will combine physics-based computational modelling with experimental validation. High-fidelity CFD-DEM models will be developed to capture fluid flow, particle dynamics and particle-fluid interactions during battery slurry mixing. A systematic parametric study will investigate the effects of material properties, mixer geometry and operating conditions on mixing performance. Laboratory experiments using a vacuum planetary mixer will provide rheological and mixing data for model validation. The validated framework will then be extended to pilot/industrial-scale mixing systems, supported by collaboration with UKBIC and CPI, to develop and assess reliable scale-up methodologies.

Battery slurry mixing is a critical step in electrode manufacturing, directly influencing slurry homogeneity, rheology, coating quality and ultimately battery performance. However, the complex interactions between active materials, conductive additives, binders and solvents make the process difficult to understand and optimise. Current scale-up from laboratory to industrial mixers still relies heavily on empirical approaches and trial-and-error, leading to high material consumption, cost and development time. listings.summary: Non-exhaust emissions from brake wear represent a major environmental and health concern, becoming tightly regulated under new Euro 7 standards. This PhD research aims to develop and validate an intelligent Electro-Mechanical Braking (EMB) control system to actively suppress brake particulate emissions.
listings.description:
Non-exhaust emissions from brake wear represent a major environmental and health concern, becoming tightly regulated under new Euro 7 standards. This PhD research aims to develop and validate an intelligent Electro-Mechanical Braking (EMB) control system to actively suppress brake particulate emissions.

- Develop control-oriented multi-physics models capturing brake dynamics, friction, thermal behaviour, and wear mechanisms.

- Formulate predictive/adaptive control strategies to modulate real-time clamp force, actively suppressing micro-slip and thermal hotspots.

This research delivers short-term academic and industrial impact through low-cost HIL validation frameworks and EuroBrake/UKACC conference presentation. In the long term, mitigating PM2.5/PM10 emissions accelerate commercial EMB deployment with partners, influencing future legislation and driving sustainable, net-zero mobility.

Vehicle emissions extend beyond the exhaust pipe; wear particles from friction braking contribute heavily to PM2.5 and PM10 air pollution. With Euro 7 enforcing strict non-exhaust limits, next-generation braking must evolve. Electro-Mechanical Braking (EMB), with evolution of Brake-by-Wire, offers precise, high-bandwidth actuation. Actively controlling transient micro-slip and thermal spikes provides an untapped opportunity to eliminate wear particles at the source without compromising stopping performance. Utilising our state-of-the-art Leeds Brake Dynamometer facility to evaluate control-driven emission reductions, this project pioneers actionable strategies for safe, net-zero mobility.

Computational: Multi-physics modelling of brake dynamics, friction, thermal behaviour, and wear mechanisms, paired with predictive/adaptive force control design.

Validation: Hardware-In-the-Loop (HIL) co-simulation using the scaled EMB bench to develop high-bandwidth control algorithms. Control force profiles generated on the desktop platform will be replayed on the Leeds Brake Dynamometer to validate real-world force response, thermal performance, and particulate emission reductions (PM2.5/PM10).

listings.description:
Floating pennywort is one of the UK’s most damaging invasive species, rapidly forming dense mats that choke waterways, reduce biodiversity, and increase flood risk. This PhD tackles the problem head‑on by developing autonomous aquatic robots capable of detecting, collecting, and managing pennywort across the Calder catchment. Building on emerging environmental robotics research, the project combines computer vision, ecological insight, and real‑world field robotic trials to create a scalable, long‑term solution that suppresses regrowth after essential large‑scale manual removal. The robot will operate continuously, monitor regrowth in real time, and respond instantly, offering a transformative new approach to ecosystem invasion resilience.

The overarching aim is to develop a pervasive, long‑term deployable autonomous field robot capable of detecting and manipulating Floating Pennywort Hydrocotyle ranunculoides in real environments. The project will develop high‑confidence detection models using computer vision and leaf reflectance spectroscopy; design and manufacture a robust aquatic manipulator; integrate detection, collection, and autonomous decision‑making; and evaluate performance through lab testing and field trials.

This PhD will advance autonomous environmental robotics and deliver evidence‑based methods for controlling pennywort. It will generate publishable results in detection, manipulation, and long‑term deployment, and has strong potential to reshape invasive species management and inform future policy and funding.

Floating pennywort is a rapidly spreading invasive species that forms dense mats which block waterways, damage ecosystems, and increase flood risk. Invasive non native species collectively cost the UK economy around £4 billion per year, with floating pennywort alone responsible for over £25 million annually in economic and environmental losses across Great Britain and Europe. Manual removal is essential but short lived, as regrowth can occur within weeks at up to 20cm a day. This project addresses a critical national need by developing autonomous aquatic robots that provide continuous monitoring and targeted intervention, protecting biodiversity and safeguarding the long term effectiveness of large scale removal efforts.

listings.title: Characterisation and Prediction of CaCO3 Growth on Subsea Infrastructure via Experimental Methods
listings.summary: Investigation of the formation and growth of calcareous deposits on subsea infrastructure and the associated effects on the performance of cathodic protection systems. The project will work with an industrial sponsor to improve the understanding of how calcareous deposits affect the polarisation of off-shore…
listings.description:
Investigation of the formation and growth of calcareous deposits on subsea infrastructure and the associated effects on the performance of cathodic protection systems. The project will work with an industrial sponsor to improve the understanding of how calcareous deposits affect the polarisation of off-shore structures under various environmental conditions.

The primary aim of this project is to determine the rate at which calcareous deposits form on subsea infrastructure, such that their protective effect can be incorporated into the design of off-shore cathodic protection systems. Using a combination of laboratory techniques and industrial field data, the candidate will:

- Experimentally determine how these parameters govern film growth under various environmental conditions and polarisation states.

- Apply advanced experimental techniques to characterise film properties and explain the observed electrochemical behaviour.

- Derive rate equations correlating the local conditions to the formation rate of CaCO3 and the degree to which this protects the surface from corrosion.

Cathodic protection systems are installed on off-shore systems all over the world. A common technique to design these systems is the use of computational models to determine the current requirements. However, as it stands, such models are not able to accurately account for the polarisation stage of the process, which is primarily driven by the growth of calcareous deposits. By understanding the formation and growth of protective films, models can be generated with much greater accuracy. In doing so, cathodic protection systems can be designed that are much safer, more reliable and economically efficient.

A comprehensive literature review should be conducted, alongside a review of provided field data to determine a range of environmental conditions relevant to subsea infrastructure. Laboratory techniques should be used to polarise steel samples and to measure the growth of CaCO3 films under varying conditions. Calcareous deposits should then be characterised using ex-situ analysis techniques and then combined with analysis of collected data to derive rate equations to predict growth rate and protective properties. Numerical modelling may also be used to verify the predictive accuracy of the derived equations.

Everyday activities such as eating, drinking, grooming and using a phone can become demanding for people with advanced cancer when pain, fatigue and weakness affect arm movement. EASE-Arm will develop a compact, non-wearable upper-limb support that uses passive mechanisms to provide adjustable weight relief while allowing users to move their arm freely.

Aim: Develop and evaluate a sensor-informed passive upper-limb support that reduces perceived effort during meaningful everyday activities while preserving comfort and voluntary movement.

Objectives: Co-design requirements with patients, carers and professionals. Design and build a compact table-mounted prototype with adjustable support and easy disengagement. Integrate load and motion sensing with activity and symptom information to generate interpretable recommendations for personalised settings through accessible patient, carer and therapist interfaces. Compare unsupported, standard-support and personalised-support conditions in laboratory testing using measures of movement, muscle activity and perceived effort. Evaluate feasibility, comfort, task completion, assistance needs, acceptability and usability in palliative care. Explore a chair-mounted proof of concept and requirements for later bedside use.

Working across mechanical engineering and palliative care at the University of Leeds, the student will develop skills in co-design, prototyping, biomechanics, sensing and mixed-methods evaluation, and contribute evidence for future assistive technology in advanced illness.

People with advanced cancer may experience pain, fatigue and weakness that make everyday arm movements difficult, reducing independence and increasing reliance on carers. Activities such as eating, drinking, grooming and using a phone can become demanding, yet the level of support needed may vary with symptoms, activity and personal preference. EASE-Arm addresses this by exploring passive mechanical assistance that can be personalised while preserving comfort and freedom of movement. By combining engineering, palliative care and co-design, the project will develop evidence for a practical approach to supporting meaningful activity and informing future assistive technology for people with advanced illness.

listings.title: Multiscale Failure Analysis and AI-Assisted Prediction of High-Voltage Dynamic Subsea Cables for Floating Offshore Wind
listings.summary: This PhD offers the opportunity to investigate real failure mechanisms in high-voltage dynamic subsea cables used in floating offshore wind. Working with ORE Catapult and an international cable manufacturer, the student will access industrial cable samples, inspection evidence, operational data and full-scale testing.
listings.description:
This PhD offers the opportunity to investigate real failure mechanisms in high-voltage dynamic subsea cables used in floating offshore wind. Working with ORE Catapult and an international cable manufacturer, the student will access industrial cable samples, inspection evidence, operational data and full-scale testing.

The project will determine how cyclic bending, contact, fretting, abrasion and marine exposure interact across cable layers and length scales.

- Validate predictions against withheld industrial cases and translate the findings into design maps, test protocols and engineering guidance.

The project provides distinctive interdisciplinary training across materials science, offshore engineering, computational modelling and interpretable AI.

Floating offshore wind relies on dynamic subsea cables that must survive millions of loading cycles while operating in aggressive marine environments. Cable failures can lead to long outages, expensive offshore intervention and premature replacement. Predicting failure remains difficult because bending, contact, fretting, abrasion and environmental degradation interact across multiple cable layers and length scales. Field observations, laboratory tests and system-level models are often considered separately. This project will connect these evidence sources to identify the mechanisms and operating conditions that govern damage progression and to support more representative qualification and life-assessment methods.

Industrial inspection records, operating histories and damaged cable samples will be used to identify priority failure mechanisms. These will be reproduced using SEM/EDX, 3D surface metrology, nanoindentation, fretting and abrasion testing, simulated marine exposure and cyclic loading. Finite-element and reduced-order models will simulate bending, layer contact, slip and local stress, calibrated against laboratory and full-scale ORE Catapult data. Physics-based features and experimental variables will then inform interpretable machine-learning models with cross-validation and uncertainty quantification. Predictions will be tested on withheld industrial cases and manufacturer samples before translation into design maps and test guidance.

listings.description:
Nuclear Decommissioning is a National Priority for the UK. Pursuing a PhD in Nuclear Decommissioning offers prospective researchers the opportunity to work on one of the country's most significant engineering, environmental, and societal challenges. The UK's future energy strategy includes both renewable energy and new nuclear power. With strong industry partnerships, excellent career prospects, and opportunities to address globally significant challenges, a PhD in Nuclear Decommissioning offers the opportunity to make a lasting impact while developing world-class research and technical expertise.

Autonomous wireless sensing, as a key technology in the era of industrial digitalisation, provides a paradigm shift in the efficient monitoring of nuclear decommissioning sites, enabling real-time data collection with minimal human interventions. A key challenge is the need for frequent battery replacement due to lack of access to the main power supply. This project aims to develop a novel solution for condition monitoring of air ducts in nuclear decommissioning sites, by designing, optimising, and testing an autonomous wireless multi-parameter sensing node.

The successful applicant will work at the intersection of science, sustainability, and innovation. Key skills are related to integrating airflow energy harvesting, multiparameter sensing and wireless communication. The airflow energy harvester-sensor will autonomously power the sensor node (including corrosion, temperature sensors and wireless communication modules). The proposed solution is an innovative way to monitor the condition of air ducts in nuclear decommissioning environment, which will create significant impact on the use of digital technologies in nuclear decommissioning.

listings.summary: Alkali metals are a vital component in many enabling technologies, such as battery and supercapacitor technologies. listings.description:
Alkali metals are a vital component in many enabling technologies, such as battery and supercapacitor technologies. While lithium currently dominates these technologies it is unsustainable due to its rarity; potassium/sodium batteries represent a sustainable alternative and have recently gained increasing attention.1 Given these batteries are in their relative infancy, there is significant scope for development of new cathode materials.

This self-funded project will use the power of advanced X-ray spectroscopic techniques to understand how the abundant alkali elements can be used to make effective energy storage materials. Utilising these techniques will enable us to directly monitor the charge carriers local structure during function. With this understanding, we will design catalysts that fully harness the potential alkali species to make a real contribution to creating a more sustainable world.

As part of our team, with expert supervisors in catalyst design (Dr Simon Kondrat at Loughborough University) and X-ray absorption spectroscopy at Diamond Light Source you will make, test, and characterise alkali battery/ supercapacitors. Specially, you will explore Prussian Blue, layered alpha nickel hydroxide and activated carbon materials. During the project you will design manufacture and commissioning bespoke X-ray spectroscopy reactor cell, which will be used to characterise alkali under reaction conditions. You will have the opportunity to building skills in inorganic and physical chemistry, applied and sustainable energy storage and advanced X-ray characterisation techniques.

We are a community based on mutual support and collaboration. Through our Doctoral College there are continual opportunities for building important research skills and networking among your peers and research academics.

listings.description:
Electric motors and the systems they drive consume half of global electricity. These systems are typically very inefficient and contribute to a significant amount of energy wasted. By physically integrating power electronic converters and electrical machines we can use common structures and systems to greatly reduce, material usage and energy consumption.

Through a multidisciplinary research approach the aim is to establish fully integrated motor drives as a key enabling technology for sustainable electricity generation, high-efficiency industrial systems, lightweight transport applications, and significant reductions in manufacturing-related CO₂ emissions. The ambition is to develop innovative technological solutions that reduce energy losses and minimise environmental impact throughout the product life cycle by:

Structural and functional integration requires the development of novel joining technologies, motor winding arrangements, and 3D-printed structures capable of mounting semiconductor devices within the motor architecture.

The harsh thermal environment within integrated motor drives demands innovative design and manufacturing solutions. Advanced additive manufacturing techniques will be explored to improve thermal management across the entire system.

The use of wide-bandgap semiconductor devices can significantly reduce the size of passive components within power electronic converters. However, their high switching speeds can introduce challenges related to electromagnetic interference (EMI) and motor winding degradation. Novel converter topologies, EMI mitigation strategies, and advanced winding technologies will therefore be investigated.

Multi-modular distributed motor-drive architectures and ultra-fast semiconductor devices present significant control challenges. Research may involve FPGA-based control platforms, advanced microcontrollers, distributed control algorithms, and artificial intelligence techniques, including neural networks and evolutionary optimisation methods, to enable the efficient operation of integrated converter-motor systems.

Applications are invited to join the Power Electronics, Machines and Control (PEMC) Research Group at the University of Nottingham. Based within a recently established £18 million research facility on Jubilee Campus, PEMC is internationally recognised as a leading centre for research in power electronics, electrical machines, and control engineering.

listings.title: Space Satellite Structures Manufacturing Using 3D Printing of Advanced Polymers and Composites
listings.summary: The rapid growth of the global space sector is creating increasing demand for lightweight, high-performance, and cost-effective satellite structures. Small satellites, particularly CubeSats, have transformed access to space by providing affordable platforms for Earth observation, communications, navigation, climate…
listings.description:
The rapid growth of the global space sector is creating increasing demand for lightweight, high-performance, and cost-effective satellite structures. Small satellites, particularly CubeSats, have transformed access to space by providing affordable platforms for Earth observation, communications, navigation, climate monitoring, scientific research, and defence applications. However, CubeSat structural frames are still predominantly manufactured from aluminium alloys, which add mass, impose design constraints, and contribute significantly to manufacturing and launch costs.

This PhD project aims to develop next-generation CubeSat structural systems using advanced polymers, polymer composites, and additive manufacturing technologies.

Building on recent advances in high-performance engineering polymers and fibre-reinforced composites, the research will investigate how 3D printing can be used to replace conventional metallic satellite structures while maintaining the strength, stiffness, durability, and dimensional stability required for space applications.

One of the most important challenges in satellite engineering is reducing overall system mass. Every kilogram launched into orbit carries a significant financial penalty.

Lightweight CubeSat structures can reduce launch costs while enabling larger payloads such as sensors, communication systems, scientific instruments, batteries, and propulsion units. Weight savings achieved through advanced polymer composite structures can therefore improve mission capability without increasing launch costs.

Additive manufacturing offers unique opportunities for the aerospace sector by enabling highly optimised geometries, lattice structures, topology-optimised designs, and reduced material waste. Unlike conventional machining and fabrication methods, 3D printing enables rapid development cycles, lower tooling costs, greater design freedom, and more sustainable manufacturing approaches. Advanced polymer composites also offer excellent strength-to-weight ratios, corrosion resistance, vibration damping characteristics, and the potential for significant structural mass reduction.

The PhD will focus on the design, optimisation, manufacture, and testing of lightweight CubeSat frames using advanced polymers and composite materials. The successful candidate will investigate material selection, structural performance, manufacturing feasibility, thermal and environmental durability, and the impact of structural mass reduction o

listings.title: Electrifying chemical reactors for Net Zero: flow, heat and particle dynamics in next-generation reactors
listings.summary: Can renewable electricity replace fossil-fuel heating in some of industry’s most energy-intensive processes? This PhD will uncover how flow, particle motion, electrical currents and heat interact inside electrified reactors, developing the fundamental understanding needed to design efficient, flexible technologies for…
listings.description:
Can renewable electricity replace fossil-fuel heating in some of industry’s most energy-intensive processes? This PhD will uncover how flow, particle motion, electrical currents and heat interact inside electrified reactors, developing the fundamental understanding needed to design efficient, flexible technologies for low-carbon fuels, hydrogen production and a Net Zero future economy.

Many industrial processes require very high temperatures and currently rely on fossil-fuel combustion. Replacing this heat with renewable electricity could significantly reduce industrial carbon emissions, but new reactor concepts are needed to use electrical energy efficiently, safely and reliably.

This PhD will investigate the fundamental behaviour of directly electrified particle and fluidised-bed reactors. In these systems, electrically conductive particles can generate heat through Joule heating while being continuously moved and mixed by a flowing gas. This creates a challenging and largely unresolved scientific problem: particle motion changes the contact network through which electricity flows, while the resulting heat generation can in turn alter the flow, particle dynamics and, ultimately, chemical reaction.

The project will develop new understanding of these coupled interactions between fluid flow, particle motion, electrical conduction and heat transfer. Advanced computational modelling, theoretical analysis and relevant experimental data will be used to determine how particle-scale behaviour controls reactor-scale temperature distributions, electrical pathways, hot spots and overall energy efficiency.

The intended outcome is a predictive framework that identifies the physical mechanisms governing electrified reactors and provides new design principles for their efficient operation and scale-up. The research will have relevance to emerging Net Zero technologies including hydrogen production, methane pyrolysis, ammonia conversion, low-carbon fuels and other high-temperature industrial processes.

The project offers interdisciplinary training spanning fluid mechanics, multiphase flows, heat transfer, computational modelling and sustainable energy technologies, providing an excellent foundation for careers in both advanced engineering research and the rapidly growing industrial decarbonisation sector.

The development of more sustainable methods for production of chemicals is one of the most important challenges in the move towards a low carbon economy. The aim of this project is to develop emulsion-based flow systems for the production of high value compounds from biomass waste from the fruit industry.

As new enzymatic or microbial routes are being proposed to replace non-renewable feedstocks and catalysts, so there is a need for the development of novel reactor technology to enable their implementation. Exciting opportunities are emerging in reactor design for biomanufacturing of fine chemicals such as pharmaceuticals, food additives and fragrances.

Here we focus on development of methods for the transformation of batch-based processes into continuous flow processing with immobilised enzyme catalysts. We will use microreactor technology with in-situ spectroscopic monitoring to enable optimisation of promising routes to valuable intermediates.

The research will also provide opportunities for feedback-based manipulation of chemical processes on the microscale using python-based programming.

The project will provide ample opportunity for student-led initiative and innovation in this exciting multidisciplinary field.

listings.description:
There is increasing concern over the widespread accumulation of Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), such as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), in our rivers and ecosystems. The aim of this project is to develop cell-like compartments for the removal of POPs that can’t be achieved by conventional methods.

Artificial cells are micro-sized structures with features allowing them to mimic some of the functions of biological cells. They provide new opportunities for chemical processing with natural catalysts and can be tuned to maximise reactivity under non-natural conditions. Exciting progress has been made in the development of artificial cells, but challenges remain in their implementation in real-world applications.

In this project you will combine experiments with computational models of artificial cells for their eventual implementation in water-treatment. The research will involve design and development of bioreactors with artificial cells. Many technologies for removal of POPs are energy intensive, expensive or inefficient.

This work will provide valuable new insights into the coupling between catalytic reaction and mass transport for efficient removal of persistent pollutants from the environment.

listings.summary: Background: The transition towards electrified automotive and aerospace transport demands electric motors with increasing power density, efficiency and operating voltage without compromising reliability. These trends, together with wide-bandgap converters and fast-switching voltage waveforms, impose increasingly…
listings.description:
Background: The transition towards electrified automotive and aerospace transport demands electric motors with increasing power density, efficiency and operating voltage without compromising reliability. These trends, together with wide-bandgap converters and fast-switching voltage waveforms, impose increasingly severe electrical stresses on winding insulation. The challenge is particularly critical in aerospace applications, where reduced air pressure can significantly increase the risk of partial discharge (PD) and accelerate insulation degradation. This PhD studentship will investigate and enhance the reliability of next-generation winding insulation systems, including emerging hairpin and Litz-wire technologies, under representative electrical, thermal, pressure and mechanical stresses. The successful candidate will combine extensive experimental testing with insulation lifetime modelling to study PD inception, degradation and endurance, and to develop approaches for predicting insulation lifetime under realistic operating conditions. The research will support improved insulation design and qualification for reliable next-generation electric motors, contributing to safer, higher-performance automotive and aerospace electrification.

Applications for this PhD position are invited at the Power Electronics and Machines Centre, University of Nottingham. Based in a recently built £18M facility at Jubilee Campus, the Power Electronics, Machines and Control (PEMC) Research Group is globally renowned and one of the leading in its field.

A master’s degree (e.g. MSc, MEng, MPhys, MRes or equivalent) in a relevant engineering or physical sciences discipline, such as electrical/electronic engineering, general engineering, mechatronics, physics, materials science/engineering, mechanical/aerospace engineering, or a closely related subject, is essential.

A strong background or relevant experience in high-voltage engineering, electrical machines, power electronics, dielectric/insulation materials, or related areas would be advantageous.

listings.title: Physics-based prediction of friction, thermal behaviour and scuffing in high-speed electric vehicle gears
listings.summary: How can electric vehicle gears run faster and more efficiently without damaging their surfaces?This project aims to develop physics-based models connecting lubricant films, surface roughness and frictional heating to predict efficiency and scuffing. Combining computational modelling with tribological experiments, it…
listings.description:
How can electric vehicle gears run faster and more efficiently without damaging their surfaces?This project aims to develop physics-based models connecting lubricant films, surface roughness and frictional heating to predict efficiency and scuffing. Combining computational modelling with tribological experiments, it will help establish the scientific foundations for efficient, durable electrified vehicle transmissions.

High-speed electric vehicle transmissions must deliver high efficiency while resisting surface damage. Lower-viscosity lubricants can reduce power losses but may compromise surface separation. Scuffing, a severe form of adhesive surface damage, can occur when lubrication and surface protection become inadequate. Predicting this failure requires understanding how lubricant film formation, asperity contact and frictional heating interact throughout gear engagement.

This project will develop a deterministic thermal mixed-lubrication framework to predict friction, temperature and scuffing risk in high-speed gears. The model will couple elastohydrodynamic lubrication (EHL), measured surface topography, asperity contact mechanics and heat transfer. It will resolve changing loads, entrainment velocities and sliding conditions along the tooth contact, accounting for lubricant rheology and temperature-dependent properties.

Controlled rolling–sliding experiments will characterise lubricant friction under selected operating conditions and support model validation. The research will distinguish heat generated through lubricant shear from that arising at asperity contacts, and investigate how their interaction influences local temperatures and damage initiation. Scuffing criteria will be critically assessed against experimental evidence, with model assumptions and predictive uncertainty explicitly evaluated.

Expected outcomes include validated predictions of frictional power loss and thermal behaviour, together with a physically informed assessment of scuffing risk. These tools could support lubricant selection, surface-finishing strategies and transmission design.

The project builds on the supervisor’s academic tribology research and electric-drive transmission development experience. You'll develop expertise in computational tribology, numerical methods, experimental testing and surface characterisation, addressing a research challenge with direct industrial relevance.

listings.description:
Project Title: Turning the Malaria Parasite's Protein Degradation Machinery Against It -Professor Katerina Artavanis-Tsakonas, co-supervised with Laura Itzhaki (Department of Pharmacology)

Malaria remains a major global health challenge, with drug resistance threatening the effectiveness of existing treatments. This project will explore a fundamentally different way to kill malaria parasites: harnessing their own protein-degradation machinery to selectively destroy proteins they need to survive. Our lab studies how the ubiquitin system works in Plasmodium falciparum, revealing important differences between parasite and human cells that could be exploited therapeutically. This project will combine parasite genetics, biochemistry and chemical biology to develop new ways of manipulating protein stability. The aim is to create powerful tools for discovering new parasite biology while exploring novel strategies for antimalarial drug development.

listings.summary: Project title: Exploring functional effects of dysregulated microRNA-mediated cellular pathways in malignant germ cell tumours - Dr Matthew Murray.
listings.description:
Project title: Exploring functional effects of dysregulated microRNA-mediated cellular pathways in malignant germ cell tumours - Dr Matthew Murray.

Malignant germ cell tumours (GCTs) are characterised by microRNA (miRNA) dysregulation. Our studies to date have identified key tumour-suppressor and oncogenic candidate miRNAs warranting further study. We have already targeted/manipulated over-expressed miR-371~373 and miR-302/367 miRNAs and replenished downregulated miRNAs (let-7 and miR-100-5p/125b-5p) in malignant GCT cell lines with phenotypic and genotypic effects. This project will extend those observations in engineered inducible malignant GCT cell lines in vitro which can, e.g., express miR-100-5p/miR-125b-5p upon doxycycline treatment. Combination treatment using miRNA replenishment/targeting approaches with cisplatin will also be investigated, and novel agents targeting identified affected cellular pathways, prior to in vivo studies.

listings.summary: Why do some viruses cause severe disease after they cross into a new species, while others don't? This project will investigate how differences in pattern recognition receptor (PRR) signalling between host species influence virus infection, adaptation and zoonotic emergence. We will compare PRR pathways and downstream…
listings.description:
Why do some viruses cause severe disease after they cross into a new species, while others don't? This project will investigate how differences in pattern recognition receptor (PRR) signalling between host species influence virus infection, adaptation and zoonotic emergence. We will compare PRR pathways and downstream immune responses across different host species to determine how variation in pathogen sensing, signalling strength and immune regulation shapes the outcomes of virus/host interactions. Using molecular virology, immunology and comparative approaches, the research will identify conserved and species-specific mechanisms that determine the outcome of cross-species infection. Understanding how PRR signalling establishes or restricts host range could provide new insights into predicting and preventing the emergence of novel viral pathogens.

listings.description:
Many viruses establish long-term or life-long persistent infections. To be maintained within their hosts, these viruses must be able to spread to new uninfected cells in the face of an active immune response to them. How such viruses balance the need to spread within their host organism while evading detection and possible clearance is not well understood. This project seeks to understand the mechanisms by which members of two diverse types of viruses (herpesviruses and polyomaviruses) promote their efficient spread from one cell to the next. Such important steps in the viral life cycle could be good targets for intervention.

listings.description:
This PhD opportunity at Cranfield University explores energy flexibility, energy policy and social inequalities in the energy transition. Applicants are invited to develop their own research proposals, with possible directions including flexibility poverty, community energy and local energy sharing. Working with Dr Pegah Mirzania, applicants will refine their ideas and explore fully funded studentship opportunities through Cranfield’s research networks. These studentships cover tuition fees and a living-cost stipend, with funding subject to eligibility and a successful competitive application.

Energy flexibility - the ability to change when electricity is used, generated or stored is central to the UK’s net-zero transition. The 2025 Clean Flexibility Roadmap recognises that some households face barriers to participation. Understanding how financial resources, digital capabilities, technology ownership and everyday needs affect access to flexibility benefits is therefore important for a fair energy transition.

Applicants are invited to develop their own PhD proposals exploring how flexibility value is created, allocated and distributed within decentralised energy systems, and how access to benefits could reduce social inequalities. Proposals could draw on “flexibility poverty” to examine participation and exclusion, or explore whether community energy, local energy sharing and energy credit allocation can extend benefits beyond households that own energy assets. Research could compare cases in the UK and one or more EU countries. Applicants will shape their questions, case studies and methods according to their interests and data availability, potentially combining comparative policy analysis with modelling of household outcomes.

Cranfield’s involvement in European community energy research provides links with academic, industry and community partners. Applicants will work with Dr Pegah Mirzania to develop a proposal for the South and East Network for Social Sciences (SENSS) student-led competition, funded by the Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC). Successful studentships cover tuition fees and a tax-free living-cost stipend. Funding is subject to eligibility and a successful competitive application.

listings.summary: We are recruiting a PhD candidate to research the fundamental materials science principles underpinning a key industrial coating deposition process, electrodeposition of platinum. Sponsored by Siemens Energy, one of the world’s leading energy technology companies, and EPSRC through the IDLA programme, this scholarship…
listings.description:
We are recruiting a PhD candidate to research the fundamental materials science principles underpinning a key industrial coating deposition process, electrodeposition of platinum. Sponsored by Siemens Energy, one of the world’s leading energy technology companies, and EPSRC through the IDLA programme, this scholarship offers a £23,805 annual stipend (tax free), access to state-of-the-art equipment for coating production (both electroplating and chemical vapour deposition – CVD) and materials characterisation and performance testing, and a combined academic and industrial supervisory team. We are looking for a motivated student able to work independently in an industry-relevant challenge using fundamentally experimental methods supported by key computational modelling.

Turbine blades survive extreme oxidative and corrosive environments thanks to protective coatings, which are manufactured following a complex series of materials deposition methods and heat treatments. Electroplating of platinum is one of those key steps, used to enhance component life and reduce diffusion of undesired elements. The electrochemistry involved is complex and sensitive to the variation of several process parameters, which can lead to inconsistent coating quality. Current industrial practices rely heavily on empirical knowledge, with limited integration of predictive modelling or systematic optimisation.

This project aims to address the current knowledge gap in platinum plating by providing a solid fundamental understanding of the electrochemical process. By integrating first-principles modelling, experimental validation via cutting-edge techniques for both coating production and characterisation, and robust design methodologies, the project seeks to enhance the platinum adhesion, reduce process variability, and improve long-term durability under extreme operating conditions.

Cranfield University is uniquely positioned to address this challenge in materials science. World-class facilities are available in our Centre for Materials to produce the full coating system and test it, together with decades of expertise of a specialised academic team with strong industrial connections. A key and active partner of this endeavour will be the industrial sponsor, Siemens Energy, one of the world’s leading energy technology companies. listings.title: Digital Biomarkers for Mobility Decline and Falls in Dementia
listings.summary: Falls and mobility problems are among the most disabling consequences of dementia, affecting independence, quality of life, and healthcare utilisation. Yet current clinical assessments often identify changes only after significant decline has occurred.
listings.description:
Falls and mobility problems are among the most disabling consequences of dementia, affecting independence, quality of life, and healthcare utilisation. Yet current clinical assessments often identify changes only after significant decline has occurred.

This PhD will investigate whether continuous real-world movement data captured using advanced wearable sensor technology can reveal subtle signs of mobility decline long before conventional assessments detect problems. By combining cutting-edge wearable devices, digital biomarker development, and artificial intelligence, the project aims to transform how mobility decline and fall risk are detected, monitored, and ultimately prevented in people living with dementia.

Working at the intersection of clinical neuroscience, biomedical engineering, and data science, you will analyse high-resolution movement data collected from people across the spectrum of cognitive ageing, including individuals at risk of dementia and those living with established disease. You will explore how patterns of gait, balance, activity, and everyday movement can be used to identify early changes, predict future decline, and improve personalised approaches to fall prevention.

The project offers a unique opportunity to work with state-of-the-art wearable technology, real-world movement datasets, and clinical cohorts. You will receive training in:

Your findings could contribute to the development of new digital tools that allow clinicians to identify mobility problems earlier, stratify fall risk more accurately, and support people with dementia to remain active and independent for longer.

We are seeking highly motivated candidates with backgrounds in Engineering, Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Mathematics, Neuroscience, Biomedical Science, Physics, or related disciplines. Applicants should have strong quantitative and analytical skills, an interest in interdisciplinary research, and enthusiasm for applying technology to address major healthcare challenges.

This studentship provides an excellent opportunity to develop expertise in one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare innovation: the use of wearable technologies and digital biomarkers to improve outcomes for people living with dementia and other age-related conditions.

listings.title: Usable security for crypto wallets
listings.summary: This project applies usable security to understand how users perceive and respond to crypto wallet threats, then design and evaluate security features, interfaces and decision-support tools that support safer behaviour and reduce human error.
listings.description:
This project applies usable security to understand how users perceive and respond to crypto wallet threats, then design and evaluate security features, interfaces and decision-support tools that support safer behaviour and reduce human error.

Crypto wallets are applications or devices that allow people to manage the cryptographic keys needed to access and use digital assets. However, users must navigate seed phrases, irreversible transactions, scams and difficult choices between convenience, privacy and security. Poorly understood security features can themselves lead to mistakes and financial loss.

This project will apply usable security, the study of how to design security mechanisms that people can understand and use effectively, to crypto wallets. You'll investigate how different users perceive, prioritise and respond to threats when choosing and using wallets. The aim is to understand the gap between the risks identified by technical security research and the risks that users recognise and act upon.

You'll develop a user-centred mental threat model capturing who users believe may harm them, which outcomes they fear and which protective actions they trust. The research will combine qualitative and quantitative methods, potentially including interviews, focus groups, co-design workshops, longitudinal studies and surveys. It may compare newcomers and experienced users, as well as users of custodial, self-custodial, mobile, hardware and multi-device wallets.

Building on these findings, you'll design and implement novel wallet security features, interface mechanisms or decision-support tools that help users make safer decisions and reduce opportunities for human error. Potential solutions may include improved risk communication, transaction warnings, recovery mechanisms or security-enhancing workflows.

The project will evaluate these interventions with end users and assess their effectiveness in improving security outcomes. The intended contributions are both a deeper understanding of user security behaviour and practical solutions for building safer crypto wallets.

listings.description:
Food processing currently relies heavily on the combustion of natural gas to provide process and space heating. Until recently, natural gas was considered the preferred fuel for heating due its lower unit cost and greenhouse gas emissions compared to alternative fossil fuels and electricity. Emissions from the combustion of natural gas, however, are fixed, and gas, unlike electricity cannot benefit from the use of renewable energy sources and nuclear power for decarbonisation.

To meet the net zero target by 2050 it is therefore imperative that the use of natural gas is phased out in the next 10-15 years. This places significant challenges on the food manufacturing industry which include changes to processing technologies to accommodate decarbonised energy vectors, the need to make informed decisions on the adoption of new technologies, and significant capital investment.

To address this challenge, we are seeking to recruit a highly motivated and enthusiastic doctoral researcher to undertake investigations on a range of emerging electrified technologies, energy recovery technologies and alternative gas burning fuels for the decarbonisation of industrial cooking.

The project will be based within the Centre for Sustainable Energy Use in Food Chains (CSEF) which has substantial expertise and experimental facilities to support the research.

Candidates are expected to hold, or about to obtain, at a minimum, one of the following: upper second-class Honours degree (or equivalent) in food science and technology, chemical or process engineering, mechanical engineering, or related discipline. Good team working, observational and communication skills are essential with the ability to work independently and as a member of a research team.

The pathway combines observational, descriptive, and trials-based methods with large population-scale datasets to provide evidence on societies most pressing health challenges. Research informs evidence-based policy making to support people to make healthy lifestyle choices and/or to live better with illness and disability. More specifically, it examines the built and social environment and the impact that these have on multiple health and/or social outcomes. For example, a project may characterise the housing or school travel environment, and investigate the impact on injuries, mental health and educational outcomes; or shifting ageing and family-size demographics in relation to the epidemiology of chronic health conditions to address the pressing issue of the ‘care -gap’. Projects may use a range of methodologies, from observational to computational and population-level modelling. Such projects and associated methods are made possible through the linkage of administrative and health data, increasing demand for suitably qualified doctoral researchers capable of applying a mix of methods to complex social science problems.

Media, Communications and Public Relations at Swansea has been consistently recognized for its excellence and is placed right at the top in UK league tables for various elements of its delivery. Priding itself on a strong sense of community, staff and students are involved at the cutting edge of the study of contemporary media and its impact. Our mix of esteemed practitioners and globally acknowledged scholars have expertise across a broad range of sub-themes within the Journalism, Democracy and Digital Media pathway.

For example, while we attend to the traditional aspects of print and broadcast journalism and the way that these cover key areas such as politics, conflict, financial affairs, the climate crisis and sport, our expertise extends into alternative digital news media, fact checking, disordered information, hate speech, racism and misogyny. Applications are invited for 4-year PhD studentship based in Cambridge Institute of Medical Research (CIMR), University of Cambridge and the new AstraZeneca Discovery Centre at Cambridge. The student will be working on a collaborative project jointly supervised by Dr Jennifer Dickens in CIMR and Dr James Garnett and Dr Catherine Overed-Sayer at AstraZeneca and will work have opportunity to work across the two sites.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive, fatal interstitial lung disease (ILD) in which alveolar type 2 (AT2) cell epithelial dysfunction plays a key initiating role. Epithelial senescence is increasingly recognised as playing a role in triggering and perpetuating disease. This project aims to develop a platform in which to assess and optimise the delivery of nanoparticle approaches to senomodulatory therapeutics in the lung.

Senescent-cell targeting nanoparticles will be engineered and loaded with exemplar senomodulatory drugs in collaboration with Prof. Ljiljana Fruk (Department of Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology) and delivered to AT2 cells, using human alveolar organoids as the primary in vitro model. Working with the AstraZeneca team, drug selection will be optimised and an automated screening platform developed to undertake proof-of-concept studies to assess the efficacy and functional effects of nanoparticle-mediated senolytic delivery to AT2 cells.

The studentship will be co-supervised by Dr Jon Roozenbeek (Department of Psychology), Dr Lee de Wit (Department of Psychology) and Moira Nicolson (UK Cabinet Office)

This studentship is part of the CAM-DTP's supervisor-led topics, and we note that the successful candidate for this position is not guaranteed to receive the studentship. Rather, it is part of a DTP-wide competition, with limited studentships being available.

Unethical decision-making is as a major societal problem. For instance, the Grenfell and Hillsborough disasters in the UK were preceded by a chain of decision failures. While there is some literature on how and why people make unethical decisions, why people tolerate or even reward those who do is understudied. This cross-cultural project will explore the psychology of unethical decision-making: what drives it, and how the public perceives it, and its connection to trust in public and private institutions.

These investments take broad form in terms of the construction of high voltage pylons to electric vehicle charging stations. Through the ripple effects in the economy, these investments may change economic growth across four nations of the UK.

According to the Office for National Statistics, disposable household income across the UK's 12 regions varies considerably, ranging from £20,562 in the North East to £36,487 in London.

This PhD examines whether low-carbon investment reduces regional gaps in employment, incomes and energy affordability. Applicants could focus on renewable energy, electricity networks or low-carbon heating. Depending on the research question and available data, methods could include spatial analysis, econometric policy evaluation or regional input-output modelling of employment and supply-chain effects. Findings would inform investment, skills and affordability policies for a just energy transition.

listings.title: Stochastic analysis and modelling of flow boiling
listings.summary: Flow boiling is one of the most efficient heat transfer mechanisms and plays a critical role in modern energy systems, including electronics cooling, renewable energy, and advanced thermal management technologies. However, its practical deployment is often limited by the lack of reliable predictive models, due to the…
listings.description:
Flow boiling is one of the most efficient heat transfer mechanisms and plays a critical role in modern energy systems, including electronics cooling, renewable energy, and advanced thermal management technologies. However, its practical deployment is often limited by the lack of reliable predictive models, due to the complex and inherently stochastic nature of multiphase flow phenomena.

This PhD project aims to develop next-generation, uncertainty-aware stochastic models for flow boiling, moving beyond traditional deterministic approaches. The research will combine advanced data-driven modelling with high-resolution experimental analysis. You will work with an established flow boiling facility equipped with state-of-the-art optical diagnostics to generate and analyse time-resolved experimental data, providing a unique opportunity to bridge fundamental science with real-world engineering applications.

The successful candidate will join a dynamic, industry-collaborative research team and will develop expertise at the interface of thermal sciences, data science, and machine learning.

Develop and implement automated image-processing algorithms to extract and quantify statistical characteristics of flow boiling processes

listings.title: Uncertainty-aware scheduling and analysis of AI-powered cyber-physical systems
listings.summary: AI and machine learning are increasingly used in cars, aircraft, robots, and other critical systems, but their performance, correctness, energy consumption, and safety are intertwined in ways that are hard to predict. We seek to untie this knot so we can build intelligent systems that are more trustworthy and…
listings.description:
AI and machine learning are increasingly used in cars, aircraft, robots, and other critical systems, but their performance, correctness, energy consumption, and safety are intertwined in ways that are hard to predict. We seek to untie this knot so we can build intelligent systems that are more trustworthy and resource-efficient.

In brief: How can modern cyber-physical systems (e.g., cars, aircraft, robots) make the right decision at the right time, without draining their batteries, while being safe to operate?

In addition, such systems increasingly rely on AI and machine learning, where computational performance, correctness, energy consumption, and safety are tightly connected. Consider the following simplified problem: A more accurate computation may require more time and energy, while a faster one may produce less reliable results. How to decide which one to use?

This challenge is already visible in space. For instance, NASA’s Perseverance rover adapts its onboard schedule to uncertain durations of science and engineering activities, which also make energy use difficult to predict. Such uncertainty can be particularly problematic if misjudged (a system can become inoperable, inefficient, unsafe, or even waste significant amount of taxpayer's money).

This project seeks to develop scheduling algorithms and analysis methods that explicitly account for uncertainty. Scheduling determines when computations run and how they share resources. Analysis assesses what these choices mean for performance, correctness, energy use, and safety. You will investigate how uncertainty in these quantities can be characterised, how their dependencies affect system behaviour, and how scheduling decisions can improve efficiency while respecting safety requirements.

The research will combine mathematical modelling, probability and statistics, algorithm design, and experimental evaluation. The aim is to provide both theoretical foundations and practical methods for intelligent systems that make better use of limited resources and offer clearer evidence of trustworthy behaviour.

If you feel you have gaps in some areas that might be required for the research, you will be able to attend any lectures across the wide range of courses offered within the School of Electronics and Computer Science to supplement your knowledge, for instance, AI, scheduling theory, computer science, embedded systems.

listings.summary: Create new computational methods for the prediction of materials structure to transform the development of medicines. listings.description:
Create new computational methods for the prediction of materials structure to transform the development of medicines. Pharmaceutical scientists routinely screen large numbers of potential crystal forms to improve drug performance, but experimental screening is time-consuming and resource intensive. This project will develop new computational methods to rapidly screen pharmaceutical materials.

Many active pharmaceutical ingredients can be co-crystallised with another small molecule (coformer) to produce materials with improved solubility, stability or manufacturability. However, identifying which coformer will produce suitable crystal forms remains a major challenge. Existing computational screening approaches provide useful guidance but often do not explicitly assess crystal packing and solid-state stability. Crystal structure prediction (CSP) can provide this information but is currently too computationally expensive for routine large-scale screening.

In this project, you will develop accelerated CSP workflows that retain predictive accuracy while dramatically reducing computational cost. Working with newly developed methods and machine-learned interatomic potentials, you will create tools capable of screening large libraries of coformers. You will investigate whether stable cocrystals or the propensity to form a cocrystal can be identified without performing a complete CSP study for every candidate system.

The research combines computational chemistry, machine learning, crystal engineering and scientific software development. You will work with the open-source mol-CSPy software package that we develop in our research group, and will collaborate closely with researchers at AstraZeneca, gaining exposure to industrial pharmaceutical development and real-world solid-form challenges. You will also have opportunities for visits or placement activities with AstraZeneca.

The outcomes of this project will include new computational methodologies for pharmaceutical crystal screening, published research papers, and software tools that support the development of future medicines.

The potential exploitation of deep-sea mineral resources is creating an urgent need for scientifically robust approaches to the conservation of planet’s most remote, remarkable ecosystems, including hydrothermal vents. Vents harbour highly distinct, endemic and vulnerable animal communities patchily distributed along ocean ridges with contrasting geological, physical and geochemical characteristics. Yet identifying representative networks of habitats for protection requires understanding how species and ecological functions change among habitats, and which habitats make unique contributions to biodiversity.

The contrasting environments of ocean ridges provide a powerful global system for investigating the poorly understood patterns and processes driving species and functional diversity change (β-diversity) among scattered habitats in the deep sea, allowing these key knowledge gaps to be addressed.

The central hypothesis of this project is that the distinct attributes of the world’s ocean ridges drive different patterns of species and functional β-diversity in hydrothermal vent ecosystems. Testing this hypothesis will reveal why vent communities become different across space and environmental gradients and provide the evidence to identify representative and complementary habitats for conservation.

You will analyse an unpublished global database of vent species and their traits compiled by the supervisory team. You will apply state-of-the-art statistical modelling, including distance-decay and joint species distribution models, to test whether geological, physical and geochemical differences among ocean ridges explain contrasting biodiversity patterns and evaluate the relative roles of dispersal limitation and ecological niche sorting. Finally, you will quantify the distinctiveness of vent habitats to identify habitats that contribute the most to species and functional diversity, providing evidence to spatial conservation priorities.

Climate warming is reshaping mountain landscapes [1,2]. Glacier retreat removes ice support, redistributes near-surface stress fields, and exposes slopes to changing hydrological and thermomechanical regimes, including permafrost thaw. These changes are increasing rockfall frequency and magnitude [3], creating escalating hazards for mountain communities, transport networks and visitors. Yet because rockfall is notoriously difficult to monitor, we lack detailed quantitative understanding of how rockfall dynamics are evolving concurrently with deglaciation. The Mont Blanc massif provides an exceptional natural laboratory, exemplifying processes driving change across deglaciating mountain regions worldwide. This project will provide evidence needed to understand how climate warming is reshaping rockfall dynamics and improve future hazard assessment for mountain communities.

You will combine field-based remote sensing and numerical modelling to quantify rockfall activity in accessible deglaciating catchments in the Mont Blanc massif. Objectives: (1) deploy long-range terrestrial laser scanning [2] and low-cost time-lapse cameras to acquire repeat high-resolution topography and imagery of glacier-adjacent rock walls; (2) undertake 3D change detection [e.g. 4] to detect and characterise new rockfalls, and 2D rockfall scar spectroscopy to identify and date abundant existing scars preserved across rock walls, creating a novel inventory spanning recent events to centuries-millennia; (3) interrogate this inventory to reveal patterns in rockfall location, geometry and timing, testing the generality of existing hypotheses (e.g. larger rockfalls occur from newly deglaciated slopes), and; (4) undertake rockfall-runout modelling [e.g. 5] to reconstruct rockfall trajectories and predict future runout pathways, informing regional hazard assessment.

listings.summary: To apply for the ARIES Doctoral Training Partnership studentship please simply select the ‘online application’ link below for

Shallow landslides (i.e., slope failures in surface material typically < 2 m thick) are a global hazard, posing significant risk to infrastructure and populations (1) especially in seismically active regions. However, it is still not possible effectively predict the location of future landslides (2, 3). A significant factor in the occurrence of shallow landslides is the amount of material available to fail; the mobile soil layer above solid bedrock called regolith. Regolith controls the size and distribution of shallow landslides across unstable landscapes. Yet, global knowledge of the thickness and physical properties of this horizon is extremely rare. Recent modelling (3) using a novel landscape evolution model component and a co-seismic landslide inventory suggests a different approach - that regional regolith thickness can instead be inferred from databases of landslide occurrences using inverse modelling.

To unlock the potential of this novel approach, this PhD will utilise the dynamic landscape of the central Italian Apennines, an accessible and data rich area prone to landslides and earthquakes (5), to test if the modelled regolith thicknesses correlate with field derived observations. This project addresses a fundamental knowledge gap, providing vital information to improve hazard modelling and mitigation strategies in vulnerable regions worldwide.

The researcher will: 1) undertake ensemble modelling of shallow landslides using the ShallowLandslider (3) Landlab component to generate and compare plausible subsurface regolith configurations; 2) assess spatial patterns of plausible landslides against a regional multi-temporal dataset to infer the best fit regolith characteristics; 3) undertake field data collection and follow-up laboratory analysis to constrain the regolith parameters and soil production rates across a number of key locations in the Central Apennines, and 4) test model outputs against field-constraints to improve landslide forecasting.

Fisheries and fish biodiversity depend on coastal nurseries which are heavily exposed to human activities. In particular, commercially important flatfish, such as turbot, sole and plaice, rely critically on knee- or waist-deep areas of sandy beaches in their first summer. Impacts of warming and human disturbance on these coastal nurseries are little studied, but likely include direct feeding interference and thermal stress as well as indirect effects through displacement to suboptimal habitats, ultimately impacting growth, survival and recruitment to the adult population.

This project aims to untangle the interactive effects of increased temperature and human disturbance on fish nurseries through applications of state-of-the-art tools, developed at Plymouth and Southampton, for measuring metabolism, growth and stress responses in situ.

Brixham Laboratory, the student will explore physiological responses of juvenile turbot to temperature increase under different feeding conditions. Turbot are commercially valuable, locally available, with well-developed husbandry practices; juveniles rely on the most-impacted, shallowest areas of beaches around Plymouth.

Physiological traits investigated will include metabolic rate, growth rate, protein synthesis, oxidative stress as well as field proxies for these processes (RNA-based indices, otolith carbon-isotope chemistry). Field investigations using the proxies will then examine influences of warming and human presence on distribution, feeding, growth energetics and stress in situ.

Bringing insights from these efforts to an existing long-term beach-sampling dataset, the student will identify drivers of nursery habitat quality and apply this to forecast changes under future scenarios.

This exciting, multidisciplinary PhD offers the opportunity to use cutting-edge ecotoxicology and molecular approaches to investigate how climate change and emerging pollutants interact to impact estuarine ecosystems.

Estuaries are among the most productive and valuable ecosystems on Earth, supporting biodiverse habitats, fisheries, and internationally significant bird populations. Within these transitional waters, invertebrates play critical ecological roles as biofilters, ecosystem engineers and prey for higher trophic levels. However, estuarine ecosystems face increasing pressures from climate change and pollution.

Estuaries receive contaminants from terrestrial, freshwater and marine sources, with many pollutants accumulating in sediments where they can persist and interact with biological communities. At the same time, estuaries are also being challenged by increased frequency, intensity and duration of heatwaves, driving increased organism stress and exacerbating the uptake and toxicity of pollutants. Despite growing concern, the combined effects of emerging contaminants and warming temperatures on estuarine ecosystems remain poorly understood.

This PhD will investigate how emerging pollutants affect ecologically important estuarine invertebrates under ambient and extreme temperatures. Working closely with the supervisory team, you will co-develop laboratory-based multi-stressor ecotoxicology experiments to assess pollutant responses of estuarine invertebrates exposed to emerging contaminants (e.g. tyre-wear particles, pharmaceuticals) and heatwaves. The project will combine controlled exposure studies with molecular and organism-level assessments to identify mechanisms of toxicity and ecological consequences. Research outputs will improve understanding of risks posed by pollutants to estuarine biodiversity and ecosystem functioning in a changing climate.

Coastal regions face the triple threat of emerging contaminants, heatwaves, and deoxygenation. Current chemical risk assessment substantially underestimates ecological risk because pollutants are evaluated in isolation and at the species-level only, overlooking synergistic stressor interactions and population-level variation in tolerance. Without accounting for these interacting pressures and natural population variability, risk assessments may fail to predict population declines, biodiversity loss, and ecosystem disruption.

This interdisciplinary project aims to develop a multi-level, risk assessment framework to evaluate vulnerability of marine invertebrate populations to emerging pollutants under climate change. By combining transcriptomics with computer vision, AI-powered physiological approaches, and linking responses to fitness outcomes, the project will identify mechanisms underpinning population resilience and sensitivity to multiple stressors. The recovery of nature is a pressing global issue. Nature recovery is difficult to predict, and different recovery strategies are implemented from tree planting to diverse forms of rewilding. Across Europe, humans transformed the vegetation of the continent through forest clearance for agriculture over millennia [1,2]. However, within that long-term transformation, multiple major population collapses occurred, in prehistory and the historic period. These collapses offer unparalleled opportunities as ‘long term’ experiments to understand natural nature recovery: reductions in population and land use pressure should result in ecological change [3]. This PhD project will develop detailed long-term data using palaeoecology and archaeology to assess past ecological recovery, using pandemics as disrupters to past human systems.

The project will focus on two time periods: the early Neolithic, and the medieval Black Death. The first has been characterised by “boom-and-bust” cycles of population growth and collapse [5], likely driven by plague [4]. The Black Death removed up to 50% of the population of Europe, with different impacts across the continent [3]. This project will therefore provide a critical assessment of how ecosystems adapted and responded to associated reductions in land-use pressure, focussing on recovery and resilience (do systems return to pre-existing conditions or states?), temporality (what sort of timescales do systems change or regenerate over) and stability (can, or do, systems reach equilibrium states?). The project will analyse the nature of pre-pandemic land use and economic/ecological systems, drawing on the archaeological/historical literature, to understand how landscape preconditioning influences recovery.

Coral reefs are under imminent threat from climate change, with 99% expected to be lost within 50 years, with profound consequences for ecosystem functioning and the services they provide. Soft coral-dominated reefs are increasingly common across the Indo-Pacific, representing the most widespread reef state after hard coral-dominated reefs. Many soft coral species can outcompete hard corals, likely due to their greater resilience to increasing temperatures, as well as the production of bioactive metabolites that are thought to promote hard coral tissue damage and inhibit their recovery. Despite their importance, there is little understanding of either mechanism, and their combined influence on soft coral competitive success remains unexplored. This timely project aims to investigate how thermal tolerance and secondary metabolite dynamics jointly contribute to the increasing ecological dominance of Indo-Pacific soft corals under climate change, and associated deterioration of coral reefs.

You will conduct field-based controlled thermal experiments on dominant Indo-Pacific soft coral species at Coral Eye, Bangka Island (North Sulawesi, Indonesia), and will quantify physiological performance and changes in metabolite production under acute and chronic heat stress. LC-MS/MS metabolomics will characterise changes in chemical defences, while bioactivity assays and experiments with hard coral adults/larvae, will evaluate the ecological functions of these chemical defences. This integrated approach will determine whether thermal stress enhances, reduces or alters the ecological function of soft coral chemical defences.

Microplastics are a widespread environmental contaminant readily ingested by marine invertebrates and negatively impacting feeding, growth, reproduction and survival. Alongside this backdrop of environmental pollution, marine invertebrates must also contend with the pressures of climate-induced ocean warming including marine heatwaves (MHWs). MHWs are periods of unusually high sea temperatures that persist for more than five days, and are increasing in frequency and severity. An organism’s capacity to recover from thermal stress will likely dictate its ability to cope with additional environmental pressures including microplastics. Equally, microplastic effects may be more severe in marine animals already dealing with the bioenergetic limitations associated with acute thermal stress. Despite this, the combined effects of these growing environmental pressures on marine invertebrates are not well understood. This project will investigate if and how microplastic exposure and MHWs interact to affect different marine invertebrates.

Using laboratory-based experimental studies, this research will focus on invertebrate feeding and digestive physiology, linking these to growth bioenergetics and performance. The student will expose two ecologically and commercially important invertebrate species: edible crabs (Cancer pagurus) and blue mussels (Mytilus edulis) to different microplastic polymers in conjunction with simulated MHWs representative of the intertidal zone. Cutting-edge experimental approaches already operated by members of the supervisory team will be used to measure e.g. gut pH regulation, digestive assimilation efficiency and oxygen consumption. This will enable an understanding of how these biologically contrasting invertebrate species will cope with predicted future temperature and plastic contamination scenarios, and the implications this may have for ecosystem health.

We know climate change threatens biodiversity, but many of the ways in which it affects individual species are shrouded in the complexity of the interactions between them(1).
