listings.title: Behavioural Sleep Dysfunction as a Mechanistic Driver of Long COVID Symptom Severity: An Integrative Psychophysiological Investigation
listings.summary: Sleep disturbances have emerged as one of the most persistent and debilitating symptoms reported by individuals with Long COVID. Prospective cohort work demonstrates that Long COVID is associated with shorter sleep duration, poorer sleep quality, and increased rates of moderate‑to‑severe sleep disturbance up to three…
listings.description:
Sleep disturbances have emerged as one of the most persistent and debilitating symptoms reported by individuals with Long COVID. Prospective cohort work demonstrates that Long COVID is associated with shorter sleep duration, poorer sleep quality, and increased rates of moderate‑to‑severe sleep disturbance up to three years post‑infection. Mechanistic reviews highlight several biological factors that may underpin these disturbances, including neuroinflammation, cytokine imbalance, autonomic nervous system dysfunction, circadian disruption, and mitochondrial impairment, all of which can alter sleep–wake regulation and contribute to insomnia‑like symptoms.

Pre‑infection sleep characteristics also appear relevant: longitudinal UK data show that poor sleep quality and greater variability in sleep efficiency are associated with an increased risk of developing Long COVID. These findings suggest that sleep may both predispose individuals to prolonged post‑viral symptoms and be adversely affected by the condition itself, underscoring a bidirectional relationship. Parallel evidence from behavioural sleep science, demonstrates that insomnia processes such as hyperarousal, irregular sleep schedules, and dysfunctional sleep behaviours negatively affect mood, psychomotor performance, daytime functioning, and overall wellbeing.

These behavioural mechanisms may amplify symptom severity in Long COVID, which is already characterised by fatigue, cognitive impairment, autonomic dysfunction, and impaired physiological recovery. Current literature indicates that sleep dysfunction in Long COVID is likely multifactorial, arising from biological, behavioural, and autonomic pathways and may play a key role in shaping daily functioning and long‑term recovery trajectories. This provides a strong rationale for examining insomnia‑related behavioural processes as potential mechanistic contributors to Long COVID symptom burden and as targets for intervention.

Long COVID (post‑COVID condition) is a chronic, multisystem disease state that persists for ≥3 months after SARS‑CoV‑2 infection and impairs daily functioning for many sufferers.

Women consistently show higher prevalence and activity limitation than men, yet the drivers, biological (immune, autonomic, endocrine), and social, are not resolved. Large, contemporary cohorts (e.g., NIH RECOVER) report a ~31% higher risk of Long COVID in females—with age, pregnancy, and menopausal status shaping risk— underscoring the need for mechanistic, sex‑aware research and clinical translation.

UK statistics similarly show higher self‑reported prevalence and greater activity limitation among women, highlighting societal and economic burdens. Mechanistically, converging evidence points to immune dysregulation (including altered monocyte/B‑cell states and low cortisol), autonomic dysfunction (e.g., orthostatic tachycardia/POTS), and endocrine perturbations, with plausible hormonal modulation of immune pathways.

Recent multi‑omic analyses suggest sex‑specific immune correlates and sustained inflammatory signalling in Long COVID, but integrated models linking symptoms to objective biomarkers across systems are rare. This project will execute a three‑part programme:

a lab‑based and ambulatory tracking study to profile immune, autonomic, and endocrine markers in a sex‑stratified cohort;

listings.title: Passive acoustic monitoring for characterisation of under-ice environments
listings.summary: The project will investigate passive acoustic monitoring in under-ice environments, combining acoustic propagation modelling with machine learning and data analytics to characterise environmental conditions, improve understanding of ice-generated acoustic processes and their influence on sonar performance, and exploit…
listings.description:
The project will investigate passive acoustic monitoring in under-ice environments, combining acoustic propagation modelling with machine learning and data analytics to characterise environmental conditions, improve understanding of ice-generated acoustic processes and their influence on sonar performance, and exploit this information to enhance under-ice situational awareness and maritime sensing capabilities.

The Arctic and High North are becoming increasingly important operating environments, however the under-ice acoustic environment is a highly dynamic and complex physical system which remains difficult to observe, predict and exploit, and for sonar systems to operate reliably. Sea ice processes such as fracturing, ridging, deformation and movement influence the generation, propagation and scattering of sound and, consequently, sonar performance. Improved understanding of these system interactions is critical for sensing and situational awareness in under-ice environments.

This project will investigate how passive acoustic monitoring can be used to characterise and understand the under-ice environment. Rather than relying solely on active sonar, the research will examine whether naturally occurring ice-generated sounds can provide exploitable information about environmental conditions. A particular focus will be placed on identifying, classifying and interpreting the acoustic signatures associated with physical ice processes and understanding their relationship to environment properties and acoustic behaviour.

The project will combine physics-based acoustic propagation modelling, signal processing, statistical analysis and machine learning to develop methods for extracting environmental information from passive acoustic observations. By integrating physics-based and data-driven approaches the research aims to identify links between observed acoustic characteristics and key environmental parameters, enabling improved environmental characterisation where direct measurements are challenging or unavailable.

The outcomes will improve understanding of under-ice acoustic environments and demonstrate how passive acoustic information can support environmental characterisation, sonar performance prediction and operational decision making. Potential applications include improved under-ice situational awareness and more effective use of maritime sensing systems in complex ice-covered regions.

listings.title: Metabolic health and fitness to serve: the impact of GLP-1 receptor agonists on pancreas–bone crosstalk
listings.summary: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs lower bone density and occasionally inflame the pancreas, but nobody knows whether the drug or the weight loss is responsible. Using micro-CT imaging of patient tissue alongside human stem-cell and organoid models, you will separate the two and uncover how the pancreas and skeleton communicate.
listings.description:
GLP-1 weight-loss drugs lower bone density and occasionally inflame the pancreas, but nobody knows whether the drug or the weight loss is responsible. Using micro-CT imaging of patient tissue alongside human stem-cell and organoid models, you will separate the two and uncover how the pancreas and skeleton communicate.

GLP-1 weight-loss drugs have changed medicine faster than almost any treatment in a generation. Millions of people are now taking them, including serving personnel in the UK Armed Forces. But two signals have appeared in the data, and nobody can yet explain either.

The first is bone. People on these drugs lose bone density, particularly at the hip and spine. Is that the drug itself, or simply the consequence of losing weight and putting less load through the skeleton? No study has been able to separate the two.

The second is the pancreas. These drugs act directly on the pancreas, and in rare cases cause inflammation. What sustained exposure does to pancreatic tissue over years, especially in people already carrying excess pancreatic fat, remains unclear.

These may turn out to be the same problem. There is growing evidence that the pancreas and bone communicate, and this project will test whether GLP-1 drugs disrupt this cross-talk.

You will work with micro-CT imaging of real patient pancreatic tissue, human stem-cell derived pancreatic models, and patient-derived organoids, then test whether signals released by drug-treated pancreatic tissue change how bone cells build and break down bone. The findings matter directly for Defence, where bone stress injury is a major cause of lost service days, and the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs are often those returning to heavy physical training.

listings.title: An AI-powered knowledge-graph approach for predicting biological threat responses
listings.summary: Interested in applying AI to solve real-world biological and security challenges? This project will bring together systems biology, machine learning and network science to build predictive models of host-pathogen interactions. You will develop cutting-edge AI approaches that could transform how we respond to novel…
listings.description:
Interested in applying AI to solve real-world biological and security challenges? This project will bring together systems biology, machine learning and network science to build predictive models of host-pathogen interactions. You will develop cutting-edge AI approaches that could transform how we respond to novel infectious and biological threats.

The human body is a complex adaptive and hierarchical system of nested biological networks. These networks continuously respond to a multitude of external and internal signals, ranging from pathogen (bacterial, viral) exposure and environmental stressors to therapeutic interventions.

The ability to predict how biological networks respond to external perturbations has important applications across healthcare, defence and biosecurity. Biological threats, whether naturally occurring, engineered, or previously unknown, represent a significant risk to military personnel, critical infrastructure, and civilian populations. Rapidly understanding how a novel biological agent interacts with the human host and how the host networks respond is therefore a major challenge.

This project focuses on developing tools for prediction of how these networks respond to biological threats such as bacterial and viral pathogens.

Knowledge graphs provide a powerful framework for integrating, representing and interrogating heterogeneous information. Biomedical knowledge graphs integrate diverse molecular and disease-related information and are comprised of 100s of thousands of entities and millions of relations between those entities.

The project will first construct an integrated multi-omics knowledge graph incorporating host-pathogen interactions, molecular pathways, diseases, phenotypes and therapeutic interventions.

We will then develop graph foundation models and explainable AI methods to quantify how biological threats perturb molecular networks, identify pathways associated with disease severity and resilience, and predict potential intervention targets.

These approaches will provide a mechanistic framework for modelling biological responses and supporting preparedness against emerging infectious and environmental threats.

listings.title: Automating synthesis in the defence industry
listings.summary: This project will develop an integrated, automated platform for rapid synthesis of isotope-labelled compounds for defence-relevant analytical and toxicological applications. Combining synthetic chemistry, automation, analytical measurement and digital optimisation, it will investigate closed-loop isotope labelling for…
listings.description:
This project will develop an integrated, automated platform for rapid synthesis of isotope-labelled compounds for defence-relevant analytical and toxicological applications. Combining synthetic chemistry, automation, analytical measurement and digital optimisation, it will investigate closed-loop isotope labelling for producing analytical reference standards and compounds supporting metabolism, toxicokinetic and chemical-threat studies.

Isotope-labelled compounds are essential tools for chemical analysis, enabling the accurate identification and quantification of chemicals and their transformation products. However, their synthesis can be time-consuming and often requires considerable manual optimisation. This project will address this challenge by developing an integrated, automated platform for the rapid synthesis of isotope-labelled compounds for defence-relevant analytical and toxicological applications.

The project will combine synthetic chemistry, laboratory automation, analytical measurement and digital optimisation to investigate closed-loop approaches to isotope labelling.

Automated experimentation will enable reaction conditions to be rapidly explored and optimised, while simultaneously generating large, structured datasets of isotope-labelling reactions. These data will be used to develop predictive approaches that relate reaction conditions and molecular structure to labelling outcomes, ultimately enabling the planning of synthetic pathways to isotope-labelled compounds. Target compounds will include analytical reference standards and molecules supporting studies of metabolism, toxicokinetics and chemical threats.

A distinctive feature of the project is its interdisciplinary nature. You will receive training spanning organic synthesis, isotope chemistry, automation, analytical chemistry, large-scale chemical datasets, predictive modelling and 3D printing, developing an unusually broad combination of practical laboratory and digital skills.

The datasets generated will also contribute to the EPSRC-funded Physical Sciences Data Infrastructure (PSDI) data collection, allowing high-quality experimental data to be reused and integrated into other researchers' workflows.

By connecting automated experimentation, predictive modelling and data sharing, the project aims to establish a more efficient and data-driven approach to designing and producing isotope-labelled molecules.

listings.title: Wide-area ocean environmental inference using networks of uncrewed maritime systems
listings.summary: Future marine operations will increasingly rely on distributed networks of autonomous platforms. This project will investigate how acoustic measurements exchanged between uncrewed vehicles and deployed sensors can be exploited to estimate ocean environmental conditions over wide areas, combining acoustic tomography,…
listings.description:
Future marine operations will increasingly rely on distributed networks of autonomous platforms. This project will investigate how acoustic measurements exchanged between uncrewed vehicles and deployed sensors can be exploited to estimate ocean environmental conditions over wide areas, combining acoustic tomography, signal processing, machine learning and environmental modelling.

Future marine operations are expected to employ large numbers of uncrewed underwater and surface vehicles operating alongside distributed environmental and acoustic sensing systems. The effectiveness of many maritime capabilities, including acoustic communications, navigation, surveillance and sonar systems, depends strongly on environmental conditions. Accurate knowledge of the ocean state is therefore critical for predicting system performance, reducing uncertainty and supporting operational decision-making. However, environmental observations are typically sparse and geographically limited, creating a need for techniques that can infer environmental conditions across much larger areas.

While conventional oceanographic sensors provide measurements at discrete locations, acoustic propagation is influenced by environmental parameters including temperature, salinity (leading to sound speed structure) and seabed properties. Acoustic signals transmitted and received across a distributed network therefore contain information about the intervening environment. Extracting and exploiting this information offers the potential to estimate environmental conditions over spatial scales far greater than can be achieved through direct sampling alone.

This project will investigate novel approaches for wide-area ocean environmental inference using observations collected by fleets of unmanned vehicles and distributed sensor networks. Drawing on concepts from underwater acoustic tomography, the research will focus primarily on signal processing, estimation and inverse methods, while also exploring the potential application of machine learning and data-driven approaches. Particular emphasis will be placed on developing techniques that are applicable to arbitrary fleets, meaning sensing networks with varying numbers of platforms, differing sensor capabilities, changing geometries and dynamic membership as assets enter, leave or manoeuvre within the network.

listings.summary: Using light to remotely control chiroptical properties represents an exciting new avenue to create advanced communication technologies. listings.description:
Using light to remotely control chiroptical properties represents an exciting new avenue to create advanced communication technologies. This project will develop fundamental new supramolecular photoswitching technologies based on mechanically interlocked molecules with a diverse application space, and will include training in organic synthesis, photophysical analysis and self-assembly.

Photoswitches are molecules which undergo reversible reactions in response to light, enabling the remote control of matter at the nanoscopic scale. Chiroptic outputs, namely circular dichroism and circularly polarised luminescence, can be modulated by appropriately functionalised photoswitches.

These are foundational to the development of variety of new technology areas, including optical computing, advanced sensing and communications.

This project will use mechanically interlocked molecules to deliver a fundamentally new class of chiroptic switch, building upon designs recently published by our group (for reference, Mechanically Interlocked Indigo Photoswitches and ‘Click’-able hemiindigo triazole photoswitches with switchable fluorescence).

You will synthesise a series of mechanically interlocked photoswitches, and will be measure their photophysical properties using a combination of spectroscopies. With successful design criteria in place, these will be adapted to use non-covalent interactions between the components of the mechanically interlocked molecules to drive chiral conformations and thus switchable chiroptic response.

listings.description:
How do maritime robots behave when operating close to one another in waves? In this project, you'll develop experimental methods to explore this question by combining simulation and experiments, with the aim of identifying opportunities to improve energy efficiency, performance and safe operating envelopes.

As the Navy and wider maritime sector move towards the use of autonomous surface vehicle operations, understanding the unsteady hydrodynamics of manoeuvres in waves, in close proximity will be needed to ensure safe and energy efficient operations. For example, in launch and recovery of autonomous systems in adverse weather, operations alongside such as re-fuelling/recharging, search and rescue and in restricted waters or ports with a variety of waterway users.

To address these complex system interactions, you'll develop and test novel Hardware in the loop (HIL) experimental methods to evaluate unsteady hydrodynamics of autonomous systems operating in close proximity in waves. The research will explore how hydrodynamic behaviours could be used to improve performance, including opportunities for energy, emissions and cost savings, as well as extending safe operating envelopes and endurance. This will be achieved by exploring and developing cyber-physical evaluation methods, coupling simulation and experimental measurements in real-time, with active control to explore complex hydrodynamic interactions.

The research ambition is to accelerate the development and ultimately design, strategies and safe deployment of maritime autonomous systems operating in close proximity. This approach, the methods and results are also expected to have significant interest and application across the wider maritime sector, e.g., for evaluating future SMART ports, energy saving technologies, and in support of the UK maritime decarbonisation goals.

You'll be based in the Maritime Engineering group and you'll have access to an array of hydrodynamics facilities including the 138x6x3.5m University of Southampton Boldrewood towing tank, the largest academic tank in the UK.

listings.title: Extension of Hall thruster spacecraft propulsion operational range through design and propellant optimisation
listings.summary: Hall thrusters efficiently propel many spacecraft but offer limited thrust flexibility. This project aims to extend their operational range, from higher thrust to high fuel efficiency. Using thruster databases, optimisation, simulations, and experimental validation, you'll investigate thruster geometries and…
listings.description:
Hall thrusters efficiently propel many spacecraft but offer limited thrust flexibility. This project aims to extend their operational range, from higher thrust to high fuel efficiency. Using thruster databases, optimisation, simulations, and experimental validation, you'll investigate thruster geometries and alternative propellants, including dynamic propellant switching, to improve mission adaptability.

Hall ion thrusters are the dominate type of propulsion used in space, used on the majority of spacecraft as their primary propulsion system. This includes many different spacecraft missions, from Earth observation constellations, geostationary satellites, to interplanetary missions. Thanks to their higher ion velocities, they are considerably more fuel efficient than chemical rockets, leading to more capable systems that can complete larger orbital changes than alternatives.

However, the operational range of Hall thrusters is relatively small, limited to lower thrusts than chemical propulsion systems, which is limiting the spacecraft’s ability to dynamically respond to mission changes, i.e. move quickly in response to mission changes. In this project you'll investigate extending the operational range of Hall ion thrusters, in terms of extending a given Hall thruster to operate towards a higher thrust operation, whilst still having the capability for fuel-efficient high ion velocity operation as well.

This will be completed using our database of existing Hall thrusters, investigating their operational range and capabilities, identifying particular thruster geometries (channel diameter, width, etc.), that can lead to potentially lead to greater operational range. You'll also investigate the potential of using different gaseous propellants, including the ability to switch dynamically the propellants to further extend the range as the mission scenarios requires. Work will be based on a data optimisation investigation, followed by Hall thruster simulation, and experimental testing and validation of the thruster.

You must have at least a UK 2:1 honours degree, or its international equivalent, in aerospace engineering and related disciplines.

This project will develop physics-informed digital twins that augment vibration qualification testing of defence systems. By combining models and measurements, the project will predict unmeasured responses, extend test evidence to new conditions, account for ageing and uncertainty, and reduce physical testing while maintaining confidence in certification, qualification and reliability assessments.

This project will develop physics-informed digital twins that work alongside physical vibration tests, enabling defence systems to be certified and qualified with fewer tests and with evidence whose reliability is understood.

Before a mechanical system enters military service, evidence must show that it will perform safely and reliably throughout its life. For dynamic loads, this comes from qualification testing against vibration and shock profiles representing expected environments. Physical testing cannot cover every environment, configuration and ageing state an asset will meet. Laboratory tests also differ from service conditions. Many critical parts sit inside sealed assemblies where sensors cannot be fitted, so their response is never measured directly.

In this project you'll build digital twins of a test article and its test setup, combining finite element and reduced-order models with measured data. You'll:

model the coupled shaker, fixture, controller and test article to plan multi-axis tests and predict where they depart from service conditions

quantify uncertainty in each prediction and develop criteria to compare the trustworthiness of twin-based evidence with traditional qualification approaches

You'll gain skills in structural dynamics and uncertainty quantification that are in demand across the defence, aerospace and nuclear sectors. You'll also benefit from inclusion in the 'Ministry of Defence and Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Centre for Doctoral Training in Complex Integrated Systems for Defence and Security' (MOD/EPSRC CISDnS CDT), which offers opportunities for interdisciplinary working, collaboration and networking with defence partners.

listings.title: Efficient optimization algorithms for large scale interdiction problems on networks
listings.summary: How can we protect vital networks against disruption? This PhD develops faster matheamtically sound optimization algorithms to reveal critical weaknesses in transport, logistics and communication networks. Combining mathematical theory with computational experiments, you will investigate how networks respond to…
listings.description:
How can we protect vital networks against disruption? This PhD develops faster matheamtically sound optimization algorithms to reveal critical weaknesses in transport, logistics and communication networks. Combining mathematical theory with computational experiments, you will investigate how networks respond to disruption and build tools that help decision makers assess vulnerabilities and improve resilience.

Networks underpin the movement of people, resources and information. When a link is disrupted, operators can reroute traffic, so the importance of a component depends on the response of the whole network. Identifying the most damaging disruptions within a limited budget is known as network interdiction. Its combination of discrete decisions and an optimising network response creates challenging bilevel/min-max problems.

Working with Dr Stefano Cipolla and Prof Alain B. Zemkoho at the University of Southampton, you will develop efficient algorithms for large networks. The project will initially study shortest-path interdiction, modelling disruption through finite increases in link costs.

You will investigate how network structure can strengthen mathematical formulations and how adaptive decomposition and sparse numerical methods can accelerate solution.

You will combine theoretical analysis with implementation and reproducible computational experiments. Algorithms will be tested on synthetic and public networks against established optimisation methods, comparing runtime, memory and solution quality. Suitable continuous relaxations will provide opportunities to explore value-function and semismooth approaches.

The intended outcomes are new algorithmic insights, documented research software and a prototype for network vulnerability assessment. The project supports defence and security resilience planning while offering potential applications in logistics and infrastructure. You will develop expertise in operational research, optimization, graph algorithms and numerical linear algebra through research and CDT training.

You should have a foundation in linear algebra and calculus and an interest in mathematical reasoning and analytical problem-solving.

Familiarity with, or experience in, any combination of numerical programming, for example using Python, MATLAB or Julia, optimisation, or graph algorithms would be useful.

You are not expected to have experience in all of these areas, and relevant specialist skills can be developed during the PhD.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) further complicates treatment, creating a critical need for antibiotic-independent approaches that can control infection while supporting tissue repair.

This PhD will investigate sex-specific phage therapies for conflict wound healing, developing engineered bacteriophages designed to reduce bacterial burden while promoting vascularised MSK tissue regeneration. The research will address whether antimicrobial treatment and tissue repair can be targeted simultaneously on the battlefield, and whether responses vary according to biological sex.

In this PhD, you will design, optimise and experimentally test novel lightweight metamaterial architectures, combining computational modelling and advanced manufacturing to enable the next generation of safer, quieter aircraft.

Smart multifunctional metamaterials offer new opportunities to enhance the performance of lightweight aerospace structures through innovative material design and tailored architectures. Their integration into aircraft composite structures could enable improved impact protection, acoustic performance and advanced sensing and non-destructive testing, combining multiple functions without unnecessary increases in weight or complexity.

This PhD will investigate how metamaterial architectures can be designed and optimised to integrate these functions into lightweight aerospace structures.

multifunctional structural metamaterials: developing resonant structures and architected lattices potentially incorporating advanced materials, including graphene-based materials and lightweight aerogels, to control energy transfer, improve impact resistance, enhance sound absorption and reduce noise transmission

advanced sensing and non-destructive testing: exploring acoustic and thermal metamaterials to manipulate and focus ultrasonic and thermal waves for structural sensing, ultrasonic inspection and thermal-wave imaging, enhancing the detection and characterisation of defects such as delaminations and barely visible impact damage.

A central challenge will be the AI-driven inverse design and performance optimisation of these architectures, balancing mechanical and acoustic performance, sensing and inspection sensitivity, weight and manufacturability.

You will use finite element modelling, parametric optimisation and machine learning to develop innovative configurations. Selected designs will be manufactured and experimentally evaluated at the University of Southampton using advanced facilities and techniques, including laser vibrometry, ultrasonic scanning, infrared thermography and dynamic impact testing.

The project offers opportunities to develop expertise in AI and machine learning, metamaterial design and optimisation, acoustics, advanced materials, structural sensing, ultrasonic and thermographic NDT, and experimental validation.

listings.summary: The Surrey Morphology Group at the University of Surrey is inviting applications for a PhD studentship that offers 3.5 years (42 months) of funding and extensive associated resources. The topic is the comparative predictability of Romance verbal inflection, and forms part of the UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship project…
listings.description:
The Surrey Morphology Group at the University of Surrey is inviting applications for a PhD studentship that offers 3.5 years (42 months) of funding and extensive associated resources. The topic is the comparative predictability of Romance verbal inflection, and forms part of the UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship project 'Scaling predictability in Morphological paradigms'.

UK or international fees covered, plus UKRI standard stipend (£21,805 for 2026-27 academic year) and support for conference travel.

The project seeks to measure the amount of information available to speakers when they make inferences about the shape of inflected words. For example, English speakers can guess that the past tense of a new verb like "glorp" might be "glorped", following the same pattern as "jump" / "jumped". This raises fundamental questions about how languages work: how hard it is to make these predictions across languages? What language structures help, and how do they vary? Do languages become more predictable over time? To answer these questions, the project will innovate new computational tools able to measure the information available to speakers when they predict forms and apply them to comparable datasets.

The PhD position is focused on Romance languages, for which ample data already exists, and the diachrony of which is well known. This will allow for a deep dive into the synchronic and diachronic properties of predictability. The PhD candidate will have the opportunity to collaborate with members of the project involved in developing the methodology and data and answering the questions in other families.

The position is based at the University of Surrey, within the Surrey Morphology Group (SMG). In addition to the collaborative activities within the project, the successful candidate will benefit from the research environment of the SMG, a world-leading centre for research on morphological theory, typology and description.

Applications should be submitted via the Linguistics PhD programme page. In addition, please send a CV along with a one-page statement of interest to Alison Stubley, specifying the title of the project and name of the supervisors.

listings.summary: We are seeking to recruit a highly motivated and enthusiastic PhD student to join our battery research team within the Nottingham Applied Materials and Interfaces Group (NAMI, https://www.thenamilab.com/) at the University of Nottingham. Our research focuses on understanding the fundamental chemistry that controls the…
listings.description:
We are seeking to recruit a highly motivated and enthusiastic PhD student to join our battery research team within the Nottingham Applied Materials and Interfaces Group (NAMI, https://www.thenamilab.com/) at the University of Nottingham. Our research focuses on understanding the fundamental chemistry that controls the performance and lifetime of advanced energy-storage technologies, and using this understanding to develop the next generation of high-energy batteries.

Lithium-ion batteries with nickel-rich positive electrodes offer some of the highest energy densities available from commercial battery technologies and are increasingly important for electric vehicles and other demanding applications. However, increasing the energy stored within these materials also introduces new challenges associated with their stability, particularly at high states of charge. Understanding and controlling the chemical reactions occurring between battery materials and electrolytes is therefore critical to developing batteries that combine high energy density with long lifetime.

This PhD project will investigate the fundamental chemistry occurring at the interfaces between high-energy positive electrode materials and battery electrolytes. The student will explore how electrode composition, state of charge, electrolyte chemistry and operating conditions influence interfacial reactions and long-term battery performance. The project will combine electrochemistry, physical-organic and battery testing with advanced chemical and spectroscopic characterisation to identify the processes controlling degradation and develop strategies to suppress them.

The successful candidate will gain broad expertise in electrochemistry, lithium-ion battery development, electrolyte chemistry and advanced materials characterisation. The project will be undertaken within a highly collaborative research environment with access to state-of-the-art battery and analytical facilities and interactions with academic and industrial researchers working across energy-storage science.

The award covers Home fees and provides an annual stipend (£21,805 for 26/27). International candidates may apply and, if successful, would receive a University of Nottingham Fee Difference scholarship to cover the difference between Home and International fee rates.

listings.title: PhD project: Microgrid Resilience
listings.summary: The deployment of renewable energy resources is a viable option to mitigate the emissions of greenhouse gases which have become one of the major concerns on a global scale, and the UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050. To ensure a reliable electricity supply using renewables, deployment of distributed energy…
listings.description:
The deployment of renewable energy resources is a viable option to mitigate the emissions of greenhouse gases which have become one of the major concerns on a global scale, and the UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050. To ensure a reliable electricity supply using renewables, deployment of distributed energy resources and their efficient operation require an interconnected energy system, known as a microgrid, which can operate autonomously when the upstream grid fails. In this way, microgrids can improve the resilience of the electricity system by reducing the amount of energy not supplied, and excess microgrid generation can be sold to the main grid to provide customers with financial benefits, such as reductions in electricity bills.

This exciting project will focus on modelling a small-scale converter-dominated microgrid, integrating renewable generation, hybrid electrical storage and hydrogen technologies. On the energy generation side, photovoltaic generation, batteries and supercapacitors will be used, and on the conversion and utilisation side, a hydrogen electrolyser and a fuel cell will allow hydrogen production, storage and reconversion to be actively controlled as part of the microgrid operation. Microgrid resilience metrics and their modelling and analysis approach will be proposed. A variety of disturbances (low/high frequency and high/low impact) and their effects on microgrid’s ability to resist incidents efficiently and provide quick recovery and restoration will be analysed under uncertainty.

listings.description:
One of the essential networks for society is water distribution networks. The delivery of water to the customers is affected through different threats to the system. These include failure of components in the system, which are accelerated through the aging of the infrastructure; climate change, due to changing weather conditions and environmental factors impacting on the system; and deliberate planned acts, such as targeted terrorist activities.

This exciting project will focus on developing a mathematical model (and a supporting research software) to predict the key performance indicators of a water network, when links in the network are fully or partially failed. It will investigate the impact of the different threat types and identify the critical links in the network, which most affect the network performance. Resilience evaluation will consist of proposing a method for the best use of resource allocation, which will make water networks robust and resilient to these threats.

listings.title: PhD project: Railway asset degradation and management modelling for climate change
listings.summary: Bridges are vital to the UK’s economic and societal infrastructure, and railway bridges are critical infrastructure for Network Rail, forming a vital part of the 30,000 bridges, tunnels and viaducts which they manage across Britain. Increased traffic demand, limited maintenance, and ageing structural systems have…
listings.description:
Bridges are vital to the UK’s economic and societal infrastructure, and railway bridges are critical infrastructure for Network Rail, forming a vital part of the 30,000 bridges, tunnels and viaducts which they manage across Britain. Increased traffic demand, limited maintenance, and ageing structural systems have pushed many bridges beyond their original design capacities. In addition, climate change is altering environmental exposure conditions, particularly temperature and relative humidity, which further accelerate the deterioration of bridges. Physics-based formulations with probabilistic models are necessary to capture uncertainty and environmental variability in bridge component degradation modelling. The processes of atmospheric and pitting corrosion, chloride-induced corrosion, thermal cycling and fatigue, protective painting and coating degradation, to name a few, are most affected by increased rainfall and humidity, extreme heat conditions and air pollution, especially due to increasing effects of climate change.

It is envisaged that the approach will incorporate climate-dependent parameters and their influence on the deterioration of a bridge, and it will allow a clear integration of regional/national climate projections. Climate projections will be taken from the UK Climate Projections (UKCP18) based on multiple Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) and used along the probabilistic models of deterioration to capture uncertainty and environmental variability. The proposed approach will consider interdependencies, providing a realistic system-level variability in condition-state evolution, ranging from baseline ageing to pessimistic climate change effects, which would indicate acceleration of deterioration.

More than 80% of the world’s energy still comes from fossil fuels. Climate change and diminishing fuel reserves mean that it is becoming essential to find alternative, sustainable technologies to supply a growing global population. With no greenhouse gas emissions, inherent safety features and virtually limitless fuels, nuclear fusion has a key role to play in the energy market of the future. Major projects, like ITER in France and STEP in the UK, are providing potential avenues for solutions of this clean, abundant, and safe energy. Robotics and remotely operated tools are a fundamental part of operating fusion power plants, therefore, a fusion power plant must be designed to be inspected, maintained, and upgraded remotely using robots.

This exciting project will focus on different qualitative and quantitative risk assessment techniques, considering their suitability for risk analysis of the robotics-based maintenance and/or decommissioning of a nuclear fusion plant. System failure modes and contributing elements in success of a mission will be identified and analysed, followed by modelling a variety of threats and their effects on the mission, as well process recovery and restoration under uncertainty.

listings.title: Architecture of Flexibility in the UK: Towards Broader Customisation in Industrialised Construction
listings.summary: One of the core benefits of Industrialised Construction (IC) is the repetitive standardised advantage gained, allowing broader efficiency, quality, and an inheritable learning process across different projects. However, one of the most obvious disadvantages of such an approach is undermining Architects’ site-specific…
listings.description:
One of the core benefits of Industrialised Construction (IC) is the repetitive standardised advantage gained, allowing broader efficiency, quality, and an inheritable learning process across different projects. However, one of the most obvious disadvantages of such an approach is undermining Architects’ site-specific designs, design flexibility, and creativity.

Given the increasing need to change ways construction projects are delivered, there is a need to critically involve architect insight to ensure the feasibility of the overall national change programme for broader IC in the United Kingdom. The project includes rethinking how manufacturing facilities producing full-scale modules, through either volumetric or modular approaches, can benefit from the best of both worlds- repetitiveness and standardisation for one, and the flexibility and customisation for another.

The PhD is expected to investigate how reconfiguring manufacturing facilities and production systems can be reconfigured to include enhanced architectural capability for variations within the same (whole) highly repetitive process. This would enhance our understanding of enhanced uses of manufacturing in construction, creating conditions of which can make offsite factories more efficient and capable of meeting various client preferences.

The project may focus on a certain building typology, such as residential or educational buildings, or a combination of residential and non-residential buildings. This PhD projects welcomes applicants from Architecture and/or Construction Management backgrounds, preferably with experience or exposure to fabrication and/or construction.

listings.title: Creep and Durability of Weakly Stabilised Clays
listings.summary: Traditionally stabilised materials in infrastructure are used near the top of earthworks to create increased performance of the overlying pavement or railway track structures. However more recently, stabilised clay fill materials are being used in lower layers of large embankments to improve stability and reduce…
listings.description:
Traditionally stabilised materials in infrastructure are used near the top of earthworks to create increased performance of the overlying pavement or railway track structures. However more recently, stabilised clay fill materials are being used in lower layers of large embankments to improve stability and reduce settlements of the embankment.

Additionally materials are being treated with lower levels of stabilising agents than may have been traditionally used to reduce costs. While the behaviours of such materials are understood in pavement applications (under low normal stresses), little is know about the durability and creep performance of weakly stabilsed materials subject to high overburden and confinement stresses, (as occurs deep in embankments). Additionally little is known about the impact of changes in environmental conditions (such as the availability of free water) over time on the durability of such materials.

listings.description:
This PhD project lies at the intersection of three topics: Occupational Safety and Health (OSH), digital technologies, and industrialised construction. Digital4OSH is a research group bringing together researchers and practitioners from Loughborough and across Europe. For several years, the group has been studying the application of digital technologies to the management of OSH in construction.

Despite governmental support to realise broader pre-manufactured value in construction through industrialised construction, our understanding of how various organisations operating in this space are leveraging digital technologies to manage building safety risks is limited. This project aligns with the Building Safety Act and aims to explore how to better maintain a clear “golden thread” of information throughout pre-manufactured construction products’ lifecycle.

The PhD project will address an emerging need to explore how various industrialised systems, components, and structures align (or not) with the Building Safety Act. This will then inform the development of an online platform which records such safety performance using digital tools. One of the core objectives of this project is to enable the benchmarking of organisations and even countries against each other via a web-based platform. This research would address questions such as: how well are existing practices in line with the Building Safety Act? How can engagement with the use of a platform be incentivised? listings.description:
The UK construction industry is undergoing a digital transformation, with growing pressure to deliver projects more efficiently, sustainably, and transparently across the entire building lifecycle. Lean Construction principles have demonstrated strong potential to reduce waste and improve project flow, yet they are rarely integrated with whole-life information management frameworks or operational digital twins.

This PhD project aims to bridge this gap by investigating how product and process information can be structured, managed, and continuously updated across design, construction, operation, and maintenance, enabling a true whole-life digital ecosystem for built assets. The research will explore how lean principles—flow, pull, value, waste reduction—can be embedded into lifecycle information workflows, creating a continuously improving feedback loop between physical assets and their digital twins.

listings.title: Learning The Dynamics Of Turbulence To Inform Practical Fluids' Modelling
listings.summary: Turbulence is the great unsolved problem in classical physics yet modelling turbulence appropriately is vital for effective engineering design of aircraft, wind turbines and combustion processes and for understanding our evolving environment.
listings.description:
Turbulence is the great unsolved problem in classical physics yet modelling turbulence appropriately is vital for effective engineering design of aircraft, wind turbines and combustion processes and for understanding our evolving environment.

This project will make use of recent theoretical developments and results from our own work to consider how to construct the next generation of practical engineering closures for turbulent flows.

The pathway to the future looks to be a stochastic differential equation approach but how best to formulate this given the nonlocal and nonlinear properties of turbulent flows is an open problem.

This project will involve looking at the equations afresh and then using machine learning methods to constrain the search of the relevant parameter space to develop a new modelling approach.

listings.title: Optimising Site Transport Deliveries: Modern Methods of Construction
listings.summary: Applications of Industrialised Construction (IC) involve producing prefabricated elements in factories, transporting such elements to prepared sites, and assembling these in suitable forms for a safe and operational end product. Variations of such approaches include either whole built modules, e.g. 3D volumetric…
listings.description:
Applications of Industrialised Construction (IC) involve producing prefabricated elements in factories, transporting such elements to prepared sites, and assembling these in suitable forms for a safe and operational end product. Variations of such approaches include either whole built modules, e.g. 3D volumetric solutions, or 2D flat-packed systems, often referred to as the Modern Methods of Construction (MMC) Categories 1 and 2. These varied applications of IC are likely to be associated with different transport needs, whereby on-site arrival via predetermined routes plays a critical role.

Designing an optimisation system that allows transport operators to select an efficient route consider material nature, environmental factors, and site readiness will be a key within a value chain that determines lead transport times of modules, which are ideally in alignment with both factory production and site readiness.

This project aims to link the changes and possible digital applications that need to be made available to optimise existing transport decision-making and arrangements. The PhD is expected to contribute to our body of knowledge around optimising transport of pre-manufactured construction modules, pods, and components under MMC Cat 1 and 2.

listings.title: Pedagogies of Disasters
listings.summary: Globally, the majority of higher education training that is somehow related to disasters risks, focuses on hazards as a “problem” posed by nature – something that can be “solved” through a technical solution. Little reflection is required as to the social implications of Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) “solutions”, and…
listings.description:
Globally, the majority of higher education training that is somehow related to disasters risks, focuses on hazards as a “problem” posed by nature – something that can be “solved” through a technical solution. Little reflection is required as to the social implications of Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) “solutions”, and knowledge too often remains analytical and distant from any sort of lived experience.

Whilst many DRR-related subjects introduce the ideas of human-centric DRR, there is still a disconnection between technical engineering subjects and broader social science subjects. This is a missed opportunity for students acquiring technical knowledge to reflect on and engage with a wider societal context.

The aim of this PhD project is to enhance the understanding of what is being taught – and how – in higher education curricular in the context of DRR, and to explore how to engage with a kind of pedagogy that would enhance equity and well-being, while avoiding the creation of risk through development and redevelopment.

It is expected that the research would draw on the liberative pedagogies of Paulo Freire, bell hooks and others, to engage educators in collectively drawing on philosophies and practices that emphasise holistic ways of knowing and learning and encourage the broader consideration of non-technical ideas.

listings.title: Personal Cooling Systems for Enhanced Thermal Comfort and Sleep Quality
listings.summary: Overheating in buildings is a growing threat to health and wellbeing of citizens. In many parts of the world air-conditioning (AC) is used to maintain thermally comfortable sleep…
listings.description:
Overheating in buildings is a growing threat to health and wellbeing of citizens. Overheating in bedrooms is of particular concern as during sleep occupants’ ability to take actions to adapt to heat is more limited. In many parts of the world air-conditioning (AC) is used to maintain thermally comfortable sleep environments. The International Energy Agency predicts a significant increase in the uptake of AC units globally and in Europe between now and 2050.

Research has shown that the bed microclimate has a greater effect on thermal comfort and sleep quality than the bedroom’s temperature. There is a potential to reduce the energy demand for cooling by using low-energy personal cooling strategies to minimise or eliminate the need for energy intensive AC. Personal cooling is a rapidly developing area with new systems emerging. However, Credible, unbiased, documented evidence about their effectiveness to enhance thermal comfort and prevent sleep deprivation is needed if they are to be widely implemented.

The aim of this project is to quantify the impact of state-of-the-art personal cooling systems on human thermal comfort and sleep quality and establish their optimised performance under various thermal conditions. The project will use the newly refurbished full-scale thermal comfort test house facility at Loughborough University.

The successful candidate will conduct controlled experiments using both advanced thermal manikins as well as human participants. The project outcomes will provide the knowledge for engineers and manufacturers to develop energy efficient personal cooling systems.

Heritage buildings often exhibit complex, irregular, and evolving geometries, making traditional inspection and monitoring methods inadequate. With the rapid improvement of terrestrial laser scanning, photogrammetry, and LiDAR technologies, point clouds offer unprecedented opportunities for digitally capturing full-shape geometry and tracking changes over time.

This PhD project will develop advanced computational methods for automated analysis, comparison, and interpretation of large-scale point cloud datasets, enabling high-precision health monitoring, deformation tracking, and quality control for heritage buildings. The research will explore the unique challenges of heritage structures, including irregular morphologies, partial visibility, environmental constraints, and historical preservation requirements.

listings.title: The Impact of Low Emission Zones in Cities
listings.summary: Low Emission Zones (LEZs) are now a core urban transport policy for reducing harmful emissions from road traffic and improving air quality in busy city centres. By restricting or charging the most polluting vehicles, they directly target a major source of nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter, supporting wider goals…
listings.description:
Low Emission Zones (LEZs) are now a core urban transport policy for reducing harmful emissions from road traffic and improving air quality in busy city centres. By restricting or charging the most polluting vehicles, they directly target a major source of nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter, supporting wider goals around public health, climate mitigation and liveable streets. LEZs are being introduced or strengthened in many European and UK cities, often alongside congestion charging, active travel investment and public transport improvements, making them central to sustainable mobility strategies.

Despite their rapid rollout, key questions remain about how, and for whom, LEZs deliver benefits. Studies report improvements in particulate pollution and some health outcomes, but findings are mixed for other pollutants and there are important uncertainties about distributional effects, behavioural responses and longer-term dynamics. This creates a strong need for rigorous, comparative research that can inform future policy design and help cities integrate LEZs into broader decarbonisation and equity agendas.

This PhD project will evaluate the direct and indirect impacts of Low Emission Zones using advanced econometric and spatial-temporal methods. The student will identify a set of plausible impact channels, such as air quality, health and well-being, traffic patterns, equity and economic activity, and assemble relevant datasets at appropriate spatial and temporal scales.

The core of the project will be the design and implementation of causal models exploiting staggered introductions, boundary changes or tightening of standards across multiple cities, using approaches such as difference-in-differences, event-study designs and related quasi-experimental techniques.

A central objective is to understand heterogeneity: why similar policies appear to have different effects across locations and population groups. The student will explore factors such as baseline pollution, vehicle fleets, enforcement intensity, complementary policies and socio-demographic characteristics, testing how these shape outcomes and distributional impacts. There will be scope to examine spillover effects, for example the displacement of traffic and pollution to neighbouring areas, and to consider dynamic responses such as fleet renewal and changes in travel behaviour.

listings.title: The Productivity Promise: A Critical Study of AI-Driven Monitoring Technologies and Their Impact on Construction Productivity
listings.summary: Construction organisations are increasingly turning to AI-enabled monitoring systems, such as machine-vision progress tracking, predictive safety and productivity analytics, and automated resource allocation, to enhance project delivery and reduce inefficiencies. These technologies promise real-time insights, faster…
listings.description:
Construction organisations are increasingly turning to AI-enabled monitoring systems, such as machine-vision progress tracking, predictive safety and productivity analytics, and automated resource allocation, to enhance project delivery and reduce inefficiencies. These technologies promise real-time insights, faster decision-making, and the ability to optimise workflows at a scale previously impossible. However, empirical evidence on their actual productivity impact remains limited, fragmented, and often driven by vendor claims rather than independent, site-based evaluation.

This PhD project will critically examine how AI-driven monitoring systems influence construction productivity and project delivery outcomes. It will investigate how these tools are integrated into everyday site practices, how project teams interpret and act upon AI-generated insights, and how the presence of monitoring technologies shapes behaviours, communication, and coordination across project stakeholders.

The research will also explore both the productivity gains and the potential unintended consequences, such as increased monitoring pressure, data misinterpretation, or workflow disruptions, that may undermine expected benefits.

The ultimate goal is to develop a robust performance evaluation framework that enables construction organisations to assess the true value, limitations, and risks of AI implementations. This framework will support more evidence-informed decision-making, helping organisations determine when, where, and how AI-enabled monitoring technologies genuinely contribute to improved productivity and project delivery.

listings.title: Utilisation of Textile Waste for Enhanced Biogas Production
listings.summary: Large amounts of textile waste are generated worldwide during their manufacture and as post-consumer waste. Textile recycling is difficult as a variety of fabric materials are used in production, and most of it ends up in landfills or get incinerated.
listings.description:
Large amounts of textile waste are generated worldwide during their manufacture and as post-consumer waste. Textile recycling is difficult as a variety of fabric materials are used in production, and most of it ends up in landfills or get incinerated.

Anaerobic digestion (AD) is an environment-friendly microbial process that can degrade organic materials and produces biogas. Cotton represents the largest fraction of textile waste that can be subjected to AD. However, its high crystallinity resists microbial degradation. An effective pretreatment is required before using cotton-rich textiles as AD feed, to aid the breakdown of organic matter and increase biogas yield.

Most pretreatment techniques are often energy-intensive, expensive and produce toxic residues that can adversely affect sensitive AD microbial communities.

The main aim of this PhD project is to study textile pretreatment process using highly reactive species produced by gas plasma and how the AD microbial system is affected by the pretreated materials (mostly experimental but may involve computational simulations). An energy-efficient and scalable plasma-microbubble pretreatment reactor that has been developed over the past few years will be used for this purpose.

listings.title: Making net-zero quieter: sustainable acoustic metamaterials
listings.summary: This project explores acoustic metamaterials that combine effective noise control with more sustainable manufacturing materials. Through modelling, optimisation and experimental testing, it investigates how manufacturing materials influence acoustic performance, durability and environmental impact, developing design…
listings.description:
This project explores acoustic metamaterials that combine effective noise control with more sustainable manufacturing materials. Through modelling, optimisation and experimental testing, it investigates how manufacturing materials influence acoustic performance, durability and environmental impact, developing design approaches that support the transition to net zero emissions.

Low-frequency noise is difficult to block using conventional treatments. Acoustic metamaterials offer an alternative: engineered structures that manipulate sound through their geometry and resonances. However, switching to greener materials can disrupt their acoustic performance. The challenge is to redesign these structures so that environmental benefits do not come at the expense of effective sound insulation.

You'll combine computer modelling, multi-objective optimisation and laboratory experiments to investigate how material choices influence acoustic performance, durability and environmental impact. You'll develop and test designs that tackle noise across a broad frequency range, identifying trade-offs and opportunities for more sustainable noise treatments.

You'll have access to the University of Southampton’s world-class research facilities, including anechoic and reverberation chambers, specialist impedance tubes, high-performance computing and advanced manufacturing capabilities. These resources will support your journey from numerical simulations and design optimisation to prototype manufacture and experimental validation.

The intended outcomes include validated metamaterial designs and evidence-based guidance for selecting materials for sustainable noise control, with potential applications in transport, buildings and low-carbon technologies such as heat pumps.

You will receive training in computational acoustics, numerical modelling, design optimisation and experimental acoustic testing, alongside prototype development and sustainability assessment. This project will also develop your transferable skills in research planning, data analysis, scientific writing and presenting your findings to academic and industry audiences. This is an opportunity to connect fundamental discoveries with practical engineering solutions, helping shape noise control technologies for a quieter, more sustainable future.

listings.summary: Lancaster University is pleased to offer a fully funded PhD studentship as part of the Faraday Institution PhD Training Programme, focused on understanding the structure-property relationships of graphene-based conductive carbons for next-generation battery electrodes.
listings.description:
Lancaster University is pleased to offer a fully funded PhD studentship as part of the Faraday Institution PhD Training Programme, focused on understanding the structure-property relationships of graphene-based conductive carbons for next-generation battery electrodes.

Conductive carbon additives are essential for battery electrode manufacturing; however, the influence of their local structural disorder on conductivity and percolation remains poorly understood. This project will investigate how structural motifs in graphene-based carbons govern electronic conductivity and electrode performance in advanced battery systems. The successful candidate will develop and apply advanced X-ray pair distribution function (PDF) analysis, supported by structural modelling and complementary characterisation techniques such as NMR and Raman to establish quantitative descriptors for carbon disorder.

The project will be hosted by Dr Xiao Hua (xiaohua.group) at the Department of Chemistry, Lancaster University, in close collaboration with HydroGraph, an industrial partner developing advanced graphene materials through patented detonation synthesis routes.

Dr Xiao Hua’s research group focuses on advanced characterisation of disordered energy materials and developing new structure-property understanding for batteries and related electrochemical systems, with expertise in X-ray total scattering, pair distribution function analysis, and operando methods. HydroGraph will provide specialised graphene materials with controlled structural properties for benchmarking and optimisation studies, alongside technical input and industrial mentorship throughout the project.

The successful candidate will undertake an industrial placement of about three months with HydroGraph during the PhD, gaining direct experience in graphene production, process optimisation, and industrial R&D challenges associated with next-generation battery manufacturing.

This project is also closely connected to major Faraday Institution research themes including thick electrodes, degradation, and next-generation energy-storage technologies. listings.title: Computability and Constrained Equations in Free Semigroups
listings.summary: Given a finite set (A), and an associative binary operation (\circ), a semigroup is a set that contains (A) and is closed under (\circ). If (|A| = n), the free semigroup (A^+) is a particular example of a semigroup.
listings.description:
Given a finite set (A), and an associative binary operation (\circ), a semigroup is a set that contains (A) and is closed under (\circ). If (|A| = n), the free semigroup (A^+) is a particular example of a semigroup.

Often in computer science, (A) is a set of symbols called letters, (\circ) is the concatenation operation, and (A^+) contains all non-empty strings (also called words) comprising symbols from (A). The first-order theory of a free semigroup is algorithmically undecidable in general; however, satisfiability for first-order quantifier-free formulas, including single equations, is well known to be decidable, at least in theory. In practice, developing sufficiently efficient algorithms remains a challenge.

The aim of this project is to study equations or quantifier-free first-order formulas in free semigroups that are augmented by additional constraints, for example by restricting the values variables may take to rational subsets of (A^+) or by placing arithmetic constraints on their lengths, and as a result to better understand the limits of algorithmic approaches in solving the resulting satisfiability problems.

Such problems have implications in a variety of areas of mathematics and computer science, including formal methods, combinatorial group theory, arithmetic and number theory, formal language theory, theory of computation, and combinatorics on words.

The project will consist primarily of producing novel definitions, theorems, and proofs, and may include some practical (programming) elements depending on the strengths and interests of a successful applicant. In all cases, a strong background in theoretical computer science and discrete mathematics is required, particularly in topics such as formal language theory, logic, algorithms, and complexity.

A successful candidate should have strong internal motivation and should enjoy problem-solving and abstract thinking. They should work well individually, although there will also be opportunities for collaboration and networking both locally and internationally. Good communication skills, both verbal and written, and experience in reading and writing formal mathematics (including proofs) are also desirable.

The candidate will be part of the theoretical computer science research theme and will work closely with the primary supervisor, supported by regular supervision meetings. They will likely share an office with other PhD students and postdocs working in a mixture of theoretical and applied

listings.description:
Over recent years the modelling and understanding of complex phases, and their interfacial interactions, has developed at pace. Phases can be a solution of components, a mixture including colloidal particles, or different states such as in a frozen or vapour state. Through our recent modelling, we are able to understand in much greater detail the formation and stability of such phases, and now the emphasis is to use this for practical benefits in manufacturing and use of products.

Examples can include manufacturing of paints and their subsequent use and disposal, printed electronics, manufacturing and storage of consumable products like food and drink, and many others. This project will initially make developments on the fundamental fluid mechanics and thermodynamics of the modelling but rapidly move to exploiting the models to find positive gains in sustainability, cost reduction, storage lifetimes and other related aspects.

listings.title: Post impact fatigue behaviour of titanium aerospace alloys
listings.summary: This projet will investigate how impact damage triggers fatigue cracking in titanium aerospace components, combining advanced materials science with real-world engineering challenges. Using state-of-the-art testing and microscopy facilities, you’ll gain sought-after expertise in fatigue, failure analysis and aerospace…
listings.description:
This projet will investigate how impact damage triggers fatigue cracking in titanium aerospace components, combining advanced materials science with real-world engineering challenges. Using state-of-the-art testing and microscopy facilities, you’ll gain sought-after expertise in fatigue, failure analysis and aerospace materials while contributing to more sustainable aviation.

Lightweight titanium alloys are central to the next generation of more fuel-efficient aero-engines, helping to reduce aircraft weight and supporting the aviation sector’s journey towards net-zero emissions. However, titanium fan and compressor components are vulnerable to impact damage throughout service. Low-velocity impacts can occur during ground handling and maintenance, while high-velocity foreign object damage (FOD) can arise in flight from the ingestion of debris. Even when impact damage appears minor, it can significantly reduce fatigue life by creating conditions for crack initiation and growth.

Working in partnership with Rolls-Royce, this project will investigate how titanium alloy composition influences the initiation and early growth of fatigue cracks caused by impact damage. Particular emphasis will be placed on understanding the strain-rate-dependent microstructural changes that occur during impact events and how these changes govern subsequent fatigue behaviour. By linking alloy chemistry, microstructure and damage evolution, the project aims to deliver new insights that will support the design of more damage-tolerant aerospace materials and components.

You'll gain hands-on experience with world-leading experimental facilities at the University of Southampton, conducting impact testing and cyclic fatigue experiments that replicate demanding service conditions. You'll develop expertise in advanced materials characterisation techniques, including scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and nanoindentation, alongside the analysis of crack initiation and propagation mechanisms. This multidisciplinary project offers an exciting opportunity to contribute to cutting-edge aerospace research while developing highly sought-after skills in materials science, fatigue and failure analysis.

listings.title: Quantifying tribofilm formation using dynamic pressure sliding and in-operando Raman
listings.summary: This project combines tribology, advanced surface engineering and real-time Raman spectroscopy to reveal how protective tribofilms form and fail under extreme conditions. Working with the National Physical Laboratory, you'll develop durable engine surfaces that could unlock cleaner, longer-lasting heavy-duty transport.
listings.description:
This project combines tribology, advanced surface engineering and real-time Raman spectroscopy to reveal how protective tribofilms form and fail under extreme conditions. Working with the National Physical Laboratory, you'll develop durable engine surfaces that could unlock cleaner, longer-lasting heavy-duty transport.

The global transport sector is facing an enormous challenge to transition to clean carbon sources of propulsion and achieve net zero emissions by 2050. One pathway to propulsion decarbonization is combustion of diesel alternatives such as hydrogen. However, efficient combustion of sustainable fuels can lead to formation of corrosive species from unburnt fuel or condensed water vapour, degrading the tribological performance of protective tribofilms on the cylinder liner surface.

This project will assess the tribological impact at the ring-liner interface of a hydrogen fuelled off-grid heavy duty combustion engine using dynamic pressure sliding, a technique that simulates the variable contact pressures along the stroke of the 4-stroke cycle. The key novelty of the project is ascertaining liner surface evolution and quantifying tribo-film formation and removal as a function of contact conditions, carried out using in-operando Raman spectroscopy at the National Physical Laboratory. The principal challenge in qualifying this technique is achieving sufficient optical penetration through the lubricant film to acquire a reliable, scattered Raman signal without excessive attenuation.

The project will quantify tribo-layer formation using in-operando Raman, to observe surface chemistry development in real-time. This will be verified through the use of scanning electron microscopy and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy before determining the influence that water contamination has on lubricant emulsification and tribo-film degradation. The goal of the project is to engineer surfaces that will enable durable operation of hydrogen fuelled combustion engines for heavy duty transport and off highway applications. You'll be trained in Raman spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy.

This PhD explores how AI can address major threats to energy infrastructure that cause widespread outages. It will develop machine learning and agent-based tools to predict and manage cascading failures—rare, high-impact events that can disrupt power, water and communications. Building on prior work such as the NTRM toolkit (https://github.com/sskazakos/NTRM), you will create simulations, analyse real datasets, and design resilience assessment tools. You’ll collaborate with industry, publish research, and gain skills in AI, energy systems modelling, and risk analysis.

This self-funded PhD project is available to UK and Overseas applicants who are able to self-fund or identify their own sources of funding. You will be supported when applying to any external sources.

How can we leverage artificial intelligence to tackle modern serious threats to energy infrastructure that leave millions without power?

This PhD project aims to investigate the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, including machine learning (ML) and agent-based control, for predicting, managing and improving the resilience of energy networks to disruption.

AI tools will be used to predict the likelihood and impact of cascading failures. Cascading failures can lead to widespread electrical blackouts, typically characterised as High-Impact Low Probability (HILP) events, potentially leaving millions of people without energy, water or communications, risking lives, and costing £ billions. Prior knowledge of the occurrence of such HILP events can enhance the response of infrastructure operators, thus limiting their impact.

You will build on prior research that has been done by the supervisor’s team on leveraging machine learning to predict large-scale blackouts, including the Network Theory Resilience Metric (NTRM) toolkit (https://github.com/sskazakos/NTRM).

listings.summary: How can we prevent cascading failures that disrupt power, water and communications for millions?
