Focusing on energy and telecom systems as multilayer “networks of…
listings.description:
How can we prevent cascading failures that disrupt power, water and communications for millions? This PhD investigates how to strengthen the resilience of interconnected critical infrastructures facing climate change, cyber threats and global shocks. Focusing on energy and telecom systems as multilayer “networks of networks”, you will develop structural resilience metrics, build cascading‑failure simulations, analyse real datasets, and extend the open‑source NTRM platform (https://github.com/sskazakos/NTRM).

This self-funded PhD project is available to UK and Overseas applicants who are able to self-fund or identify their own sources of funding. You will be supported when applying to any external sources.

The University of Sussex believes that the diversity of its staff and student community is fundamental to creative thinking, pedagogic innovation, intellectual challenge, and the interdisciplinary approach to research and learning. We celebrate and promote diversity, equality and inclusion amongst our staff and students. As such, we welcome applicants from all backgrounds.

This PhD explores cutting-edge approaches to understanding and strengthening the resilience of interconnected critical infrastructure systems, at a time when climate change, cyber threats and global disruptions are increasing system vulnerability.

Interdependent critical infrastructure, such as power, gas, telecommunications, water, transport and other networks, can be vulnerable to emerging threats like climate change, pandemics and cyber-terrorism, potentially leaving millions of people without energy, water or communications, risking lives, and costing £ billions. The root cause of the widespread nature of these disruptions can often be traced to the interconnected and interdependent structure of these infrastructure systems, which resembles a “network of networks”, otherwise referred to as multilayer networks.

Develop a prototype toolkit of holistic metrics, which can be used to assess the resilience of interdependent energy and telecommunications networks, simply by considering their fundamental structure, types of interactions and locations of potential interventions.

You will build upon an existing open-source research platform (Network Theory Resilience Metric [NTRM] - https://github.com/sskazakos/NTRM), offering a strong practical starting point and opportunities to make visible, publishable contributions early in the PhD.

listings.description:
Applications are invited for a four-year, AstraZeneca-funded PhD studentship in the Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics, commencing in October 2027.

The successful candidate will be jointly supervised by Prof Sergio Bacallado (University of Cambridge), Dr Dino Oglic (AstraZeneca), and Dr Jon Paul Janet (AstraZeneca). The studentship offers an opportunity to conduct cutting-edge research at the interface of statistical machine learning, molecular simulation and drug discovery.

The project, entitled Physics-Guided Representation Learning from Free Energy Perturbation Data for Affinity Prediction and Candidate Down-Selection, aims to develop novel machine-learning methods for predicting molecular binding affinities and supporting decision-making in drug discovery.

Free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations provide valuable information about how strongly candidate drug molecules bind to their biological targets, but these calculations are computationally expensive. This project will investigate how machine-learning models can extract richer information from FEP data and experimental measurements, combining physical principles with modern representation-learning techniques.

The research will involve developing and evaluating new statistical and machine-learning methods, with access to both public benchmark datasets and AstraZeneca's industrial drug-discovery expertise and data.

listings.title: Developing Luminescent Supramolecular Receptors for the Selective Detection and Removal of Toxic Heavy Metals from Aquatic Environments
listings.summary: Heavy metal contamination of freshwater systems is a major environmental challenge, posing significant risks to ecosystems, biodiversity, and human health. Toxic metal ions such as mercury, lead, cadmium, and nickel are persistent pollutants that can accumulate within food chains, resulting in long-term environmental…
listings.description:
Heavy metal contamination of freshwater systems is a major environmental challenge, posing significant risks to ecosystems, biodiversity, and human health. Toxic metal ions such as mercury, lead, cadmium, and nickel are persistent pollutants that can accumulate within food chains, resulting in long-term environmental and public health consequences.

There is an urgent need for innovative technologies that can both detect and remove these contaminants from complex environmental systems. Existing remediation approaches, including adsorption, ion exchange, photocatalysis, and electrochemical treatment. Many of these can be effective but often suffer from limitations such as poor selectivity, high energy requirements, or the generation of secondary waste. These challenges are particularly pronounced in natural waters, where competing ions can reduce performance and efficiency.

This PhD project will explore how supramolecular chemistry can address these limitations through the development of highly selective molecular receptors and self-assembled cage architectures for heavy metal capture. The successful candidate will design, synthesise, and characterise novel supramolecular systems capable of recognising and encapsulating environmentally relevant metal ions. The project provides an exciting opportunity to contribute to next-generation sensing and water remediation technologies with real-world impact.

listings.description:
United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 15 calls for the protection and restoration of terrestrial ecosystems, halting biodiversity loss and land degradation. Achieving this requires deeper understanding of how environmental change impacts biodiversity, and reliable estimation of microclimatic conditions is key to understanding how ecosystems function and is increasingly recognised as essential for predicting ecological consequences of climate change and pest invasions. Forests host two-thirds of the world’s terrestrial biota, yet their microclimatic conditions vary considerably in space and time. Effective monitoring demands high-density sensor networks capable of continuous, long-term data collection across challenging terrain.

This PhD project will design a nature-inspired hardware that enables the deployment of IoT sensors within forest ecosystems, integral to environmental research and effective environmental management. SPS nodes harvest energy directly from the ambient environment, eliminating batteries, and transmit data wirelessly, dramatically reducing human intervention and enabling monitoring in difficult geographical terrains.

The proposed investigation will develop an SPS node integrating a bespoke energy harvester (electromagnetic or piezoelectric) with sensors measuring temperature, rainfall, wind speed, humidity, soil moisture, and CO₂ levels. The node will be autonomous and self-sustained with marginal human involvement. A hardware demonstrator assessed in real environmental operating conditions will be the main deliverable.

listings.summary: Urban landscapes contain numerous small waterbodies that may collectively provide important habitat and connectivity. listings.description:
Urban landscapes contain numerous small waterbodies that may collectively provide important habitat and connectivity. Garden ponds in particular, may represent a significant, but overlooked, component of urban freshwater networks. Previous research has demonstrated that ponds in the wider landscape can support diverse aquatic communities. However, little is known about garden pond biodiversity and the spatial / biotic variables structuring their communities. We have limited understanding of whether garden ponds function as isolated habitat patches or collectively form interconnected networks that contribute to urban freshwater biodiversity.

Urbanisation and connectivity may however facilitate the spread of non-native and invasive species. Garden ponds may therefore function as both biodiversity refuges and potential invasion pathways, with landscape connectivity and human activity interacting to influence the distribution of native and non-native species.

ii) Quantify native and non-native aquatic diversity within garden ponds, and determine the environmental, spatial and biotic drivers;

iii) Assess the role of garden ponds in maintaining and enhancing urban freshwater connectivity including in the spread of invasive species; and;

iv) Evaluate the effectiveness of wildlife ponds and garden pond-management practices in supporting aquatic biodiversity.

listings.title: Hidden Signals Beneath Our Feet: AI and Soil eDNA for Predicting Ecosystem Health and Drought Resilience
listings.summary: Can multimodal and agentic AI reveal hidden signals in soil biodiversity and help predict ecosystem resilience to drought?
listings.description:
Can multimodal and agentic AI reveal hidden signals in soil biodiversity and help predict ecosystem resilience to drought?

Led by Computer Science at Loughborough University, in partnership with Defra’s DNA Centre of Excellence, this PhD will develop AI methods to identify indicators of soil ecosystem health and predict responses to drought. Soil microorganisms support nutrient cycling, carbon storage and water regulation, making their resilience vital for environmental sustainability.

You will develop a unified AI framework integrating soil eDNA data from Defra’s Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment programme and Forest Research with soil measurements, climate, hydrological and spatial records. Multimodal learning will combine these data with ecological knowledge extracted from scientific literature and environmental reports to guide predictions of soil health and ecosystem responses to drought. AI agents will support evidence retrieval, analytical workflows and identification of knowledge gaps, recommending additional data or expert review where uncertainty is high. The framework will track uncertainty from data integration to prediction and address explainability and transferability across habitats and drought scenarios.

Outputs will support biodiversity monitoring, conservation, climate adaptation and sustainable land management. Training will cover multimodal learning, AI agents, uncertainty quantification, data engineering and GPU/HPC computing, complemented by eDNA methods, ecological interpretation and fieldwork opportunities. A Defra placement will provide experience translating AI research into environmental policy and practice.

listings.title: Low-Cost Monitoring of Dynamic River Channels to Improve Flood and Drought Forecasting
listings.summary: Flood and drought models routinely treat river channels as fixed, yet erosion and deposition continuously reshape them, introducing unquantified error into flow estimates across the UK’s monitoring network.
listings.description:
Flood and drought models routinely treat river channels as fixed, yet erosion and deposition continuously reshape them, introducing unquantified error into flow estimates across the UK’s monitoring network.

This PhD investigates how shifting riverbeds distort flood and drought predictions. Using low-cost continuous sensing and numerical modelling, it will identify which stations are most exposed to sediment-driven forecasting error.

Working in partnership with the Floods & Droughts Research Infrastructure (FDRI), the findings will directly inform future instrumentation of water monitoring networks. This will support the shift from static to dynamic flood risk assessment, and build resilience to increasingly frequent and severe hydrological extremes.

Year 1: Literature review; training in research skills, Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) operation and data processing, and Structure-from-Motion survey techniques; sensor installation and testing on the River Soar.

Year 2: Sensor deployment in the Upper Tweed in partnership with FDRI; training in hydraulic and hydrodynamic numerical modelling; propagation of observations through stage-discharge rating curves to quantify discharge error.

Year 3: Numerical modelling extending the Year 2 error relationships across the wider monitoring network to identify the stations most exposed to sediment-driven forecasting error.

listings.title: Seeing extreme winds - Machine learning applied to video clips to better estimate site-specific wind hazard
listings.summary: Extratropical cyclones such as Storm Eunice inflict extreme winds on the UK, causing billions of pounds in insured losses. Yet the peak 3-second gusts that drive damage vary greatly over short distances in cities, and weather stations and models cannot capture this. This PhD tackles the problem with visual anemometry:…
listings.description:
Extratropical cyclones such as Storm Eunice inflict extreme winds on the UK, causing billions of pounds in insured losses. Yet the peak 3-second gusts that drive damage vary greatly over short distances in cities, and weather stations and models cannot capture this. This PhD tackles the problem with visual anemometry: extracting gust speeds from short video clips of trees. Building on pilot work showing that optical flow tracking of tree motion captures peak gusts, you will set up a campus-scale “living lab” at Loughborough University, installing four to five camera and anemometer sets for at least a year. You will combine this dataset with machine learning, laser scanning and a physics-based digital twin of trees to test how well video measures wind, even in extreme conditions. You will then link these small-scale observations to historical weather data such as ERA5 and show how buildings shelter or expose sites.

The work collaborates with the ArboKlim project (Prof. Theresa Blume), which is instrumenting trees in Potsdam, Germany. The aim is a low-cost, proof-of-concept hazard-mapping tool. It could scale nationally using CCTV networks and inform the (re)insurance sector.

listings.title: Volcanoes and microplastics: microplastic abrasion and degradation by pyroclastic materials
listings.summary: Microplastic pollution is a pressing global challenge; microplastics are recognised as a pervasive, near-unmanageable pollutant, with consequences for human and animal health, biogeochemical cycling and ecosystem functioning.
listings.description:
Microplastic pollution is a pressing global challenge; microplastics are recognised as a pervasive, near-unmanageable pollutant, with consequences for human and animal health, biogeochemical cycling and ecosystem functioning.

Microplastics have been discovered in nearly all global environments, from the deepest oceans to the highest mountains. Whilst transport and abrasion of microplastics have been studied in fluvial, marine and aeolian settings, to date volcanic environments have not been considered.

This studentship will evaluate how the processes of abrasion by volcanic particles affects the physical and chemical properties of microplastics. In comparison with studies on aeolian abrasion, the project will seek to understand the extent to which plastic breakdown and transport is exacerbated in volcanic environments. Novel experiments will simulate microplastic transport in volcanic settings, using pyroclastic materials sourced from different volcanoes worldwide.

Using state-of-the-art materials characterisation facilities (Loughborough’s Centre for Analytical Science and Materials Characterisation Centre), the project will quantify any resulting surface chemical and morphological changes of microplastics to assess the extent of abrasion and degradation.

The project will contribute new insights into the environmental fate of plastic [pollution] in a previously unstudied environmental setting. Findings will have implications for human and ecosystem health, biogeochemical cycling, and pollution management in volcanic regions.

listings.title: More data, more and better distances: Improving on Gaia parallaxes with multi-modal machine learning
listings.summary: Accurate stellar distances underpin our understanding of the Galaxy. This project will develop a neural network that combines diverse astronomical observations to estimate distances, even when Gaia parallaxes are uncertain or missing, and improve existing estimates. It will advance stellar astrophysics while…
listings.description:
Accurate stellar distances underpin our understanding of the Galaxy. This project will develop a neural network that combines diverse astronomical observations to estimate distances, even when Gaia parallaxes are uncertain or missing, and improve existing estimates. It will advance stellar astrophysics while developing machine learning methods with applications beyond astronomy.

The Gaia mission has recently provided photometric (brightness) and astrometric (positional) information for nearly 2 billion astronomical objects. Perhaps most importantly, it has provided parallaxes -- and hence allowed distance estimates -- for roughly 1.5 billion sources. However, only about 10% of these have "good" parallaxes sufficient for inferring distances robustly.

In this project, we will develop, train and exploit a machine learning algorithm that will provide useful distances estimate even for sources with highly uncertain Gaia parallaxes -- or perhaps no parallaxes at all. At the same time, it will also improve the quality of the distance estimate for sources that do have good-quality parallaxes.

The core idea is that almost every astronomical measurement contains at least some information about the distance to that source. For example, distant sources will appear fainter, whereas sources located behind dense interstellar clouds may be closer than they appear.

We will develop and train a neural network combines source observations to provide the best possible distance estimate for the source. Machine-learning algorithms that can work with different kinds of data simultaneously are known as "multi-modal", and they are extremely powerful tools for extracting critical information hidden in complex data sets.

The specific distance-estimation tool we aim to develop will be immensely valuable to stellar astrophysics. The machine learning methodology we will learn about, implement and exploit has an even wider range of applicability, well beyond the astronomical context.

listings.description:

Accreting black holes are the most luminous steady stellar sources in the Galaxy when they actively swallowing matter. Their extreme powers are generated in their accretion discs, and they feed back huge energies to their surroundings through superfast winds and relativistic streams of jet plasmas. Much remains to be understand about the conditions under which these structures form, and how black holes grow via accretion.

In this PhD, you will exploit state-of-the-art multiwavelength observations from frontline facilities to carry out comprehensive novel studies of the immediate environments of Galactic black holes. You will:

use timing and spectral observations in X-rays to measure the physical conditions responsible for feedback changes with accreting of matter using NASA's JWST complemented by a suite of radio, optical and X-ray datasets

test some of the leading theories regarding the formation and evolution of discs and jets. The aim is to test and refine models of the immediate accreting environments around black holes, which can help to test the growth of black holes across cosmic time.

listings.title: A new theory for the most bizarre supermassive black holes in the cosmos
listings.summary: Supermassive black holes evolve across billions of years. But a new population that changes rapidly in just months is challenging our understanding of black-hole growth. In this project, you will determine the space density of changing-look black holes, and develop a new physical theory on their origin and evolution.
listings.description:
Supermassive black holes evolve across billions of years. But a new population that changes rapidly in just months is challenging our understanding of black-hole growth. In this project, you will determine the space density of changing-look black holes, and develop a new physical theory on their origin and evolution.

Changing-look active galactic nuclei (AGN) are supermassive black holes that evolve faster than is currently thought possible according to our best understanding of accretion. Instead of millions to billions of years, these sources display dramatic evolution in just months. This is puzzling because inflow of matter through viscous processes in accretion discs and ultimately on to the black hole is thought to proceed at a much slower pace. The discovery of these cosmic monsters implies that our understanding of accretion remains incomplete.

with these measurements, you will then test new physical theories on their origin and evolution by comparing the measured space densities, host-galaxy properties, and timescales of change. Connections will be drawn with other populations of stellar- and super-massive accreting sources across the cosmos.

Training will be provided in all aspects of observational astronomy and data science. Applicants should be comfortable with some scientific computing.

listings.title: Testing the foundations of cosmology with quasars
listings.summary: Does the Universe look the same in every direction? Distant quasars, powered by giant black holes, hint that it might not. Using public telescope surveys, this project will investigate whether that surprising signal reveals a problem with our understanding of the Universe or arises from how we observe the sky.
listings.description:
Does the Universe look the same in every direction? Distant quasars, powered by giant black holes, hint that it might not. Using public telescope surveys, this project will investigate whether that surprising signal reveals a problem with our understanding of the Universe or arises from how we observe the sky.

Is the Universe statistically isotropic on the largest scales? This assumption underpins our standard cosmological model, yet observations of distant quasars have revealed a possible challenge. Their sky distribution shows a dipole whose amplitude and direction may differ from expectations based on our motion relative to the cosmic microwave background. Whether this reflects new physics, cosmic structure or observational biases remains unresolved.

In this project, you will use supermassive black holes as beacons to test this assumption. You will analyse public WISE and Gaia quasar catalogues, supported by public spectroscopy and complementary SPHEREx and Euclid releases where available. Infrared spectra will help establish how quasar colours and spectral shapes influence the expected signal, while high resolution imaging will help identify blended sources and contaminants.

developing simulations and Bayesian methods that distinguish observer motion, cosmic clustering and additional anisotropy

The project combines observational astrophysics, cosmology and data science. You will develop analysis tools and publish constraints on cosmic isotropy, with valuable outcomes whether the anomaly persists or is explained by survey effects. Training will cover scientific computing, statistical inference, survey analysis and scientific communication. You will need to be comfortable with scientific computing in any language of your choice.

listings.title: The making of bulges and giant elliptical galaxies
listings.summary: How did the Universe’s most massive galaxies build their bulges? Using new observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), you'll test whether galaxy collisions or internal processes shaped galaxies 10 billion years ago, comparing your findings with…
listings.description:
How did the Universe’s most massive galaxies build their bulges? Using new observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), you'll test whether galaxy collisions or internal processes shaped galaxies 10 billion years ago, comparing your findings with theoretical models to uncover the origins of the bulges we observe today.

Most stars in the present-day Universe are found in spheroids: giant ellipticals and the bulges of massive discs. These systems formed most of their stars more than 10 billion years ago and have little cold gas left, yet their progenitors were vigorously forming stars in extended, gas-rich discs. How those discs build compact bulges remains a major open challenge in astrophysics.

Recent observations suggest that we may be witnessing the early stages of this transformation in distant galaxies with centrally concentrated reservoirs of cold gas fuelling intense nuclear star formation. However, we still do not know what drives this process. Are galaxy collisions primarily responsible, or can galaxies build their central structures through their own internal evolution? These scenarios predict different observables, notably the spatial distribution of stars and the properties of their cold gas.

In this project, you'll combine observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) of these progenitors at the peak epoch of galaxy formation, 10 billion years ago, and test which mechanisms best explain the observed structures. Supervised by Dr Puglisi, you will start from in-hand datasets and expand the sample with archival and new observations to measure the spatial distribution of stars (JWST) and cold gas (ALMA). You'll collaborate with Southampton Cosmology researchers to interpret your observations using their state-of-the-art galaxy evolution models. You will obtain robust statistical constraints on which mechanisms drive the assembly of bulges and spheroids.

You'll receive training in the reduction, analysis and interpretation of state-of-the-art astronomical observations, including high-resolution JWST imaging and ALMA interferometric data. You'll develop expertise in multi-wavelength image analysis, structural modelling of galaxies, and spatially resolved measurements of stellar populations. listings.title: Why do galaxies stop forming stars, and why do they end up with bulges?
listings.summary: In this project you'll build transparent, data-driven models that switch quenching ingredients on and off, one at a time, and test them against new data from the Euclid space telescope, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Rubin-LSST telescope to reveal what really shuts galaxies down.
listings.description:
In this project you'll build transparent, data-driven models that switch quenching ingredients on and off, one at a time, and test them against new data from the Euclid space telescope, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Rubin-LSST telescope to reveal what really shuts galaxies down.

Galaxies come broadly in two main flavours: blue, star-forming discs and red, quenched systems with a prominent central bulge. The drivers behind such a dichotomy are still a matter of intense debate.

This project aims to tackle this fundamental mystery in astronomy making use of flexible and transparent, data-driven numerical models that connect observations directly to theory. You'll build and extend semi-empirical models in which galaxies grow along their host dark matter halo merger trees at the rate imposed by observed star formation rates, and central supermassive black holes grow following observed Eddington-ratio distributions and duty cycles. With such flexible tools, you'll be able to test one ingredient at a time:

does quenching happen when a black hole reaches a threshold mass, or when the halo becomes massive enough, or after mergers and disc instabilities?

Because every assumption is explicit and can be switched on or off, these models show clearly what the data demand and what they do not. Your predictions will be tested against new data from Euclid, JWST and Rubin-LSST, covering millions of galaxies, and compared with outputs from simulations such as TNG and EAGLE. If you have a creative and curious mind, this is the project for you.

listings.title: How did the first supermassive black holes grow so fast?
listings.summary: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has found black holes that seem too massive, too early. How did they grow so fast? In this project you will build transparent, data-driven models that trace black hole growth from the first seeds, test light, heavy and primordial scenarios against JWST data, and set constraints on how…
listings.description:
James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has found black holes that seem too massive, too early. How did they grow so fast? In this project you will build transparent, data-driven models that trace black hole growth from the first seeds, test light, heavy and primordial scenarios against JWST data, and set constraints on how the Universe’s first giants formed.

JWST is finding supermassive black holes within the first billion years of cosmic time, which already weigh millions to billions of suns, comparable to the masses of their host galaxies, and roughly ten times more common than we expected. How did they get so big and numerous so quickly?

This project tackles that question with semi-empirical models: transparent, data-driven numerical tools that connect observations directly to theory. You'll grow black holes along dark matter halo merger trees through gas accretion and mergers, with accretion rates drawn from Eddington-ratio distributions and duty cycles consistent with current data. You'll then start them from different seeds: light (about 100 solar masses, left by the first stars), heavy (10,000 to a million solar masses, from direct collapse) or primordial black holes. Using statistical approaches, you'll ask which seeds and accretion histories can reproduce the JWST active galaxies, including the “Little Red Dots”, and X-ray quasars.

Because every assumption is explicit and can be switched on or off, you'll transparently dissect the main supermassive black hole growth channels and set clear constraints on viable seeding mechanisms by comparing with a variety of data sets both in the local and the high-redshift Universe. If you have a creative and curious mind, this is the project for you.

listings.description:
Applications are invited for a funded PhD studentship through the NERC-funded CENTA Doctoral Training Partnership and Cranfield University. The award will cover UK tuition fees, provide a tax-free stipend at the UKRI rate and include research and training support. The project will investigate acid sulfate soils: sulfide-rich soils that can generate sulfuric acid and release metals following drainage, excavation, drought or rewetting. Combining soil classification, LandIS legacy data, field sampling and predictive mapping, the researcher will identify where these soils occur and determine how land management history influences acidification hazards across agricultural peatlands and coastal wetland restoration sites.

Acid sulfate soils contain sulfide minerals that generate sulfuric acid when exposed to oxygen through drainage, excavation or drought. Rewetting can then mobilise stored acidity and metals into surrounding waters. These processes can damage aquatic ecosystems, reduce agricultural productivity and complicate wetland restoration. Climate-driven drought, changing water management and expanding restoration programmes make it increasingly important to identify these soils before disturbance and understand how they may respond.

This PhD aims to establish how reliably existing soil information can predict acid sulfate soil occurrence and whether land management history improves predictions of acidification responses. The researcher will combine soil classifications, historical profile descriptions and information from Cranfield’s LandIS Soils Data Portal with geological, terrain and hydrological data, archived samples and fresh, depth-resolved field observations. Statistical and machine learning models will be developed and independently validated across contrasting UK landscapes. Agricultural and coastal restoration case studies will then test whether drainage, disturbance and rewetting obscure, preserve or reveal diagnostic soil signals.

The project will be based at Cranfield University, which has extensive expertise in soil science, environmental data and predictive soil mapping and curates the LandIS national soil information resource. The studentship is funded through the NERC-funded CENTA Doctoral Training Partnership and Cranfield University. listings.summary: This 3.5-year PhD, supported through the Central England NERC Training Alliance (CENTA3), will investigate how changing weather controls whether fungi remain attached to terrestrial surfaces, recover after disturbance or redistribute to new locations. You will combine fungal experiments with controlled rainfall,…
listings.description:
This 3.5-year PhD, supported through the Central England NERC Training Alliance (CENTA3), will investigate how changing weather controls whether fungi remain attached to terrestrial surfaces, recover after disturbance or redistribute to new locations. You will combine fungal experiments with controlled rainfall, airflow, simulated sunlight and drying-rewetting, together with dynamic modelling, to understand how successive weather events shape fungal persistence and dispersal. The studentship provides a tax-free stipend and Home-rate tuition fees for 3.5 years.

Fungi colonise surfaces across terrestrial environments and play important roles in decomposition and carbon cycling. These networks are repeatedly exposed to rainfall, wind, sunlight and changes in moisture. Such events can detach fungal material, affect its survival and alter its ability to resume growth. However, we still have limited understanding of how successive weather events interact to determine whether established fungal networks persist, progressively decline, recover after disturbance or redistribute to new locations.

You will use a model filamentous fungus to investigate these processes under controlled environmental conditions. Wild-type and defined mutant strains will be compared on model surfaces with controlled roughness and wettability to determine how fungal attachment mechanisms and material surface properties influence retention, regrowth and release. Experiments will vary the order, spacing, intensity and combination of rainfall, airflow, simulated sunlight and drying-rewetting. Material transported by air and rainwater will be collected to determine whether spores, fungal fragments and colonised particles remain viable and can establish on new surfaces. Selected findings will then be tested on natural substrates.

The project will be based at Cranfield University and bring together expertise in fungal biomaterials, material interfaces, environmental testing and modelling. Fungal cultivation, attachment and surface characterisation will be carried out within the Magan Centre of Applied Mycology, while controlled weather experiments will use Ocean Systems Test Laboratory. The project also brings together modelling expertise from City St George’s, University of London, and fungal biology expertise from Utrecht University. As part of CENTA3, you will join a wider doctoral training programme in environmental science supported by NERC.

listings.title: How do the languages that we speak affect numerical processing and mathematics achievement?
listings.summary: A growing body of research suggests that different aspects of language influence the way we think about, represent, and apply numbers and mathematical concepts. One aspect of language that has repeatedly been shown to affect numerical processing concerns the way numbers are named. Indeed, number-naming systems vary…
listings.description:
A growing body of research suggests that different aspects of language influence the way we think about, represent, and apply numbers and mathematical concepts. One aspect of language that has repeatedly been shown to affect numerical processing concerns the way numbers are named. Indeed, number-naming systems vary significantly across languages.

For example, in English, two-digit numbers above twenty are named in the same order as they are written: first the tens and then the units (“forty-eight”). In Dutch or German, however, it is the opposite (“48” in Dutch or German is named “eight and forty”).

Increasingly more studies show that such irregularities in number words can be a stumbling block for children’s mathematical development and can even affect numerical processing in adulthood. Given that bi- and multilingualism is becoming increasingly common in our globalised world, considering how language influences the processing of numerical information in bilingual speakers and second-language learners becomes increasingly relevant.

This project aims at increasing our understanding into how the languages that we speak affect numerical and mathematical development which will in turn inform interventional approaches for multi-lingual language contexts and enhance educational practice.

The successful applicant will join the vibrant community of the Centre for Mathematical Cognition, one of the world's leading research centres for the study of mathematics education and numerical thinking. The Centre for Mathematical Cognition brings together academics who conduct research in three different areas: basic research on mathematical cognition, the design of research-based educational resources, and the evaluation of educational interventions.

listings.title: Nuclear-spin control of translation and rotation in levitated optomechanics
listings.summary: Can nuclear spins steer a levitated nanoparticle? This project develops theory for using nuclear magnetic resonance to control its centre-of-mass motion and rotation. Working closely with experimentalists, you will explore spin–motion coupling as a route to quantum states of massive objects and new approaches to…
listings.description:
Can nuclear spins steer a levitated nanoparticle? This project develops theory for using nuclear magnetic resonance to control its centre-of-mass motion and rotation. Working closely with experimentalists, you will explore spin–motion coupling as a route to quantum states of massive objects and new approaches to quantum sensing and information processing.

How can nuclear spins be coupled coherently to the motion of a levitated nanoparticle? This project will develop theoretical models for controlling both translation and rotation through nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Magnetic-field gradients can convert spin dynamics into forces on a particle’s centre of mass, while spin–rotation interactions can exchange angular momentum with its mechanical rotation.

You will investigate realistic control schemes, including radio-frequency pulse sequences, magnetic-field gradients and resonant driving, and assess how spin relaxation, mechanical damping, thermal noise and optical readout affect their performance.

For rotation, the work will examine coupling associated with the Einstein–de Haas and Barnett effects, including the roles of nuclear-spin anisotropy and quadrupolar interactions. The aim is to identify practical regimes in which spin states can prepare, control or read out mechanical motion, and to establish how these ideas could progress towards spatial quantum superpositions of massive objects and the use of nuclear spins coupled to mechanical modes for quantum computation and sensing.

This is a theory project with close interaction with experimental researchers working on levitated optomechanics and NMR. You will build skills in quantum and classical dynamics, numerical modelling and magnetic-resonance methods, helping guide future experiments in quantum metrology and information processing.

listings.title: Engineering quantum measurements to test the Zeno effect in levitated mechanics
listings.summary: The quantum Zeno effect suggests repeated measurements can slow a system’s evolution. Could this be tested with a levitated nanoparticle? You will develop and calibrate measurements, model their effects on motion, and investigate how measurement changes its state. This project probes how measurement shapes quantum…
listings.description:
The quantum Zeno effect suggests repeated measurements can slow a system’s evolution. Could this be tested with a levitated nanoparticle? You will develop and calibrate measurements, model their effects on motion, and investigate how measurement changes its state. This project probes how measurement shapes quantum behaviour near the classical boundary.

Can repeated measurements hold a quantum system still? The quantum Zeno effect predicts that frequent measurement can inhibit a system’s evolution. This project will investigate the effect using a levitated nanoparticle, a mechanical system whose motion can be controlled and measured with light.

You will work with Southampton’s non-cavity optical tweezer platform, which uses parabolic mirrors to trap and collect light from a nanoparticle and feedback cooling to prepare its motion near the ground state. The challenge is to develop the complete measurement needed for a convincing test: identifying both measurement outcomes and determining how each changes the nanoparticle’s state.

You will improve and calibrate optical detection, model realistic effects such as optical loss, heating and imperfect control, then carry out repeated-measurement experiments. Results will be compared with matched controls to distinguish genuine Zeno dynamics from technical disturbance or simple state resetting.

The project aims to deliver a validated measurement protocol, an experimentally grounded model, reusable control and analysis software, and survival statistics that establish how closely the experiment can test quantum predictions. This work addresses a fundamental question: how does measurement shape the transition between quantum and classical behaviour in a massive object?

The project combines hands-on experimental physics with quantum measurement theory and modelling, supervised by Southampton.

listings.title: Digital twins for sustainable robotic systems using noise and vibration
listings.summary: This PhD will develop digital twins that use noise and vibration measurements to estimate hidden indicators of robot performance. Combining physics-based modelling, sensing and state estimation, the project will create virtual sensing technologies that improve the efficiency, reliability and sustainability of future…
listings.description:
This PhD will develop digital twins that use noise and vibration measurements to estimate hidden indicators of robot performance. Combining physics-based modelling, sensing and state estimation, the project will create virtual sensing technologies that improve the efficiency, reliability and sustainability of future robotic systems in support of the UK's net-zero ambitions.

Robots are playing an increasingly important role in manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, infrastructure inspection and autonomous transport. As the UK progresses towards its net-zero ambitions, robotic systems are expected to improve productivity, reduce waste, support sustainable manufacturing and enable the efficient operation of critical infrastructure. To maximise these benefits, robots must operate efficiently, reliably and safely throughout their lifetime.

However, many quantities that determine robot performance remain difficult or expensive to measure directly. Examples include cutting forces in robotic surgery, wheel-ground interactions in autonomous mobile robots, component degradation and energy-loss mechanisms. At the same time, robots naturally generate noise and vibration that contain valuable information about the dynamic processes occurring within the system.

This PhD project will investigate how noise and vibration measurements can be transformed into estimates of robot performance using next-generation digital twins. The successful candidate will develop physics-informed virtual sensing techniques that combine numerical models with sensor measurements using state-estimation and data-assimilation methods. The resulting digital twins will act as virtual sensors, providing estimates of quantities that are difficult or impossible to measure directly.

The developed methods could enable robots to operate more efficiently, reliably and sustainably by improving condition monitoring, reducing maintenance requirements, extending asset life and supporting intelligent control strategies.

The project combines aspects of robotics, structural dynamics, acoustics, sensing, artificial intelligence and digital twins.

You will have access to world-leading experimental facilities and expertise of the Institute of Sound and Vibration Research (ISVR) while contributing to the development of the next generation of intelligent robotic systems.

listings.title: Active Noise Control of Automotive Tyres
listings.summary: Automotive vehicles are becoming heavier with wider tyres to support this weight. Above a speed of around 30 miles per hour, the noise produced by the tyres is the dominant source. Environmental noise pollution is only one design attribute for vehicles and yet is one of the most important attributes relating to people…
listings.description:
Automotive vehicles are becoming heavier with wider tyres to support this weight. Above a speed of around 30 miles per hour, the noise produced by the tyres is the dominant source. Environmental noise pollution is only one design attribute for vehicles and yet is one of the most important attributes relating to people who don't purchase the vehicle but are impacted by it. Society is relying on building homes closer to roads, yet the mitigation methods currently predicted will be limited by the higher vehicle weights. Traditional barriers are also insufficient and take up valuable road space. Instead in this PhD, it is the source of the sound which will be reduced.

This PhD will aim to reduce the environmental noise pollution from automotive tyres using active noise control techniques. This will advance the possible methods used to reduce the impact of vehicles on society. As the tyre rolls on the rough road surface, it vibrates, causing noise to be radiated in all directions. This noise pollution reflects from the road surface, and underside of the vehicle, scattering in a 3D sound field. Due to the shape of the tyre meeting the road surface, the sound can be amplified significantly, which complicates the mitigation.

Reducing the noise has traditionally relied on passive damping methods to wheel arches, however, in this project, you will apply active noise control techniques to reduce the carcass vibration frequencies in a 3D environment. Typically, the cancellation sound field is generated by a loudspeaker, however, this is impractical as it would then cause more sound radiation and pollution in some directions. Instead, a highly novel directional noise generation source will be employed to direct the cancellation sound to exactly the location where the noise is produced, whilst being located away from the tyre surface. This will involve making 3D maps of the sound field using an acoustic camera and creating directional cancellation signals. You will have access to experimental tyre test rigs and vehicles.

Active noise control of the vehicle interior has been successfully implemented to reduce the interior tyre noise, but this PhD research is focused on the impact on society and the potential reductions which can be achieved. The directional sound source will be used to generate sound waves which are focused in a tight beam, which cannot be achieved with traditional speaker designs which radiate unwanted sound in all directions. listings.title: AI-Guided Discovery of Immunotherapy Resistance Mechanisms
listings.summary: This PhD will investigate strategies to improve immunotherapy efficacy in cancer, integrating single-cell RNA sequencing and machine learning with experimental immunology to understand T-cell exhaustion and the tumour micro-environment. The student will identify and experimentally validate mechanisms of treatment…
listings.description:
This PhD will investigate strategies to improve immunotherapy efficacy in cancer, integrating single-cell RNA sequencing and machine learning with experimental immunology to understand T-cell exhaustion and the tumour micro-environment. The student will identify and experimentally validate mechanisms of treatment resistance, informing the development of more effective cancer immunotherapies.

A major challenge for cancer immunotherapy is understanding why immune cells that can eliminate cancer in the laboratory often become ineffective within cancers in patients. This PhD will investigate the mechanisms underlying this loss of function and identify strategies to improve the effectiveness of immunotherapies such as chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy.

Jointly supervised by experts in machine learning/data-driven biology and cancer immunotherapy, the project offers a distinctive opportunity to develop expertise across both computational and experimental research. The student will develop advanced skills in analysing and integrating single-cell RNA sequencing datasets from tumours to identify cellular states associated with treatment resistance. They will apply, critically evaluate and adapt machine-learning and gene-regulatory network approaches to predict interventions capable of maintaining or restoring effective anti-tumour immunity.

Crucially, these predictions will not remain in silico. The student will take discoveries from computational prediction through to experimental validation, testing the most promising candidates experimentally using cell culture, multi-colour flow cytometry, functional immunological assays and molecular biology techniques. The project will therefore provide unusually broad training spanning computational biology, machine learning, immunology and molecular

biology, equipping the student to work at the increasingly important interface between data science and experimental biomedical research

The supervisory teams have strong track records in translating research towards clinical application, commercialisation and collaboration with the pharmaceutical industry, providing exposure to potential careers across academia, biotechnology, healthcare and industry.

This fully funded studentship is reserved for international students, with applications from Malaysians and Singaporeans particularly encouraged.

listings.title: Safety validation and assurance of autonomous navigation systems
listings.summary: How can we demonstrate that autonomous navigation systems are safe within their intended operating conditions? This project will develop Operational Design Domain (ODD)-based safety validation and assurance methods. it will use representative, critical and degraded scenarios to evaluate system performance, identify…
listings.description:
How can we demonstrate that autonomous navigation systems are safe within their intended operating conditions? This project will develop Operational Design Domain (ODD)-based safety validation and assurance methods. it will use representative, critical and degraded scenarios to evaluate system performance, identify operational safety boundaries, and generate credible evidence supporting the safe deployment of autonomous ships.

Autonomous navigation systems must operate safely across complex and changing maritime environments. Demonstrating this safety is challenging because it is impossible to test every combination of traffic, environmental and system conditions that an autonomous ship may encounter. New approaches are therefore needed to determine whether sufficient evidence exists to support safe operation within a defined Operational Design Domain (ODD).

This project will develop ODD-based methods for the safety validation and assurance of autonomous navigation systems. The research will investigate how maritime operational conditions can be systematically represented as a scenario space covering traffic situations, environmental conditions, vessel behaviour and autonomous system states. Historical maritime data will be used to identify representative navigation scenarios, while simulation-based methods will be developed to generate critical, rare, boundary and degraded scenarios that may expose system vulnerabilities.

The project will investigate how autonomous navigation performance can be evaluated across these scenarios using safety-related measures such as collision avoidance, vessel separation, navigational risk, international regulations for preventing collisions at sea (COLREGs) compliance and successful fallback. Particular attention will be given to identifying the boundaries within which autonomous functions can operate safely and understanding how safety performance changes as conditions approach or exceed those boundaries.

The research will further examine how scenario coverage, system performance, uncertainty analysis and validation results can be transformed into structured safety evidence. Safety-case approaches may be used to establish traceable relationships between safety claims, operational risks, test scenarios and supporting evidence. listings.title: Risk-aware decision-making under uncertainty for autonomous navigation
listings.summary: How should an autonomous ship respond when navigational risk is uncertain and continuously changing? This project will develop risk-aware decision-making methods that combine predicted traffic situations, navigational risk, uncertainty, international regulations for preventing collisions at sea (COLREGs) and…
listings.description:
How should an autonomous ship respond when navigational risk is uncertain and continuously changing? This project will develop risk-aware decision-making methods that combine predicted traffic situations, navigational risk, uncertainty, international regulations for preventing collisions at sea (COLREGs) and operational constraints to support safe navigation decisions, including collision avoidance, operational adjustment, supervision and fallback.

Autonomous ships must make navigation decisions in complex environments where the behaviour of other vessels, future traffic developments and associated risks are uncertain. Avoiding collision alone is not sufficient: decisions must also consider navigational rules, operational constraints, safety margins and the consequences of uncertainty.

This project will investigate risk-aware decision-making for safe autonomous navigation. The research will explore how dynamic navigational risk can be incorporated explicitly into autonomous decision processes, enabling navigation actions to respond to both the estimated level of risk and confidence in that assessment.

The project will investigate decision-making during vessel encounters, including crossing, head-on and overtaking situations. Potential actions may include maintaining course and speed, altering course, reducing speed or increasing separation. The research will examine how these decisions can balance navigational safety, COLREGs compliance and operational efficiency, particularly when the intentions or future trajectories of surrounding vessels remain uncertain.

The project will also consider situations in which continued autonomous operation may no longer be appropriate. Methods will be investigated for linking changing risk conditions to operational responses such as increased safety margins, function degradation, remote supervision, mode switching or fallback. The project will advance autonomous navigation from collision avoidance towards risk-informed decision-making, contributing to safer and more explainable autonomous ship operations under complex and uncertain conditions.

listings.title: Dynamic risk intelligence for safe autonomous shipping under changing operational conditions
listings.summary: How can autonomous ships recognise when changing traffic, environmental or system conditions make continued autonomous operation unsafe? This project will develop dynamic risk intelligence methods to assess operational conditions against autonomous ship capability boundaries, identify evolving risk states, and support…
listings.description:
How can autonomous ships recognise when changing traffic, environmental or system conditions make continued autonomous operation unsafe? This project will develop dynamic risk intelligence methods to assess operational conditions against autonomous ship capability boundaries, identify evolving risk states, and support explainable decisions on continued operation, degradation, fallback and contingency.

Maritime autonomous surface ships must operate safely in environments that change continuously. Traffic density, weather, visibility, communication availability, sensor performance and autonomous system capability can all affect whether an autonomous ship or individual autonomous function remains able to operate safely. A key challenge is therefore to determine when autonomous operation can continue and when intervention, degradation or fallback becomes necessary.

This project will develop dynamic risk intelligence methods for safe autonomous shipping. The research will investigate how Operational Envelopes (OEs) and Operational Design Domains (ODDs) can be represented as capability boundaries for autonomous ships and their functions, and how changing operational conditions can be assessed against these boundaries.

The project will develop methods for modelling the relationships between operational conditions, autonomous functions, vessel interactions and navigational risk. Particular attention will be given to uncertainty and dynamic risk evolution, including transitions between normal, degraded, fallback-required and contingency-required operating states. Potential approaches include probabilistic risk modelling, Bayesian Networks, Dynamic Bayesian Networks, system-theoretic safety analysis and data-driven methods.

The research will also investigate how dynamic risk assessment can be translated into explainable operational information to support decisions such as continued autonomous operation, increased safety margins, function degradation, remote supervision, mode switching and fallback. The proposed methods will be evaluated using representative autonomous navigation scenarios, historical maritime traffic data and simulation-generated scenarios. The research will contribute to risk-aware autonomous navigation and provide methods supporting the safety assurance and future deployment of Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships.

listings.title: Data-driven urban aerodynamics for net-zero cities
listings.summary: This project combines cutting-edge 3D particle tracking, machine learning and fluid mechanics to measure and predict urban airflow around buildings. The research will support safer, healthier and lower-carbon urban environments while providing world-class experimental and computational training.
listings.description:
This project combines cutting-edge 3D particle tracking, machine learning and fluid mechanics to measure and predict urban airflow around buildings. The research will support safer, healthier and lower-carbon urban environments while providing world-class experimental and computational training.

Engineering net-zero cities requires better methods for predicting wind loading, designing ventilation, ensuring pedestrian comfort and mitigating pollutant dispersion in complex urban environments. Current high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods can provide detailed flow information but are often too computationally expensive for design and planning. This project addresses the challenge of obtaining accurate flow and pressure data around buildings using a combination of advanced experiments, physics-informed machine learning and data assimilation.

You'll develop novel object-aware 3D Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) methods based on retroreflective shadowgraph imaging, enabling flow measurements in complex urban geometries with significant visual occlusions. These measurements will be combined with state-of-the-art data assimilation techniques, such as our PIGLET framework, to reconstruct velocity and pressure fields while enforcing known flow physics and quantifying uncertainty. An extension will investigate reduced-order models for predicting unsteady flow and pollutant dispersion using resolvent analysis and Gaussian process regression.

The measurements will be validated against large eddy simulations of urban flows and applied to problems including pedestrian-level wind comfort, natural ventilation and structural wind loading. Improved prediction capability could support reduced embodied carbon in buildings through less conservative wind-loading estimates, improved passive ventilation strategies, and safer, more liveable urban environments.

You'll join a thriving research community of over 50 PhDs, postdoctoral researchers and academics within the Aerodynamics and Flight Mechanics Group. You'll have access to our world-class Centre for Experimental Fluid Mechanics laboratories equipped with state-of-the-art flow diagnostics, which are complemented by our IRIDIS high-performance computing facilities.

listings.summary: The Universities of Bristol, Exeter, Bath, Bath Spa, Bournemouth, Plymouth, Plymouth Marjon and West England form one of the UK’s largest Centres of postgraduate research training for social scientists in fields ranging from economics and human geography to quantitative methodology and psychology
listings.description:
The Universities of Bristol, Exeter, Bath, Bath Spa, Bournemouth, Plymouth, Plymouth Marjon and West England form one of the UK’s largest Centres of postgraduate research training for social scientists in fields ranging from economics and human geography to quantitative methodology and psychology

The Economic and Social Research Council has granted doctoral training partnership status to the collaboration. The South West Doctoral Training Partnership (SWDTP) has been accredited to offer a hub of world-class social sciences research. As one of only 15 Partnerships in the UK, the SWDTP is part of a national network which will train a new generation of social scientists. The SWDTP has been allocated 34 studentships per annum.

The SWDTP offers funding for PhD studentships that are typically 3 years and 3 months plus 3 months ‘Research in Practice’. It also funds a Masters + PhD for applicants without a prior Masters or equivalent professional experience. For applicants with a previous Masters or equivalent professional experience where this does not fully meet the ESRC’s training requirements set out (here), then the student is required to undertake ‘top up’ training during their PhD, which may extend the length of the funding.

Fully-funded ESRC studentships are offered at Exeter through eleven disciplinary pathways that span the social sciences and four innovative interdisciplinary pathways, to offer students the broadest possible approach to their studies with us.

Applicants should read Exeter’s Eligibility Information below and then apply directly to the relevant pathway through the ESRC SWDTP Pathway PhD Studentships Available tab below. Exeter applicants to the SWDTP are not required to submit a second application for a place at the University prior to applying for a SWDTP studentship.

Data Skills: Any proposal using large and complex qualitative and/or quantitative social science datasets within any pathway (bar AQM) can request to be considered for this steer.

Advanced Quantitative Methods: Any proposal using and developing advanced quantitative social science data can apply to the AQM pathway to be considered for this steer.

Each SWDTP pathway at Exeter University has an identified Masters programme that provides methods training in line with the ESRC’s training requirements. This will typically comprise: i) An introduction to research methods in social science; ii) advanced training in either quantitative or qualitative social science methods;

listings.title: 3D Concrete-Printed Scour Protection for Offshore Wind Foundations
listings.summary: Offshore wind is essential to the UK's transition to clean energy, but the foundations that support wind turbines face a major challenge: scour. Waves and currents can erode the seabed surrounding foundations, threatening long-term stability and leading to costly maintenance and repair. As offshore wind farms continue…
listings.description:
Offshore wind is essential to the UK's transition to clean energy, but the foundations that support wind turbines face a major challenge: scour. Waves and currents can erode the seabed surrounding foundations, threatening long-term stability and leading to costly maintenance and repair. As offshore wind farms continue to expand into deeper waters and more demanding environments, developing effective and sustainable scour protection solutions has become increasingly important. This PhD project will explore how 3D concrete printing can revolutionise scour protection for offshore wind infrastructure.

Unlike conventional solutions that rely on large quantities of rock armour or standard concrete units, additive manufacturing enables the creation of complex, optimised geometries that can better control water flow, reduce seabed erosion, and minimise material use. Working at the intersection of renewable energy, advanced manufacturing, materials engineering and marine science, the project will investigate how innovative 3D-printed designs interact with waves, currents and sediments.

Through a combination of experimental research and engineering analysis, the student will develop and evaluate next-generation scour protection concepts that improve performance while reducing environmental impact.

The outcomes of this research could help increase the resilience, efficiency and sustainability of offshore wind farms by reducing maintenance requirements, extending asset lifetimes and lowering the material demands of scour protection systems. More broadly, the project will demonstrate how digital manufacturing can contribute to the delivery of smarter and more sustainable offshore infrastructure, supporting the continued growth of renewable energy worldwide.

The successful candidate will join Loughborough University, one of the UK's leading engineering institutions, and have access to its world-leading expertise in construction materials, advanced manufacturing and offshore infrastructure. The project will leverage Loughborough's internationally recognised 3D concrete printing facilities, providing a unique opportunity to develop, manufacture and test innovative scour protection solutions at the forefront of research and industrial practice.

listings.title: Digital Social Licence for Offshore Wind: Misinformation, Public Discourse and Coastal Community Resilience
listings.summary: Offshore wind is central to the UK energy transition. Its long-term success depends on more than technology and infrastructure. Public trust, community resilience and the quality of public discussion also matter. Coastal communities increasingly encounter offshore wind through digital spaces including local Facebook…
listings.description:
Offshore wind is central to the UK energy transition. Its long-term success depends on more than technology and infrastructure. Public trust, community resilience and the quality of public discussion also matter. Coastal communities increasingly encounter offshore wind through digital spaces including local Facebook groups, community forums, regional news and national social media. These spaces bring together information, misinformation, local concerns, community identity and wider debates about energy transition.

This PhD will investigate how offshore wind is discussed online across different stages of the wind farm lifecycle. These will include new development proposals, operation and maintenance, life extension and decommissioning. The research will use a mixed methods computational social science approach. It will combine netnographic research with advanced computational analysis and large-scale analysis of social media and other digital data.

The student will explore themes including misinformation, emotional framing, trust, digital social licence and community resilience. The research will compare discussion within selected UK coastal communities with wider national debate.

The project offers an opportunity to work at the intersection of digital society, computational social science and sustainable energy transitions. It will generate new insight into how digital public discourse can shape community perceptions of offshore wind. The findings will be relevant to developers, policymakers, local authorities, community organisations and other stakeholders working to support socially sustainable energy transitions.

The programme includes a structured training component delivered through compressed teaching weeks during the six-months, with CDT funding covering travel costs for students based at partner universities. The project will also provide additional specialist methods training opportunities tailored to the student’s experience and the developing research, including advanced social media analysis, computational social science, digital ethnography/netnography and responsible digital research.

listings.summary: Offshore wind is at the heart of the UK's transition to a clean-energy future. listings.description:
Offshore wind is at the heart of the UK's transition to a clean-energy future. As wind farms move into deeper waters, engineers and scientists face new challenges that have never been encountered at scale before. Understanding how these complex ocean conditions affect renewable-energy infrastructure is essential for developing safe, sustainable and cost-effective technologies for the next generation of offshore wind energy.

This PhD offers the opportunity to work at the intersection of fluid dynamics, computer vision, big data and renewable energy, to explore the dynamics behind these fluid-water interactions. You will develop and apply cutting-edge experimental and data-driven techniques to investigate how complex water motions interact with offshore wind structures under controlled conditions.

Working in partnership with leading manufacturers of Optical Measurement Systems, you will combine advanced established imaging technologies (PIV and LIF) with novel approaches (Tomographic BOS) to explore new ways of visualising and quantifying complex flow phenomena. The project will generate unique datasets and provide insights that can help accelerate the deployment of both fixed and floating offshore wind technologies.

This research project will equip the candidate with highly competitive skills in experimental fluid mechanics, scientific programming, image analysis, big-data processing and scientific visualisation. You will learn first-hand how image-based data acquisition systems work and acquire the skills to develop physics-informed AI tools, extract knowledge from large and complex datasets, and tackle real-world engineering problems with direct relevance to the global energy transition.

This project is particularly suited to applicants with a strong background in mathematics, physics, engineering, or a related quantitative discipline, and an enthusiasm for computational methods, data analysis, machine vision and solving challenging scientific problems. It is desired that the candidate possesses strong aptitude for laboratory work, so an aptitude for independent work and strong planning skills are expected.

listings.title: Predicting Safety Risks in Offshore Wind
listings.summary: Can organisations identify safety risks before accidents happen? Help develop the next generation of proactive safety management in offshore wind. Offshore wind is one of the world's fastest-growing renewable energy sectors.
listings.description:
Can organisations identify safety risks before accidents happen? Help develop the next generation of proactive safety management in offshore wind. Offshore wind is one of the world's fastest-growing renewable energy sectors.

As the industry expands, organisations are collecting increasing amounts of information on incidents, near misses, workforce wellbeing and operational performance. However, despite this wealth of data, many safety interventions remain reactive, responding to problems in isolation after they occur rather than preventing and addressing them systematically in the first place.

This PhD project will explore how organisations can use existing workforce, safety and operational data to identify early warning signs of emerging risks and support more proactive approaches to safety management. Working closely with industry partners, you will investigate leading indicators and causation of safety performance, examine how organisations assess and respond to risk, and develop practical approaches to support evidence-based decision-making.

The project will draw on a range of methods, including data analysis, interviews, workshops and stakeholder engagement. The findings will help organisations improve safety performance, strengthen organisational learning and support the development of healthier, safer and more resilient workplaces across offshore wind. This studentship forms part of the Workforce Health, Safety and Wellbeing Research Cluster, a group of three interconnected PhD projects examining workforce safety, wellbeing and resilience in offshore wind.

listings.title: Multimodal learning and sensor fusion for vessel monitoring using vision and underwater acoustics
listings.summary: How can underwater sound and shore-based vision work together to monitor vessels more effectively? This PhD explores machine learning and multimodal fusion to improve vessel detection, characterisation and tracking in rivers and coastal waters, and to enhance acoustic monitoring using knowledge gained from vision when…
listings.description:
How can underwater sound and shore-based vision work together to monitor vessels more effectively? This PhD explores machine learning and multimodal fusion to improve vessel detection, characterisation and tracking in rivers and coastal waters, and to enhance acoustic monitoring using knowledge gained from vision when cameras can no longer observe.

Cameras provide information about vessel positions, sizes, types, numbers, speeds and directions of travel. Underwater sound provides complementary evidence beyond camera coverage and when visual observations are unreliable. How can these modalities improve maritime monitoring together, and how can visual knowledge strengthen acoustic monitoring?

You will develop machine learning and sensor fusion methods combining hydrophone arrays, shore-based cameras and, where available, Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. The research will investigate when multimodal sensing outperforms individual modalities, how knowledge and prior information gained from multimodal observations can enhance acoustic-only monitoring, and how uncertainty associated with each modality can inform vessel localisation and tracking.

Potential approaches include cross-modal representation learning, knowledge transfer between modalities, uncertainty-aware fusion, and probabilistic tracking informed by vessel characteristics and motion. Particular attention will be given to associating acoustic and visual observations and maintaining robust monitoring as sensing conditions and sensor availability change.

Initial studies will focus on rivers and constrained coastal navigation routes, using known sensor locations and waterway geometry to support acoustic localisation. Multimodal, vision-only and acoustic-only approaches will be evaluated for vessel detection, characterisation and tracking, testing robustness to degraded sensing and missing modalities, and generalisation to previously unseen vessels.

You will build on an existing field dataset, with hydrophone arrays, cameras and the University of Southampton’s Iridis high-performance computing facilities available. Further field measurements can extend the dataset. The supervisory team brings complementary expertise in underwater acoustics, signal processing and maritime engineering, supporting research with applications in waterway management and future autonomous vessel operations.
