listings.title: Wake, Mix, Repeat: Engineering the Environmental Footprint of Deep-Water Wind
listings.summary: The future of UK offshore wind farms lies in deep waters, a dynamic physical environment where water column density varies with depth. Understanding how currents generate foundation wakes in stratified environments is recognised as critical to the sustainability of £75bn of immediate offshore wind development.…
listings.description:
The future of UK offshore wind farms lies in deep waters, a dynamic physical environment where water column density varies with depth. Understanding how currents generate foundation wakes in stratified environments is recognised as critical to the sustainability of £75bn of immediate offshore wind development. However, a key barrier is the sector's lack of knowledge regarding the environmental footprint of offshore wind farms across a stratified water column. This doctoral studentship, fully funded by the EPSRC CDT in Offshore Wind Energy Sustainability and Resilience, offers an exceptional opportunity for a high-calibre graduate to directly impact this challenge.

You will benefit from developing a rare dual-track skill set: hands-on physical experimental fluid dynamics, in a specialised tow tank using advanced multi-sensor arrays; and state-of-the-art computational fluid dynamics, using open-source Large-Eddy Simulation. This pairing will allow you to explore how ocean mixing, which controls marine ecosystem dynamics, is artificially forced by offshore wind farm layout configuration. These outputs will help shape how Environmental Impact Assessments are made for future offshore wind. Supported through optional secondments with world-leading academic or industry collaborators, you will graduate with advanced technical expertise in big data management, advanced signal processing, high-performance computing, and complex numerical simulation.

By applying fluid mechanics to understand physical and ecosystem dynamics, you can directly support a sustainable offshore wind future.

Your technical training will bridge hands-on physical experimentation in specialized test facilities and state-of-the-art numerical modelling using open-source Large-Eddy Simulation (LES). You will gain advanced competencies in high-performance computing (HPC), big data management, and complex signal processing, backed by specialized workshops (for example, OpenFOAM CFD - Theories and Practical Applications) and international programs like the Joint EU-US Summer School on High-Performance Computing. Your development will be further supported by dedicated academic and pastoral mentoring, bespoke external mentoring, fully funded attendance at specialised research forums like the Wind Energy Science Conference (WESC) or the APS Division of Fluid Dynamics Annual Meeting, and optional secondments with academic and industry partners. listings.summary: The Darwin Trust of Edinburgh funds a number of Scholarships each year to study for a PhD in Microbiology in the Biosciences Graduate Research School.
listings.description:
The Darwin Trust of Edinburgh funds a number of Scholarships each year to study for a PhD in Microbiology in the Biosciences Graduate Research School.

The Darwin Trust of Edinburgh funds a number of Scholarships each year to study for a PhD in Microbiology in the Biosciences Graduate Research School, with supervisors who are part of the Institute of Microbiology and Infection at The University of Birmingham, U.K. Scholarships are available to graduates from non-UK countries from October each year and cover full tuition fees for 3 years and a maintenance grant for 4 years.

Students must be of the highest calibre and normally hold a First or Upper Second-Class honours degree or its equivalent.

A studentship may not be held by a student who is already a graduate of the University of Birmingham. A studentship may not be awarded to an applicant who is eligible for the home/UK tuition fee.

Applicants will normally have obtained either their first (Bachelors) degree, or their first Masters degree, no more than five years prior to the closing date for applications to the Trust.

A studentship will only be awarded to an individual who has been accepted as a postgraduate student by the University of Birmingham. A student who has already started a PhD at the University of Birmingham, no matter how this has been funded, may not be awarded a Darwin Trust studentship.

Send your CV and a covering letter to a supervisor in the School of Biosciences or Institute of Microbiology and Infection with whom you would like to work, explaining that you would like to apply for a Darwin studentship. They will review your application and may then ask your referees for a letter of recommendation. Research designed to inform the next global IUCN Red List assessment of reef-building corals and the biodiversity indicators that use them.

A global project, working alongside an international network of the world’s coral experts, including the IUCN SSC Coral Specialist Group, ZSL and Red List practitioners.

Reef-building corals are among the most threatened animals on Earth: 44% of species assessed through the IUCN Red List are now at high risk of extinction, with climate change and myriad interacting local threats as drivers. Their IUCN Red List assessments guide where conservation effort and funding go and feed high-level indicators use to track progress under the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

Yet for almost every coral species, assessors must judge extinction risk without direct population data. Filling this information gap for nearly 900 species before the next assessment cycle is unfeasible, and therefore a more strategic approach is needed. The questions that matter most then, is which gaps should be prioritised to reduce uncertainty and increase trust in the use of other proxies of decline.

Identifying genes associated with tolerance of hypoxia and control of symbiotic microbes, with relevance to predicting climate-change resilience and to potential biotechnological applications (biosensing and antimicrobial peptides).

Joining an interdisciplinary team spanning marine biology, evolutionary genomics and molecular biology, with opportunities to present at conferences and support from the University of Portsmouth Graduate School Development Programme.

Deep-sea hydrothermal vents are among the most extreme habitats for animal life, with steep gradients in temperature, oxygen, sulphide and heavy metals. Decapod crustaceans have colonised vents independently on several occasions, forming intimate symbioses with chemosynthetic microbes and evolving to tolerate chronic hypoxia and chemically reducing conditions. As climate change drives ocean deoxygenation and the expansion of oxygen minimum zones, these animals offer natural models for understanding which species and mechanisms are likely to prove resilient, as well as a potential source of novel biomolecules.

Pioneering the understanding of tectono-volatile cycle in the early-earth retrieved from the information obtained in ancient apatite inclusions in zircon.

Plate tectonics exerts a first order control on Earth’s volatile cycles and habitability. Atmospherically altered surface materials are recycled to the mantle via subduction, while volatiles from the mantle are liberated to the atmosphere via volcanism. This cycle regulates much of Earth’s climate, ocean levels and metallogenetic processes within the continental crust. However, it is uncertain when the balance between volatile cycles and plate tectonics started to operate on Earth. This PhD offers a unique approach using novel techniques that simultaneously measures volatile and elemental contents in apatite inclusions shielded in zircon grains to try and characterise the Earth’s volatile cycle in key tectonic settings. The evidence for Earth's volatile evolution using inclusions trapped in zircons will then be applied to magmas that crystallised more than 3 billion years ago, shedding light into the development of plate tectonics on Earth.

In exceptional cases, we may consider equivalent professional experience and/or qualifications. English language proficiency at a minimum of IELTS band 6.5 with no component score below 6.0.

Developing an innovative multi-strand child-led and adult-led methodology for examining water-related knowledge and behaviours.

This project seeks to deconstruct environmental habit forming in early childhood in order to develop an effective early years water literacy programme to help address the real-world problem of water scarcity and damage to ecologically sensitive and globally unique freshwater environments.

Water availability in the UK is spatially uneven, and climate change is increasing water scarcity, particularly in Eastern and Southern England. The Environment Agency warns of an estimated 5 billion litre per day deficit by 2055. Water abstraction by water companies such as Portsmouth Water and Southern Water to meet demand is known to impact ecologically sensitive and globally unique chalk streams in Hampshire.

The UK’s water industry trade body recognises the UK’s low water literacy levels especially amongst younger age brackets and this has been identified as a blocker to sustainable water use.

Current education programmes rely on the theory of rational choice, linking behaviour change to the acquisition of new information. However, recent work in the nascent field of water literacy calls for greater attention to how social and emotional components (i.e. values, social norms, ethics, cultural background) shape people’s reasoning and decision-making in relation to sustainable water use.

UoP research demonstrates the importance of habit formation within childhood in shaping the water use of HE students. Yet research is needed on how and why such habits form. Interdisciplinary research: This project bridges endocrinology, pharmacology, and molecular signalling of GPCRs to uncover new mechanisms of hormone regulation in diabetes.

Metabolic complications associated with some commonly prescribed medications, such as antipsychotic drugs, represent an important and growing clinical challenge. However, the cellular mechanisms underlying the metabolic side effects of these medications, and why some individuals or metabolic pathways may respond differently to therapeutic intervention, remain incompletely understood.

This PhD will investigate how key signalling pathways within pancreatic endocrine cells interact to regulate hormone secretion and metabolic function. The project will combine molecular and cellular pharmacology with studies in human pancreatic islets to investigate receptor signalling, pathway interactions and their consequences for endocrine function.

The successful candidate will use a multidisciplinary range of approaches, including live-cell biosensors, receptor signalling assays (BRET, nanoBRET, luciferase complementation), pharmacological tools, molecular approaches and hormone secretion assays. Studies using human pancreatic islets will provide an important translational component, allowing mechanisms identified in cellular models to be investigated in a physiologically relevant system.

The project will provide training in GPCR pharmacology, cell signalling, live-cell imaging, experimental pharmacology and analysis of human islet function, alongside broader research and transferable skills.

Using eye tracking technology to learn more about how people engage with police appeals for information, such as missing persons appeals, and what strategies they use when on the lookout for missing persons.

Understanding more about how these appeals are processed will allow us to make recommendations on the type of information that should be included in missing persons appeals.

In the UK alone, someone is recorded missing every two minutes, adding up to over 300,000 incidents a year; two-thirds of which involving people under 18 years of age (National Crime Agency, 2023). When a person goes missing, the police or other non-governmental organizations usually distribute appeals asking the public to be on the lookout for that individual and to report any sighting to the authorities. Given the documented large numbers of missing and wanted people, it is critically important that we maximise the likelihood that these alerts will be effective. To do this, it is important to understand the type of information that people engage with when presented with missing persons appeals (i.e., during encoding), as well as the type of information people engage with while looking for missing persons in different contexts (i.e., during testing). We will use the innovative method of looking at participants’ eye gaze behaviour to advance understanding of how public members engage with different missing persons appeals.

Eye-tracking technology will be used to measure the visual attention and engagement patterns of participants as they view different types of missing persons appeals. Audio books and stories are an increasingly accessible form of screen-free entertainment for young children (Arif, Clark & Picton, 2026). Audiobooks allow children to access complex narratives and vocabulary without requiring them to decode written text. This may be particularly valuable during the early years of primary education, when children's reading abilities are still developing, but audiobooks may also provide an additional source of language exposure, cognitive stimulation and relaxation for fluent readers.

There is substantial evidence that children's engagement with books and stories supports language development (see Dickinson et al, 2012, for a review), but much of this research concerns adult-mediated reading or shared reading, rather than children's independent listening to audiobooks. Currently, it is unclear whether audiobook listening provides measurable developmental benefits. This PhD will:

Examine how audiobooks fit into children’s free time alongside other activities, and what parents/guardians see as the benefits, drawbacks and barriers to use.

Examine correlates of recreational audiobook use, such as vocabulary, focused attention, formal educational outcomes and wellbeing.

Test whether a 12-week audiobook intervention improves children’s outcomes relative to reading physical books or watching equivalent video-based stories.

The project will involve building links with schools, conducting qualitative and quantitative research with parents/guardians and children, presenting work at conferences, publishing the research in peer-reviewed journals, and disseminating findings to teachers and parents. The findings of this project have the potential to benefit children, families and schools.

Investigating how patient-reported, functional and biomechanical outcomes relate to meaningful quality of life for those with limb difference.

Working alongside leading researchers, NHS clinicians and people with limb difference to develop and evaluate patient-centred approaches to measuring recovery.

Lower-limb difference can significantly affect mobility, independence, physical activity and quality of life. Whilst prosthetic rehabilitation aims to restore function and support individuals in returning to meaningful activities, understanding what constitutes successful quality of life, and in turn recovery, remains a challenge. Traditional clinical assessments provide valuable information about physical function and walking performance but may not fully capture the experiences and priorities of people living with limb difference.

This PhD offers an exciting opportunity to bridge the gap between what matters to patients and what we measure in rehabilitation. By bringing together patient-reported experiences, clinical function and objective biomechanics, the project aims to advance how meaningful recovery is understood, assessed and supported within prosthetic rehabilitation.

The successful candidate will undertake a mixed-methods research programme, working directly with people with limb difference and healthcare professionals. Research activities will include patient-centred co-design, longitudinal assessments of recovery, instrumented gait analysis, wearable technology and clinical functional testing. Findings will inform an integrated approach to measuring quality of life and recovery, culminating in a proof-of-concept study within a specialist NHS prosthetic rehabilitation centre.

This project aims to develop a computational framework combining computer vision, computer graphics, and machine learning to accelerate and improve the design and simulation of camera lenses. Traditional lens design is slow, labour-intensive, and relies on expert-led iterative methods. We propose instead to learn mappings between lens design parameters and image-quality metrics using data-driven, differentiable rendering models. The framework will support two modes: forward simulation (predicting the imaging output of candidate lens configurations) and inverse design (proposing lens architectures to meet a target imaging/perceptual objective).

We are seeking a highly motivated and technically strong candidate with a background in computer science, electronic engineering, applied mathematics, physics, or a closely related discipline.

Excellent programming skills in Python and/or C/C++, with experience using machine learning frameworks such as PyTorch or TensorFlow.

Familiarity with rendering, simulation, or physics-based modelling (e.g., ray tracing, differentiable rendering, optics, or photometric modelling) is desirable.

We particularly welcome applicants who are excited about translating cutting-edge AI research into real-world engineering systems through close collaboration with industry. Strong problem-solving ability, creativity, and the capacity to work both independently and within a collaborative research team are essential.

Prior experience with optical systems, inverse problems, generative models, or high-performance computing would be advantageous but is not required.

This is a fully funded PhD studentship opportunity to help advance our understanding of EIPH, a serious welfare issue for performance horses with particular focus on racing Thoroughbred’s. The successful candidate will join a vibrant and nurturing group of senior and early career academics with well-established clinical and research experience in equine veterinary medicine, biomarker and cellular fields.

This project sits at the cutting edge of equine biomedical research and aims to transform our understanding of a condition that significantly impacts racehorse welfare and performance. Building on the supervisory group's emerging molecular insights into EIPH, the project will explore microvasulaturedysfunction in the initiation and progression of disease, with the ultimate goal of identifying novel therapeutic targets and strategies to improve clinical outcomes. The successful candidate will develop skills in 3D cell culture models, multi-omics and more.

We are seeking a highly motivated and curious candidate with a strong interest in translational veterinary research. The ideal applicant will bring enthusiasm for interdisciplinary science, a willingness to engage with both laboratory and clinically relevant research, and a commitment to improving animal health and welfare. Experience in cell biology, vascular biology, or molecular techniques would be advantageous, but above all, we are looking for someone with drive, critical thinking skills, and a passion for discovery.

Exercise-induced pulmonary haemorrhage (EIPH) affects 50–75% of racehorses in fast work and is a major cause of poor performance and, in severe cases, sudden death. Despite its high prevalence, the mechanisms driving disease onset and progression remain poorly understood, limiting effective treatment options.

EIPH shares features with the human condition pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), where dysfunction of vascular support cells—pericytes—drives pathology. Pericytes play a key role in maintaining microvascular stability and lung integrity, yet their role in EIPH has not been explored. This project will provide the first comprehensive investigation of pericytes in equine EIPH, with the aim of identifying novel therapeutic targets to improve racehorse health and welfare. listings.title: PhD Engineering Safer Healthcare Water Systems: Evaluating Cold Water Recirculation for Water Quality and Pathogen Control
listings.summary: Do you want to help shape the future design of safer and more sustainable healthcare buildings through cutting-edge engineering research? listings.description:
Do you want to help shape the future design of safer and more sustainable healthcare buildings through cutting-edge engineering research? We are seeking an ambitious PhD candidate to investigate the role of cold water recirculation systems in healthcare buildings and their implications for water quality, infection prevention, and sustainable water management

At the Institute for Sustainable Built Environment (ISBE) at Heriot-Watt University, this exciting project will address a critical and emerging challenge facing healthcare providers. Healthcare water systems must deliver safe drinking water while minimising the risk of waterborne infections. Current guidance emphasises maintaining cold water temperatures below 20°C and reducing stagnation to limit the growth of opportunistic premise plumbing pathogens (OPPPs), including Legionella pneumophila, non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

As healthcare organisations pursue sustainability and Net Zero objectives, cold water recirculation systems are receiving increasing attention. These systems have the potential to improve water turnover, reduce water age, minimise flushing requirements, and decrease water wastage. However, there is currently limited scientific evidence to support their widespread adoption within healthcare buildings.

While recirculation may reduce stagnation, it may also introduce unintended consequences, including heat gain, disinfectant decay, biofilm formation, and conditions that favour microbial growth. Understanding these competing mechanisms is essential in healthcare environments where infection prevention is paramount and patient populations are particularly vulnerable.

Working in collaboration with NHS Scotland Assure, this PhD project will provide one of the first comprehensive evaluations of cold water recirculation systems within NHS healthcare facilities. The research will combine engineering analysis, environmental monitoring, operational data assessment, and healthcare infrastructure investigations to determine whether these systems provide a net benefit or introduce additional risks.

The successful candidate will undertake a national assessment of cold water recirculation systems across NHS Health Boards, examining system design, operation, maintenance practices, and performance. The project will involve analysing Building Management System (BMS) data, temperature monitoring records, and dedicated logging campaigns to evaluate operational effect

Are you interested in improving healthcare water quality through innovative engineering research? We are seeking an outstanding PhD candidate to investigate how pipework materials and commissioning practices influence water quality in healthcare buildings, helping to shape future NHS guidance and improve patient safety.

At the Institute for Sustainable Built Environment (ISBE) at Heriot-Watt University, this exciting project sits at the intersection of public health engineering, water quality science, and healthcare infrastructure. Safe and reliable water systems are essential within healthcare facilities, where water quality can directly affect both clinical operations and vulnerable patient populations.

Modern healthcare buildings utilise a wide range of metallic and polymeric pipework materials. These materials can interact with water in complex ways, releasing organic compounds, additives, metals, particulates, and other substances, particularly during system commissioning and the early stages of operation. Although flushing procedures are routinely carried out before buildings are handed over, there remains limited scientific understanding of how effective these practices are in stabilising water quality and reducing material-derived contaminants.

Working in collaboration with NHS Scotland Assure, this project will investigate the relationships between pipework materials, environmental conditions, commissioning procedures, and water quality outcomes. The research will address important questions surrounding material selection, flushing effectiveness, and the long-term performance of healthcare water systems.

The successful candidate will undertake laboratory-based investigations to characterise commonly specified healthcare pipework materials and evaluate their physical and chemical properties. The project will explore how material composition, ageing, surface characteristics, water temperature, stagnation periods, hydraulic conditions, and other operational factors influence the release of contaminants into drinking water.

A major component of the research will involve quantifying material leaching under representative healthcare operating conditions. The candidate will develop experimental approaches to assess how different pipework materials behave over time and identify the variables that most strongly influence water quality performance.

The project will also evaluate current commissioning and flushing practices used within healthcare const

listings.title: PhD Engineering Safer Healthcare Water Systems: Tackling Opportunistic Waterborne Pathogens
listings.summary: Are you passionate about improving public health through innovative engineering solutions? listings.description:
Are you passionate about improving public health through innovative engineering solutions? We are seeking an outstanding PhD candidate to undertake interdisciplinary research to investigate how healthcare water systems can be designed and operated to minimise the risk of opportunistic premise plumbing pathogens (OPPPs). This research will help create safer healthcare environments for some of society’s most vulnerable people.

At the Institute for Sustainable Built Environment (ISBE) at Heriot-Watt University, we are offering an exciting opportunity to undertake research at the interface of public health engineering, water microbiology, and healthcare infrastructure. This project will address a critical challenge facing healthcare providers worldwide: the persistence of opportunistic pathogens within building water systems and the associated risk of healthcare-associated infections.

OPPPs, including Legionella pneumophila, non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, can colonise plumbing networks, storage vessels, fixtures, and outlets, where they proliferate within biofilms and water systems. While current guidance largely focuses on controlling individual organisms, there is increasing recognition that broader engineering approaches are needed to reduce the risk posed by the full spectrum of waterborne pathogens. The challenge is further compounded by modern healthcare buildings increasingly incorporating water-saving technologies, low-flow fixtures, and complex plumbing configurations that may inadvertently promote water stagnation and microbial growth.

Working in collaboration with NHS Scotland Assure, this PhD project will investigate the relationship between water system design and the emergence, persistence, and transmission of OPPPs within healthcare environments. listings.title: Intelligent maritime situational awareness and risk assessment for autonomous shipping
listings.summary: How can autonomous ships understand complex maritime traffic and recognise emerging navigational risks? This project will investigate intelligent maritime situational awareness using Automatic Identification System (AIS) trajectories and video, focusing on vessel behaviour, traffic interactions, trajectory prediction…
listings.description:
How can autonomous ships understand complex maritime traffic and recognise emerging navigational risks? This project will investigate intelligent maritime situational awareness using Automatic Identification System (AIS) trajectories and video, focusing on vessel behaviour, traffic interactions, trajectory prediction and uncertainty-aware risk assessment to identify potentially hazardous situations in busy and constrained waterways.

Safe autonomous navigation depends on more than detecting surrounding vessels. Autonomous systems must understand how vessels are moving, anticipate their interactions and recognise situations that may develop into navigational hazards. Achieving reliable maritime situational awareness remains challenging, particularly in busy waterways where vessel behaviour is uncertain and traffic conditions change rapidly.

This project will investigate intelligent maritime situational awareness and navigational risk assessment for autonomous shipping, using Automatic Identification System (AIS) trajectories and video as complementary sources of maritime traffic information. The research will first examine how vessel observations can be integrated to reconstruct traffic situations and provide reliable information on vessel movements and interactions. It will then investigate methods for understanding vessel behaviour, predicting traffic developments and identifying potentially hazardous encounters, including crossing, overtaking and head-on situations.

A central research challenge will be to account for uncertainty in vessel behaviour, trajectory prediction and risk assessment. The project will explore how these uncertainties influence the identification and assessment of emerging navigational risks and the interpretation of evolving traffic situations.

Potential methods include computer vision, trajectory modelling, machine learning, probabilistic risk assessment and maritime traffic simulation. The research will focus on ports and constrained coastal waters, with evaluation using historical traffic data and representative navigation scenarios. The project will contribute to intelligent maritime situational awareness and risk-informed autonomous navigation, supporting the development of safer maritime autonomous surface ships and future maritime traffic management systems.

Roughening or loss of protection coatings on leading edges causes loss of energy capture or thrust and thus reduces efficiency.

listings.title: Realising upconversion luminescence in supramolecular [d-f] complexes
listings.summary: Do you want to help develop the next generation of medical imaging diagnostics? This PhD project will explore new light-emitting compounds for advanced bioimaging applications. By combining lanthanide and transition-metal complexes, you will develop supramolecular systems capable of converting low-energy light into…
listings.description:
Do you want to help develop the next generation of medical imaging diagnostics? This PhD project will explore new light-emitting compounds for advanced bioimaging applications. By combining lanthanide and transition-metal complexes, you will develop supramolecular systems capable of converting low-energy light into higher-energy emission, known as upconversion.

Upconversion luminescence is a process in which two low-energy near-infrared photons are combined to produce a single higher-energy photon. Because near-infrared light can travel deeper into biological tissue, UC offers exciting opportunities for high-contrast imaging with reduced background interference.

You will design, synthesise, and study new supramolecular systems capable of efficient upconversion, helping to advance the next generation of medical imaging technologies.

The project aims will utilise molecular and supramolecular [d-f] heteropolynuclear assemblies, through the use of transition-metal complexes (e.g. RuII, IrIII), in combination with lanthanide complexes (e.g. YbIII, NdIII). This will include multistep organic synthesis and coordination chemistry of the proposed ligands and complexes, and in-depth photophysical characterisation by investigating fundamental energy-transfer processes via luminescence spectroscopy.

This multidisciplinary project combines inorganic chemistry, supramolecular chemistry, and photophysics, providing training in molecular synthesis, spectroscopy, and advanced optical characterisation techniques. The research has the potential to contribute to new imaging approaches that could improve healthcare outcomes and quality of life.

You will acquire proficiency in synthetic chemistry, coordination chemistry, photoluminescence spectroscopy, and single-crystal X-ray crystallography. You will have full access to a suite of techniques via state-of-the-art facilities including Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy facility, IR, HPLC and Mass-Spectrometry, in addition to world-leading X-ray diffraction facilities.

You will also participate in group-meetings, school seminars and represent the group at conferences. This will give you the opportunity to disseminate your research results with world-leaders in the area. The University of Southampton will give professional training and transferable skills through the PGR Development Hub which provides a suite of training courses and support services which promotes well-being and employability.

listings.title: Multiagent market design for circular industrial symbiosis
listings.summary: This project uses game theory, agent-based modelling and mechanism design to support circular industrial symbiosis, where one company’s waste becomes another’s resource. It investigates economically viable partnerships, fair cost-sharing contracts and effective government incentives. The aim is to develop novel…
listings.description:
This project uses game theory, agent-based modelling and mechanism design to support circular industrial symbiosis, where one company’s waste becomes another’s resource. It investigates economically viable partnerships, fair cost-sharing contracts and effective government incentives. The aim is to develop novel multiagent research methods to reduce waste, improve resource efficiency and sustain long-term, mutually beneficial industrial collaborations.

Industrial symbiosis allows companies to use one another’s waste, by-products or surplus resources, reducing demand for virgin materials and waste disposal. However, technically feasible exchanges do not always become viable partnerships. Firms must agree on how to share benefits and the costs of transportation, treatment and transactions, while responding to uncertainty and changing market conditions, including shifts in prices and demand.

This PhD will develop multiagent market design methods that help establish and sustain these collaborations. Companies will be modelled as autonomous decision makers with different objectives, information and capabilities. The research will connect three complementary directions.

First, game-theoretic models will identify when firms benefit from collaborating and which partnerships can remain stable. Second, mechanism design will support fair cost-sharing, dynamic contracts and incentives that encourage participation and continued cooperation. Third, agent-based modelling will investigate how these arrangements evolve over time and how government policies, including taxes and subsidies, influence their economic and environmental outcomes.

Possible research questions include how to distribute costs when waste quality or supply changes, how to discourage opportunistic behaviour, and how to target public incentives effectively. Evaluation will compare alternative mechanisms and policy scenarios using measures such as participation, stability, resource reuse, emissions and public expenditure.

The project offers scope to develop formal models, computational algorithms and simulation tools. Its precise focus can be shaped around the successful applicant’s interests. It would suit applicants with a background in computer science, artificial intelligence, mathematics, economics, operations research or a related discipline, and an interest in sustainability.

listings.title: Acoustic mode detection using large microphone arrays
listings.summary: Characterising the sound fields measured both inside and outside of aeroengines is essential to support the understanding, prediction and mitigation of future noisy designs. Several challenges exist regarding the design and installation of suitable sensors (e.g., dynamic range and phase response) as well as the…
listings.description:
Characterising the sound fields measured both inside and outside of aeroengines is essential to support the understanding, prediction and mitigation of future noisy designs. Several challenges exist regarding the design and installation of suitable sensors (e.g., dynamic range and phase response) as well as the calibration, data streaming and signal quality assessment of large-channel-count arrays. Improvements are also required to the signal processing beamforming algorithms required to reconstruct the true location, amplitude and directivity of a source when the measured signal has been subjected to decorrelating effects (e.g., flow turbulence scattering, reverberation). This project aims to design, build and test a specific array and beamforming algorithm to support an upcoming Rolls-Royce aeroengine test.

Microphone array measurements are a key technology in the field of aeroacoustics to localise and quantify acoustic sources. Characterising the tonal sound fields generated by rotating components measured by surface-mounted sensors both inside and outside of an aeroengine within a reverberant wind tunnel is a particularly challenging task due to various signal decorrelating effects, including reverberation and turbulent flow-acoustic boundary layer interaction.

In this project, you will develop custom in-duct and on-wall wind tunnel microphone arrays and algorithms to reconstruct the true source levels and far-field directivity of Rolls-Royce’s next generation Ultra-High-Bypass-Ratio turbofan aeroengine.

This PhD project will be hosted within the Rolls-Royce University Technology Centre (UTC) in Propulsion Systems Noise at the Institute of Sound and Vibration Research at the University of Southampton. The UTC is a world-leading hub for aeroacoustics research, offering close collaboration with the global Rolls-Royce noise engineering team in the UK and Germany. This provides a unique opportunity to contribute to real-world challenges and make a tangible impact on the future of quieter, more sustainable aviation.

You will benefit from a dynamic research environment at ISVR, with access to specialist facilities and a vibrant postgraduate community.

You will have opportunity to attend international conferences, workshops and training events, and to engage with researchers and industry experts.

listings.title: Reliable forecasts of multiple sclerosis progression using conformal prediction
listings.summary: Multiple sclerosis progresses differently in every patient, and knowing who is likely to decline fastest could change their care. This project will develop machine learning methods that forecast disability progression with reliable, guaranteed uncertainty, built on conformal prediction and shaped with neurologists at…
listings.description:
Multiple sclerosis progresses differently in every patient, and knowing who is likely to decline fastest could change their care. This project will develop machine learning methods that forecast disability progression with reliable, guaranteed uncertainty, built on conformal prediction and shaped with neurologists at University Hospital Southampton.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) affects more than 150,000 people in the UK, and no two patients follow the same course. Machine learning can forecast disability from clinical scores, MRI and wearable activity data, but a forecast only helps if a clinician knows how far to trust it for that particular patient.

Conformal prediction attaches a range to each forecast that is guaranteed to contain the true outcome at a chosen rate, without assuming the model is correct. Our recent work on a Southampton MS cohort showed that this guarantee can hold on average while hiding which patients are missed.

The project combines new methodology with clinical impact, and is part of a wider programme on reliable machine learning for MS. You'll join a growing team of students working on uncertainty in MS, collaborate closely with the neurology team at University Hospital Southampton, and have access to the University's Iridis supercomputer.

This project will unite distributional and distribution-free uncertainty quantification into one theory, and turn it into reliable tools for high-stakes clinical decisions, such as diagnosing glaucoma and modelling neurodegeneration.

Uncertainty in a prediction has several sources: limited training data, differences between hospitals and patient groups, and the inherent unpredictability of each outcome. Knowing which source dominates tells a clinician what to do next.

distributional approaches, such as hierarchical models, capture the full spread of plausible predictions and show where uncertainty comes from

This is foremost a fundamental research project: most of your time will go into theory and new methods for uncertainty quantification, while applications keep the work grounded. Clinicians at University Hospital Southampton, our collaborators, will help you validate and refine the methods.

listings.title: The attentive ear: AI to decode listening fatigue from wearables
listings.summary: Listening in noisy environments is mentally exhausting, but human physiological responses move at fundamentally different speeds. This project uses multimodal deep learning transformers to combine asynchronous wearable signals (EEG, pupillometry, heart rate, skin conductance and others), creating an AI engine that…
listings.description:
Listening in noisy environments is mentally exhausting, but human physiological responses move at fundamentally different speeds. This project uses multimodal deep learning transformers to combine asynchronous wearable signals (EEG, pupillometry, heart rate, skin conductance and others), creating an AI engine that isolates genuine cognitive listening fatigue from everyday acoustic arousal to power next-generation smart hearables.

Understanding speech in noisy environments demands heavy cognitive effort. However, identifying when a listener crosses from effortful listening into mental exhaustion remains an unsolved challenge. Traditional attempts search for single biomarkers—like pupil dilation, heart rate, or skin sweat. But the human body does not respond in lockstep: eyes react in milliseconds, while autonomic sweat and cardiovascular responses lag by seconds. Standard algorithms struggle to make sense of these misaligned speeds.

This project reframes the problem as an asynchronous multimodal machine learning challenge. You will design and train multimodal transformer architectures and self-supervised models to fuse disparate physiological time series. The primary goal is to disentangle non-specific sensory arousal (e.g., sudden loud noises) from genuine cognitive listening fatigue (working memory depletion).

You will use the world-class acoustic laboratories and calibrated listening booths at the Institute of Sound and Vibration Research (ISVR). You will work with rich, multi-channel physiological datasets (EEG, pupillometry, ECG, galvanic skin response, fNIRS) collected during speech-in-noise paradigms, building neural networks in PyTorch. The resulting algorithms will provide the foundation for closed-loop hearables and assistive listening devices that automatically adapt their signal processing when the user is struggling.

You will receive comprehensive interdisciplinary training bridging modern machine learning and experimental hearing science:

advanced technical & AI training: hands-on training in state-of-the-art deep learning architectures (multimodal transformers, self-supervised learning, sequence modelling) using PyTorch, alongside access and training on the University's High-Performance Computing cluster (Iridis)

experimental and biosignal methods: specialist training in the world-class acoustic facilities of the Institute of Sound and Vibration Research (ISVR), covering calibrated audio reproduction, psychophysical speech testing, ethi

listings.title: Supernovae and dark energy with the Rubin Observatory
listings.summary: This project tackles one of the biggest questions in astrophysics: the nature of dark energy. Using new datasets from the Rubin Observatory, you will analyse tens of thousands of supernovae, develop expertise in data analysis and machine learning, and work at the forefront of international astrophysics.
listings.description:
This project tackles one of the biggest questions in astrophysics: the nature of dark energy. Using new datasets from the Rubin Observatory, you will analyse tens of thousands of supernovae, develop expertise in data analysis and machine learning, and work at the forefront of international astrophysics.

Type Ia supernovae, thermonuclear explosions of white dwarf stars, are astronomers’ best tool to measure distances in the universe and trace its expansion across cosmic time. They were central to the discovery of cosmic acceleration and dark energy. There are now hints from several analyses that dark energy may evolve, challenging the assumption of Einstein’s cosmological constant, the leading theory for its nature.

The project will test this possibility using new samples of type Ia supernovae from the Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Time Domain Extragalactic Survey (TiDES) on 4MOST. Both surveys have just started taking data and will discover and measure tens of thousands of distant supernovae and the galaxies in which they explode, samples 50 times larger than those available today.

This project will provide immediate access to the incoming data, placing you at the forefront as the supernova datasets are assembled. You will pioneer the use of photometric techniques to classify the supernovae and estimate their redshifts, and use the sample to investigate fundamental unknowns in supernova physics: their progenitor systems and links to the stars and dust in their host galaxies. By disentangling how factors such as age and metallicity affect supernova luminosities, and thus inferred distances, the project will underpin future state-of-the-art measurements of dark energy.

You'll be among the first to explore these datasets. You'll gain advanced skills in the analysis of large datasets, statistical modelling, machine learning and AI, alongside exposure to international teamwork and experience in scientific communication, preparing you for careers in astrophysics or any technology-driven or data science industry.

listings.summary: How do we know whether a feature in a 3D image is real? X-ray CT and electron microscopy now shape research in carbon storage, geothermal energy, subsurface hydrogen and critical minerals. Yet the number most often quoted for an image, its voxel size, does not tell us what the instrument and reconstruction actually…
listings.description:
How do we know whether a feature in a 3D image is real? X-ray CT and electron microscopy now shape research in carbon storage, geothermal energy, subsurface hydrogen and critical minerals. Yet the number most often quoted for an image, its voxel size, does not tell us what the instrument and reconstruction actually resolved. That uncertainty can change the pore networks, mineral surfaces and flow predictions derived from the image.

How do we know whether a feature in a 3D image is real? X-ray CT and electron microscopy now shape research in carbon storage, geothermal energy, subsurface hydrogen and critical minerals. Yet the number most often quoted for an image, its voxel size, does not tell us what the instrument and reconstruction actually resolved. That uncertainty can change the pore networks, mineral surfaces and flow predictions derived from the image.

This fully funded PhD will tackle that problem with Heriot-Watt University and Carl Zeiss X-ray Microscopy. Working directly with ZEISS scientists and instrument developers, you will help turn a new 3D resolution measurement into a robust method that can be used across laboratories, instruments and materials. You will test how reliably it measures resolution, carry it from controlled phantoms into real porous rocks, and establish how image uncertainty affects scientific conclusions. You will also investigate whether AI super-resolution recovers physically supported structure or creates convincing features that the original measurement cannot justify.

The research combines advanced X-ray microscopy, electron microscopy, quantitative image analysis, uncertainty measurement, scientific programming and responsible machine learning. You will join the DigiPorFlow research group at Heriot-Watt’s Institute of GeoEnergy Engineering, a leading centre for subsurface energy research, and work within an international network of academic facilities and industry experts. Find out more about the group at https://digiporflow.site.hw.ac.uk/.

The project is designed to give you experience beyond a single laboratory. Subject to facility access and project needs, you will travel within the UK and Europe, and potentially to the United States, for instrument campaigns, training and collaboration. You will present your work at international conferences, publish research papers and build professional links across academia, national facilities and the imaging industry.

listings.title: Cultural Currents in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Century: Continuities between 'Victorian' and 'Modernist' Literature
listings.summary: This PhD project provides an opportunity to investigate and challenge the boundaries and definitions of ‘Victorian’ and ‘modernist’ literature across the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
listings.description:
This PhD project provides an opportunity to investigate and challenge the boundaries and definitions of ‘Victorian’ and ‘modernist’ literature across the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

Key issues to be explored include: how do we define Victorian and modernist writing? How do these concepts relate to historical periodisation; for example, the idea of a radical transformation between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries? What about the so-called transitional period of the fin de siècle or turn of the century? What are some of the continuities and affinities that we can identify in literature and culture across the nineteenth and twentieth centuries? Does literature have to be ‘new’, experimental and demonstrably modern or modernist to be worthy of study? And what role does genre fiction, such as the sensation novel, the Gothic, the weird tale, play in our definitions of nineteenth and twentieth-century literature?

The English department at Loughborough has particular research expertise in these areas. The Cultural Currents: Nineteenth to Twentieth Century research group has a wealth of knowledge relating to several areas of nineteenth and twentieth-century literature and culture, including Victorian literature, decadence and aestheticism, the fin de siècle, Edwardian literature, the Gothic, sensation fiction, Weird fiction, and modernism.

PhD researchers in these areas would be embedded and supported by a lively and diverse research culture, within the English department, the School of Social Sciences and Humanities, and the wider University.

listings.title: Luminescent Anion Receptors for High-Throughput Bioassays in Drug Discovery
listings.summary: The aim of this PhD project is to synthesise luminescent molecules that bind reversibly to target biological anions, which are produced during pharmaceutically important enzyme reactions. Anion binding to the molecular receptor will induce a luminescence response that enables measurement of enzyme activity in real…
listings.description:
The aim of this PhD project is to synthesise luminescent molecules that bind reversibly to target biological anions, which are produced during pharmaceutically important enzyme reactions. Anion binding to the molecular receptor will induce a luminescence response that enables measurement of enzyme activity in real time. The receptors will be developed into novel bioassays, enabling better selection and validation of new drug candidates at an early stage in drug discovery.

Enzymes that consume and produce nucleoside polyphosphate anions (e.g. kinases) represent a major target in cancer drug discovery. Many drugs act by inhibiting enzyme activity; therefore, to increase confidence in the selection of lead drug compounds, it is crucial that pharmaceutical companies have robust assays to measure enzyme activity accurately. Most existing assays require expensive, unstable antibodies or chemically modified substrates, which are time-consuming to prepare and place a strain on the drug development process.

The aim of this project is to develop molecular probes that bind reversibly to specific nucleoside polyphosphate anions (e.g. ADP), which are produced during pharmaceutically important enzyme reactions. Upon binding to the anion, the probe will provide a luminescent signal that enables precise measurement of enzyme (e.g. kinase) activity in real time.

The molecular probes developed in this project will provide a vital step towards the rapid, accurate determination of enzyme kinetics and mechanisms. This would enable better selection and validation of new drug candidates at an early stage in drug discovery, reducing effort pursuing compounds destined to fail at the more lengthy and costly development phases.

Strategies for promoting cellular uptake of the probes will be investigated to enable monitoring of biochemical processes in specific compartments of living cells. To achieve this, we will explore how changes to the structure and geometry of the molecular probes affect anion binding selectivity and cellular uptake behaviour.

This project is multidisciplinary in nature, spanning the areas of synthetic organic chemistry, supramolecular chemistry, and bioassay development. The student will gain excellent training in a range of techniques including organic synthesis, study of host–guest interactions using optical spectroscopy, bioassay development, and cellular imaging.

The student will be very well trained for roles in industry. Pharmaceutical and biotechn

listings.title: Luminescent Molecular Probes to Detect Phosphate in UK Waterways
listings.summary: A major unsolved challenge for environmental agencies is to monitor inorganic phosphate in water, to predict the breakout of harmful algae blooms that lead to aquatic “dead zones”. To solve this challenge, in this PhD project we will synthesise molecular probes that bind selectively to phosphate anions and generate a…
listings.description:
A major unsolved challenge for environmental agencies is to monitor inorganic phosphate in water, to predict the breakout of harmful algae blooms that lead to aquatic “dead zones”. To solve this challenge, in this PhD project we will synthesise molecular probes that bind selectively to phosphate anions and generate a sensitive luminescent signal that enables precise measurement of phosphate in water. In collaboration with the Loughborough EcoSENSE team, we will encapsulate our luminescent probes into hydrogel materials using our patented technology, thereby delivering new tools for the measurement of aqueous phosphate levels.

This project will provide a vital step towards the accurate mapping and prediction of harmful algae blooms, alerting environmental and health agencies to take appropriate action to maintain and improve water quality.

High levels of inorganic phosphate released into waterways through sewage, fertiliser, and pesticides are a primary cause of the spread of environmentally detrimental algae. A major unsolved challenge for environmental agencies is to monitor excess phosphate in water to predict the breakout of harmful algae blooms, which lead to aquatic “dead zones” and danger to human health. The cost of responding to water-based phosphate pollution in the UK alone is estimated at £170 million per year.

Crucially, there are no existing sensors or devices capable of detecting phosphate that have been miniaturised for point-of-need testing and mapping of large waterways (e.g. rivers and lakes).

To solve this challenge, this PhD project will synthesise molecular probes that bind selectively to phosphate anions and generate a sensitive luminescent signal that enables precise measurement of phosphate in water. We have established the design principles to create luminescent probes that exhibit high binding selectivity for target biological phosphate anions (Chem. Sci., 2022, 13, 3386). We will build on this knowledge to develop probes with enhanced sensitivity for inorganic phosphate and minimal interference compared with existing sensing methods.

We will encapsulate these luminescent probes into hydrogel materials using our patented technology, thereby delivering a new method for the measurement of aqueous phosphate levels. listings.title: Stimuli-Responsive Polymeric MRI Contrast Agents for Advanced Imaging Applications
listings.summary: The aim of this PhD project is to synthesise small molecule MRI contrast agents and incorporate them into responsive polymers. The resulting polymeric particles will be designed to respond to their surrounding environment by a measurable change in MRI signal, thereby reporting on physiological parameters such as local…
listings.description:
The aim of this PhD project is to synthesise small molecule MRI contrast agents and incorporate them into responsive polymers. The resulting polymeric particles will be designed to respond to their surrounding environment by a measurable change in MRI signal, thereby reporting on physiological parameters such as local pH in human tissue, aiding the diagnosis and better understanding of diseases such as cancer.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a medical imaging technique which provides 2 and 3-dimensional anatomical information on soft tissues in a non-invasive manner. In the clinic, MRI relies upon small molecule contrast agents to enhance the image quality, enabling the diagnosis of neurological, cardiovascular and oncological disorders. However, these MRI contrast agents suffer from low sensitivity and fast excretion from the body. We have shown that these properties can be improved dramatically by linking the contrast agent to polymer scaffolds, thereby increasing their size and restricting their local motion.

Recently, we developed a novel synthetic strategy to create macromolecular MRI contrast agents with enhanced imaging capabilities, by using a combination of organic chemistry and controlled polymerisation techniques. The resulting polymeric MRI agents display substantially higher image contrast compared to those used in the clinic, potentially allowing lower and safer doses of the contrast agent to be used. Building on this exciting work, this project will focus on synthesising small molecule contrast agents and incorporating them into responsive polymers, which are capable of reporting on physiological parameters such as local pH in human tissue, aiding the diagnosis and better understanding of diseases such as cancer.

The student will gain excellent training in a range of techniques including organic synthesis, polymer chemistry, materials characterisation, and molecular imaging. They will be supported by postdoctoral researchers within the Butler Group and will be very well trained for roles in industry. Pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies increasingly require scientists with combined synthetic and bioanalytical skills. Therefore, there are many potential employability options for the student, in addition to postdoctoral opportunities in this active research field.

listings.title: Heterogeneously integrated TFLN-on-SiN platform for ultra-high-speed photonics
listings.summary: Combining low-loss optical routing with high-speed modulation requires complementary photonic materials. This project will integrate thin-film lithium niobate with silicon nitride to develop a scalable electro-optic platform. Research will address material integration, optical transitions and radio-frequency design…
listings.description:
Combining low-loss optical routing with high-speed modulation requires complementary photonic materials. This project will integrate thin-film lithium niobate with silicon nitride to develop a scalable electro-optic platform. Research will address material integration, optical transitions and radio-frequency design for high-bandwidth devices and advanced photonic circuits.

Silicon nitride (SiN) provides low-loss passive photonic circuits, while thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) offers a strong Pockels effect for high-speed electro-optic control. Integrating these capabilities requires simultaneous control of material interfaces, optical mode transfer and radio-frequency propagation.

This project aims to develop a heterogeneous TFLN-on-SiN platform for high-bandwidth electro-optic devices. The central research question is how integration processes and optical and electrode designs can be coordinated to achieve efficient modulation while preserving low-loss passive routing and fabrication tolerance.

The research will investigate bonding or transfer processes and develop optical transitions between SiN waveguides and TFLN device regions. Modelling and experimental characterisation will quantify transition loss and sensitivity to geometry, alignment and process variation.

High-speed modulators will provide the primary device demonstrator. Optical and radio-frequency simulations will guide electrode design, addressing electro-optic overlap, impedance matching, velocity matching and electrode loss. Fabricated devices will be assessed through measurements of modulation efficiency, insertion loss and electro-optic bandwidth. The validated platform will also provide a basis for investigating wavelength conversion or electro-optic frequency-comb generation.

The expected contribution is an experimentally validated integration process, high-bandwidth device designs providing at least 100GHz electro-optical bandwidth, and quantified fabrication tolerances. These outcomes will support reusable electro-optic building blocks for high-speed optical interconnects, microwave photonics and frequency-comb systems.

listings.title: Wafer-scale co-designed metasurface-PIC platform for free-space optical I/O and sensing
listings.summary: Precise control of light between photonic chips and free space is central to optical communication and sensing. This project will co-design metasurfaces and integrated photonic circuits to realise compact beam-shaping interfaces, with experimentally validated performance and fabrication tolerances supporting…
listings.description:
Precise control of light between photonic chips and free space is central to optical communication and sensing. This project will co-design metasurfaces and integrated photonic circuits to realise compact beam-shaping interfaces, with experimentally validated performance and fabrication tolerances supporting wafer-scale integration.

Free-space optical communication, sensing and chip-to-chip interconnects require integrated photonic circuits (PICs) to generate controlled optical beams. Metasurfaces provide compact beam-shaping capabilities, but their response depends on the field delivered by the PIC and the tolerances of the combined structure.

This project aims to establish a wafer-scale metasurface-PIC platform through joint electromagnetic design and experimental validation. The central research question is how the guided optical field, coupling structure and metasurface can be engineered together to achieve prescribed free-space beam properties under practical fabrication constraints.

The research will develop co-design methods for selected functions, including focusing, collimation and beam steering. Electromagnetic simulations will link PIC output fields and metasurface geometry to beam profile, coupling efficiency and angular response. The designs will explicitly account for polarisation, optical bandwidth, alignment errors and fabrication variation.

Selected devices will be fabricated and characterised to test the accuracy of the models and quantify integration tolerances. A free-space optical I/O or sensing demonstrator will evaluate performance beyond the individual component.

The expected contribution is a validated design framework and reusable metasurface-PIC components suitable for inclusion in a process design kit (PDK). This will establish a route from beam-shaping structures to manufacturable optical interfaces, supporting free-space communication, LiDAR and optical interconnects.

Comprehensive training will be provided in photonic and optical modelling using Ansys Lumerical, COMSOL Multiphysics and Zemax, alongside full equipment training in the University of Southampton’s cleanroom facilities. You'll also receive hands-on training in optical measurements and silicon photonic chip testing, including optical alignment, fibre-to-chip coupling and device characterisation. Together, these activities will develop the skills required to design, fabricate and experimentally validate integrated photonic devices.

listings.title: Ultra-low-loss SiN platform for quantum, nonlinear and precision photonics
listings.summary: Optical loss sets the performance limits of quantum, nonlinear and precision photonic circuits. This project will develop an ultra-low-loss silicon nitride platform by linking loss mechanisms to fabrication and device design. Validated components and models will support reproducible high-Q resonators and advanced…
listings.description:
Optical loss sets the performance limits of quantum, nonlinear and precision photonic circuits. This project will develop an ultra-low-loss silicon nitride platform by linking loss mechanisms to fabrication and device design. Validated components and models will support reproducible high-Q resonators and advanced quantum computing applications.

Ultra-low-loss silicon nitride (SiN) photonics enables long optical interaction lengths and high-Q resonators, supporting quantum light generation, nonlinear frequency conversion and precision sensing. Achieving these capabilities reproducibly requires control of material absorption, scattering and fabrication variability.

This project aims to establish an ultra-low-loss SiN platform supported by validated fabrication processes and predictive device models. The central objective is to determine how material properties, waveguide geometry and processing conditions govern propagation loss and resonator performance.

The research will combine optical modelling, fabrication studies and experimental characterisation to distinguish the contributions of sidewall roughness, material absorption and device geometry. Process and design variations will be evaluated systematically to identify routes to lower loss and quantify their reproducibility. Waveguide and resonator measurements will connect fabrication parameters to propagation loss, quality factor and device variability.

These results will inform a process design kit (PDK) library containing high-Q resonators, with more than 1 million Q-factor, delay lines and filters, with models that incorporate measured performance and fabrication tolerances. A selected quantum, nonlinear or sensing demonstrator will test whether component-level improvements translate into application-level benefits.

The expected contribution is a quantitative understanding of loss mechanisms, a reproducible fabrication approach and a validated library of low-loss photonic building blocks. Together, these outcomes will establish a reusable foundation for quantum, nonlinear and precision photonic circuits.

listings.title: Wafer-scale pluggable optical I/O platform for high-density photonic packaging
listings.summary: Reliable optical connections are essential to scaling photonic systems. This project will develop a foundry-compatible platform for low-loss, high-density, pluggable optical interfaces. It will combine broadband edge couplers, passive alignment and wafer-level testing to establish repeatable connections for optical…
listings.description:
Reliable optical connections are essential to scaling photonic systems. This project will develop a foundry-compatible platform for low-loss, high-density, pluggable optical interfaces. It will combine broadband edge couplers, passive alignment and wafer-level testing to establish repeatable connections for optical interconnects and photonic packaging.

Optical packaging is a critical barrier to scaling integrated photonics. High-density interfaces must provide low coupling loss while accommodating fabrication and assembly tolerances. For pluggable connections, these requirements must also be maintained through repeated attachment and detachment.

This project aims to establish a foundry-compatible optical I/O platform that integrates device design, connector architecture and packaging. The central research question is how optical mode engineering and passive alignment can deliver repeatable, low-loss connections (<1dB per fibre) at high interface density.

The research will develop broadband edge couplers with expanded optical modes and evaluate the trade-offs between coupling efficiency, bandwidth, footprint and alignment tolerance. These designs will be integrated with fibre arrays and expanded-beam interfaces to investigate detachable connector architectures. Optical simulation, fabrication and experimental characterisation will establish the effects of process variation, assembly errors and repeated mating on performance.

Wafer-level optical testing will be investigated alongside packaging methods to support reproducible device screening and assembly. A prototype interface will validate coupling loss, operating bandwidth, alignment tolerance and connection repeatability.

The expected contribution is a set of experimentally validated interface designs and testing methods that provide a route towards scalable photonic packaging. The platform will address optical connectivity requirements in pluggable modules, near-packaged optics and co-packaged optics with collaborating with ORC fiber group.

listings.description:
This is a full-time PhD opportunity sponsored by Cranfield University under the UK’s EPSRC Future Telecommunications Hubs (FTH) ecosystem, which provides training and research as part of a larger ecosystem. The financial offering includes UK home fees, a bursary, and the focus area is in distributed AI over radio access networks.

This is a project focused on how AI will provide a seamless service to mobile users of tomorrow. It is expected the student will have a background in AI with a curiosity on wireless networking.

Machine learning that occurs over a distributed network is attractive to reduce latency, ensure data and compute is sovereignly hosted, and utilise available edge computation resources. There are many challenges when the demand is spatially and temporally mobile, and when the inference is computationally heavy. This PhD studentship will advance the research in AI on Radio Access Networks (AI-on-RAN) by exploring how to optimise distributed and mobile inference of large language models by adapting how tokens, memory, and network bandwidth is used in real time.

Cranfield University is a post-graduate only university focused on critical technologies such as aerospace, defence, AI, robotics, and telecoms. It is situated just north of London between Milton Keynes and Bedford. There is a proposed merger with King’s College London in 2027.

The outcomes are expected to shape how future AI algorithms are designed, as well as how future computation and communication resources are invested in 6G telecommunication networks.

There is both university-based and wider FTH ecosystem training with other PhD students from other universities across UK. The experience gained is not only cross-disciplinary (AI and telecoms), but also there will be exposure to different stakeholders beyond these including defence, government, and infrastructure.

Applicants should have a first or second class UK honours degree or equivalent in a related discipline of computer science, statistics, or electronic / information engineering. This project would suit students with a fundamental curiosity to how foundation models work at the algorithmic level.

We will take an inclusive approach during your recruitment process and consider students from underrepresented groups and different social economic groups.

listings.title: Data-driven modelling and intelligent management for modern electrical power systems
listings.summary: This project aims to develop data-driven asset criticality ranking and maintenance optimisation methods. By integrating machine learning with operational, condition-monitoring, and environmental data, it investigates multi-stress degradation, predicts asset failure risks, and prioritises critical assets to improve…
listings.description:
This project aims to develop data-driven asset criticality ranking and maintenance optimisation methods. By integrating machine learning with operational, condition-monitoring, and environmental data, it investigates multi-stress degradation, predicts asset failure risks, and prioritises critical assets to improve maintenance efficiency and power system reliability.

Effective asset management in electrical power systems is essential for ensuring operational reliability, minimising downtime, and optimising maintenance costs. However, traditional maintenance strategies often overlook the combined effects of environmental and operational stresses on asset degradation, limiting the accuracy of asset risk assessment and maintenance prioritisation.

This project aims to develop a data-driven framework for asset condition assessment, failure risk prediction, criticality ranking, and maintenance optimisation. Particular attention will be given to understanding how multiple stress factors influence asset health and long-term reliability.

The research will combine laboratory-based experiments with the analysis of available datasets, published research findings, and relevant environmental and operational information. Experimental investigations will provide insights into degradation mechanisms, while data analysis and modelling will support the assessment of asset performance and failure risks.

Expected outcomes include improved understanding of asset degradation mechanisms, more accurate risk assessment, systematic asset criticality ranking, and optimised maintenance strategies, supporting proactive decision-making and enhanced power system reliability.

You'll join an interdisciplinary and diverse academic team in the Electrical Power Engineering research group that will support you in expanding your transferrable skills, such as critical review of the literature, academic writing and publishing, as well as collaborating with your team members and organising activities. You'll acquire hands-on experience with testing facilities and operate state-of-the-art equipment in the Tony Davies High Voltage Lab (TDHVL) as part of your experimental research.

listings.description:
Future aeroengines are expected to use shorter nacelles to reduce weight and drag. This may bring the fan and outlet guide vanes closer together, affecting fan-stage noise generation and emphasising the performance of interstage acoustic liners. This project will investigate these coupled effects to support quieter and more efficient aeroengines.

Ultra-high bypass ratio (UHBR) aero-engines offer a route to improved propulsive efficiency, but their larger fan diameters can increase nacelle weight and drag. Shorter nacelles may therefore be required, potentially also reducing the spacing between the fan and outlet guide vanes (OGVs). This can affect the noise generation within the fan stage and emphasise the performance of interstage acoustic liners.

This project will investigate the noise implications of reduced fan–OGV spacing, with particular emphasis on the design and performance of interstage liners. The research will combine experimental measurements with analytical, reduced-order and numerical modelling to improve understanding of noise generation and attenuation within UHBR fan stages. The aim is to support liner designs that remain effective under representative source and flow conditions while helping to reduce noise at source.

This project will be hosted within the Rolls-Royce University Technology Centre (UTC) in Propulsion Systems Noise at the Institute of Sound and Vibration Research (ISVR). You'll benefit from a dynamic research environment with access to specialist facilities and a vibrant postgraduate community. You'll have opportunities to attend international conferences, workshops and training events, and to engage with researchers and industry experts. Join a team of ambitious researchers for a once in a lifetime opportunity to become part of the sustainability challenge in aviation at the forefront of research for the next generation of ultra efficient and quiet aircraft.

In recent years, simulated analytical experiments have become an increasingly valuable tool for supporting undergraduate learning. Virtual laboratory environments allow students to familiarise themselves with analytical instrumentation prior to practical sessions, to engage with experimental work during periods where laboratory access is restricted, and to explore techniques that may be too costly or time intensive to deliver routinely in an undergraduate setting.

Our project aims to develop a suite of interactive learning resources to enhance the teaching of analytical chemistry. A range of simulations will be created and trialled at Loughborough University and in partnership with external institutions.

A key priority of the project is to work collaboratively with universities that have limited access to specialised equipment, supporting their teaching through shared digital resources and knowledge exchange.

listings.title: Smart contracts for fair and sustainable energy sharing
listings.summary: How can households, businesses and public organisations share renewable energy fairly?
