Join an exciting PhD at the University of Southampton, where you will harness cutting-edge Physics-Informed Neural Networks to transform environmental flow modelling. Combining fluid mechanics, machine learning and world-class supercomputing, you will develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges, from flood simulations to sustainable engineering design, within a collaborative, internationally renowned research community.

Are you passionate about leveraging artificial intelligence to address pressing environmental challenges? Join our innovative team at the University of Southampton as we explore groundbreaking applications of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) in solving complex environmental flow problems.

This exciting PhD project focuses on using advanced machine-learning techniques to simulate environmental flows, including the 2D Shallow Water Equations, pivotal for understanding flood dynamics, to guide engineering design of submerged infrastructure, and in water resource management.

The project builds on our latest research in PINNs, merging fluid mechanics with state-of-the-art AI to achieve faster, more accurate, and robust solutions for real-world environmental challenges.

As part of this research, you will join a vibrant community of PhD students working on cutting-edge tools at the intersection of machine learning and fluid dynamics. Our Water and Environmental Research Group is a world leader in computational modelling and environmental science, providing an inspiring and collaborative environment to help you excel in your studies.

In addition, you will have access to one of the fastest supercomputing facilities in the UK, enabling high-performance simulations and data analysis to push the boundaries of current environmental flow modelling techniques.

We welcome applications from talented students around the world and encourage individuals from diverse backgrounds to apply. Funding is awarded competitively based on academic excellence.

Embark on a journey where machine learning meets environmental engineering, and contribute to a sustainable future with AI-driven solutions. Apply now to make your mark in this transformative field!

listings.title: Multiscale understanding of oxide-strengthened magnesium alloys for extreme space environments
listings.summary: What if oxide particles, usually viewed as defects, could help magnesium alloys survive the extreme conditions of space? This project will investigate how nanoscale oxides improve resistance to radiation, thermal cycling, using advanced electron microscopy and testing to develop next-generation lightweight materials…
listings.description:
What if oxide particles, usually viewed as defects, could help magnesium alloys survive the extreme conditions of space? This project will investigate how nanoscale oxides improve resistance to radiation, thermal cycling, using advanced electron microscopy and testing to develop next-generation lightweight materials for future spacecraft and satellites.

Magnesium alloys are among the lightest structural metals and offer significant opportunities for reducing the weight of future spacecraft and satellites. However, their wider adoption is limited by radiation damage, microstructural instability and the extreme temperature fluctuations encountered in space. Oxide particles present in magnesium alloys are traditionally regarded as defects that reduce performance. This project challenges that view by investigating whether nanoscale oxide particles can instead be engineered to improve strength, thermal stability and radiation tolerance.

The project will investigate how oxide particles interact with grain boundaries, dislocations, deformation twins and radiation induced defects in advanced friction processed magnesium alloys. The research will determine how oxide chemistry, size and distribution influence microstructural evolution during thermal cycling and helium ion irradiation, replicating conditions relevant to space applications. Particular attention will be given to understanding whether oxide interfaces can absorb radiation induced defects and thereby reduce damage accumulation.

The project combines advanced materials characterisation and testing techniques, including scanning electron microscopy, electron backscatter diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, low temperature thermal cycling, residual stress analysis, small scale mechanical testing and ion beam irradiation. You'll gain extensive training in state-of-the-art experimental methods and access world leading facilities at the University of Southampton and national ion beam research infrastructure.

The outcomes will establish design principles for oxide strengthened magnesium alloys and support the development of lightweight materials for space, aerospace and defence applications, while providing excellent opportunities for interdisciplinary research, collaboration and professional development.

listings.description:
Hollow-core fibres (HCFs) guide light through air. Considered the next generation of optical fibre, they are attracting strong industrial interest. However, there are many designs and applications still to be exploited. This project will explore designs for larger cores suitable for transmitting high power laser light.

Hollow Core Fibres are a new generation of optical fibre that guide light in air, with very little material overlap. Optical fibre underpins the internet, this new fibre brings many improvements such as ultra-low latency and increased data rates. As a result of recent progress here at the University of Southampton, we are seeing a surge in industrial interest, but there are many challenges that remain. Beyond the telecoms application lie many industrial and scientific applications and the fibres might look very different. In this project we will look at much larger structures that guide more spatial modes of light. The project will explore how the light propagates, how the fibre can work with different lasers and how new designs can open up applications.

This project would particularly suit you if you're someone who enjoys understanding how things work, developing ideas and finding creative ways through technical problems. You should be willing to work independently while also contributing to a supportive team, sharing ideas openly and learning from colleagues with different expertise. You'll join a collaborative research environment bringing together expertise in fibre design, fabrication, optical characterisation and numerical modelling.

We maintain many collaborations with industrial partners in both the fibre production and application spaces. The project will provide opportunities to build skills in both a laboratory setting as well theoretical and numerical modelling. Regular interaction with the wider team will help you connect detailed modelling to real fabrication challenges and wider research goals.

listings.title: Next-generation granular pharmaceuticals via ultrasonic spray drying
listings.summary: This project will investigate how ultrasound can produce more uniform, stable and high-quality granular pharmaceutical powders while reducing energy use. Combining experimental research, advanced particle characterisation and process modelling, the work will enable more efficient, scalable drug manufacturing.
listings.description:
This project will investigate how ultrasound can produce more uniform, stable and high-quality granular pharmaceutical powders while reducing energy use. Combining experimental research, advanced particle characterisation and process modelling, the work will enable more efficient, scalable drug manufacturing.

The pharmaceutical industry increasingly requires manufacturing technologies that can deliver powders with tightly controlled particle size, morphology, flowability and dissolution performance, while maintaining product stability and reducing energy consumption. Conventional spray drying, particularly using two-fluid nozzles, can provide limited control over droplet size and particle characteristics and may expose heat-sensitive pharmaceutical materials to undesirable thermal and shear stresses.

This project will develop an innovative spray drying system incorporating ultrasonic atomisation to produce granular pharmaceutical powders with improved and more consistent properties. Ultrasonic atomisation uses high-frequency sound waves to generate fine droplets with controlled size, offering a promising route to improved atomisation efficiency, reduced shear and lower energy consumption. The research will establish the relationships between key processing parameters, including ultrasonic frequency, feed concentration, drying temperature and airflow rate, and the resulting particle characteristics, including size, morphology, density, flowability, compressibility and dissolution behaviour.

The project will combine experimental investigation, process optimisation and modelling to develop a validated understanding of the mechanisms governing ultrasonic atomisation and spray drying. Advanced characterisation techniques, including scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and laser diffraction, will be used to evaluate particle properties and support process–structure–performance relationships.

Expected outcomes include an optimised and scalable ultrasonic spray drying process, a validated process model, mechanistic understanding of ultrasound-assisted atomisation and prototype granular pharmaceutical formulations. The research will provide valuable training in pharmaceutical processing, particle engineering, experimental design, advanced characterisation and process modelling, while addressing an important industrial challenge in the manufacture of high-quality pharmaceutical powders and drug delivery systems.

listings.title: AI for cybersecurity and trustworthy AI systems
listings.summary: Artificial intelligence is transforming cybersecurity while creating new challenges for the security and trustworthiness of AI systems. This PhD opportunity addresses research challenges across AI for Security and Trustworthy AI, developing novel methods, systems and frameworks for cybersecurity and trustworthy…
listings.description:
Artificial intelligence is transforming cybersecurity while creating new challenges for the security and trustworthiness of AI systems. This PhD opportunity addresses research challenges across AI for Security and Trustworthy AI, developing novel methods, systems and frameworks for cybersecurity and trustworthy artificial intelligence.

Artificial intelligence is becoming a critical component of modern digital infrastructure. Machine learning and large language models are increasingly used to detect cyber threats, automate security operations and support decision-making. At the same time, AI models and AI-enabled applications introduce new security challenges, creating a growing need for secure, robust and trustworthy AI systems.

This PhD forms part of a broader research programme in AI for Security and Trustworthy AI. Research projects may focus on AI for cybersecurity, trustworthy and secure AI systems, or the intersection of these areas.

A central theme of the programme is the design and study of systems that remain effective under realistic conditions. Research may involve developing new algorithms, security mechanisms, system architectures or evaluation frameworks that account for adaptive attackers, emerging threats, distribution shifts and operational constraints.

You will join an active research environment spanning cybersecurity and trustworthy AI, with opportunities to contribute to internationally recognised research while addressing some of the most pressing challenges in securing modern AI systems and digital infrastructures. listings.summary: This project will develop quantum-enhanced Mid-IR sensing by integrating Photonic Integrated Circuits, 2D-materials and engineered metasurfaces. Combining enhanced light-matter interactions with quantum sensing and machine learning, the research aims to achieve compact, highly sensitive detection of disease…
listings.description:
This project will develop quantum-enhanced Mid-IR sensing by integrating Photonic Integrated Circuits, 2D-materials and engineered metasurfaces. Combining enhanced light-matter interactions with quantum sensing and machine learning, the research aims to achieve compact, highly sensitive detection of disease biomarkers, VOCs and toxic gases for biosensing and environmental monitoring.

This project focuses on developing an advanced quantum sensing platform based on Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs), two-dimensional (2D) materials such as Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDCs), and engineered metasurfaces for highly sensitive point-of-care diagnostics and environmental monitoring. Quantum sensing, which exploits phenomena such as coherence and superposition, offers the potential to achieve sensitivities beyond conventional detection limits. TMDCs, with their tunable optical properties, can enhance light-matter interactions, while metasurfaces can amplify specific optical resonances and enhance Mid-IR spectroscopic signals.

The project will integrate TMDC-enhanced PICs with advanced metasurface structures in Attenuated Total Reflection (ATR) and waveguide configurations to develop compact, highly sensitive Mid-IR sensors. The platform will exploit quantum sensing principles to detect subtle changes associated with molecular absorption, enabling real-time detection of low concentrations of environmental pollutants, such as volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and toxic gases, and disease biomarkers associated with cancer and ARDS. The resulting molecular fingerprints will enable identification and quantitative analysis of target molecules.

The research will involve the design and fabrication of 2D material-enhanced PICs and metasurface chips, followed by spectroscopic characterisation and proof-of-principle testing. Machine learning and advanced data analysis will be explored to improve molecular identification, quantification and classification. The ultimate aim is to develop a compact, scalable and cost-effective sensing platform combining quantum-enhanced detection with the integration and portability of photonic technologies.

listings.description:
This project will develop AI-assisted vibrational spectroscopy for early cancer detection using circulating tumour DNA (ct-DNA), epigenetic markers and microRNA (miRNA). Combining Mid-IR and Raman spectroscopy with innovative on-chip photonic devices and machine learning, the research aims to enable sensitive, non-invasive biomarker detection and precise cancer characterisation.

Cancer remains one of the most prevalent diseases worldwide and is associated with a high mortality rate, with only around 50% of patients surviving 10 years, largely because many cancers are diagnosed at a late stage. Although significant advances have been made in early cancer detection, current assays remain largely experimental, are often expensive, and can suffer from limited sensitivity and specificity. We have recently demonstrated that vibrational spectroscopy, including Mid-IR and Raman spectroscopy, can quantify DNA fragment lengths and epigenetic modifications, both of which are effective markers of cancer.

This project will advance cancer diagnostics using vibrational spectroscopy, with a particular focus on novel biomarkers including circulating tumour DNA (ct-DNA), epigenetic markers, and microRNA (miRNA). Using infrared and Raman spectroscopy, the project will investigate the unique vibrational profiles associated with these biomolecules in biological samples. An innovative on-chip photonic device platform that we have recently developed will be used to enhance the sensitivity and precision of biomarker detection.

The project will integrate machine learning with vibrational spectroscopy to develop computational models for the identification, classification, and prediction of cancer based on these specific biomarkers. The anticipated outcomes include a robust platform for vibrational spectroscopy-based biomarker detection, providing a significant step towards personalised cancer diagnostics through non-invasive and real-time assessment of ct-DNA, epigenetic markers, and miRNA expression. This research has the potential to transform cancer diagnosis by enabling earlier detection and more precise characterisation of cancer subtypes.

listings.description:
Robots and embodied agents that collaborate need ways to share what they perceive, intend and need. This PhD investigates how embodied agents learn to communicate through the modalities available to them, such as vision, sound, touch, and gesture, to collaborate effectively with one another and people, without a pre-designed language.

Most research on emergent communication takes place in abstract, disembodied settings using discrete tokens. Real collaborative systems, such as robot teams, human–robot teams and autonomous vehicles, act in physical or simulated space with different sensors, bodies and constraints, and cannot assume a pre-shared language. Recent work shows that agents with different perceptual modalities invent different, grounded protocols, raising the question of how heterogeneous embodied agents learn to coordinate.

Communication in these settings is shaped by what each agent can sense, do and afford to transmit, so effective protocols must be grounded in the body and the task rather than imposed from outside. Understanding how they arise is a prerequisite for deploying collaborative robots that people can understand and trust.

listings.title: Can machines invent a visual language we can read? Emergence and interpretability of agent-made symbols
listings.summary: When artificial agents have to communicate by drawing rather than by exchanging words or tokens, what kind of visual language emerges, and when does it become stable, efficient and understandable to humans? This project studies how populations of agents invent shared visual symbol systems through interaction. You will…
listings.description:
When artificial agents have to communicate by drawing rather than by exchanging words or tokens, what kind of visual language emerges, and when does it become stable, efficient and understandable to humans? This project studies how populations of agents invent shared visual symbol systems through interaction. You will investigate which properties of the task, the agents and the population determine whether and how such systems arise, and develop the experimental tasks and analysis methods needed to characterise them.

Humans communicate through drawings, diagrams and sketches that are grounded in perception and work across linguistic boundaries. Research on communication between artificial agents, by contrast, has mostly relied on discrete tokens or natural language, and there is no systematic account of how visual communication systems emerge and stabilise. Previous work showed that agents can develop sketch-based communication protocols through interaction using differentiable drawing. This project asks the next question: under what conditions do populations of agents converge on stable, efficient and human-interpretable visual communication?

Unlike tokens, visual messages have no predefined vocabulary: any structure or convention must emerge purely from the pressure to communicate, and many existing measures do not carry over. Characterising what emerges is therefore part of the research. The project will combine interactive, cooperative tasks with new measures of compositionality, abstraction, stability and interpretability, to examine questions such as:

The emphasis can be adapted to your background and interests, whether computational (learning dynamics), analytical (measures and evaluation) or empirical (human studies). The project spans machine learning, cognitive science, linguistics and human–computer interaction, and informs the design of AI systems that communicate transparently with the people who work alongside them.

listings.title: From interfaces to structural integrity: design and durability of cryogenic composites for aerospace
listings.summary: This PhD project investigates the design and durability of advanced composites under cryogenic conditions, focusing on fibre–matrix interfaces, thermal mismatch, microcracking and fracture mechanisms. Through experimental characterisation and damage assessment, it aims to establish relationships between material…
listings.description:
This PhD project investigates the design and durability of advanced composites under cryogenic conditions, focusing on fibre–matrix interfaces, thermal mismatch, microcracking and fracture mechanisms. Through experimental characterisation and damage assessment, it aims to establish relationships between material architecture, damage evolution and structural integrity, enabling safer, lightweight composite structures for aerospace applications.

Achieving Net Zero aviation requires disruptive technologies for lightweight, hydrogen-powered aircraft. Advanced composite materials are crucial to this transition, particularly for liquid hydrogen storage at −253°C. However, extreme cryogenic environments introduce significant challenges associated with thermal mismatch, fibre–matrix interfacial degradation, microcracking and progressive damage evolution.

This PhD project aims to develop a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms governing the structural integrity and durability of advanced fibre-reinforced polymer composites under cryogenic conditions, supporting the development of safer and lighter hydrogen storage systems.

The research will combine experimental fracture mechanics, advanced imaging and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to investigate damage initiation and evolution across multiple length scales. Particular attention will be devoted to fibre–matrix interfaces, matrix cracking, delamination and the effects of thermal cycling on mechanical performance.

A central innovation will be the application of AI-driven image analysis to high-resolution microscopy and X-ray computed tomography, enabling automated damage detection, microcrack segmentation, quantitative microstructural characterisation and identification of relationships between material architecture and damage evolution.

The resulting experimental and imaging datasets will support the development of predictive approaches linking microstructural damage to macroscopic structural performance, informing material selection and interface engineering strategies.

Ultimately, the project will establish new knowledge and AI-enabled methodologies for designing damage-tolerant cryogenic composites, accelerating the development of reliable lightweight hydrogen storage technologies and contributing directly to the transition towards Net Zero aerospace transportation.

Multimodal LLMs can process text, speech, images, and video, but still struggle to understand how claims, evidence, and counterarguments connect across these different forms of communication. listings.description:
Use fibre-optic cables as large-scale sensors across cities, coasts, and oceans. This PhD will develop machine-learning and signal-processing methods for state-of-the-art distributed acoustic sensing datasets. You will analyse complex spatiotemporal signals, combine them with environmental and operational data, and investigate applications in infrastructure, transport, environmental monitoring, and marine sensing.

Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) turns optical fibres into a dense array of vibration sensors. It could transform how we monitor infrastructure, transport, environmental processes, human activity, and marine environments. However, DAS produces large, noisy datasets that are difficult to label, creating challenges for signal processing and machine learning.

This PhD will develop computational methods for analysing DAS data across urban and maritime settings. You will have access to state-of-the-art datasets collected across the south of England and London, alongside maritime datasets. DAS measurements can be combined with secondary datasets, including vehicle counts, air-pollution records, and local-authority information to contextualise and validate the signals detected by the fibre. These datasets create opportunities for data fusion, cross-environment comparison, and rigorous validation.

You will shape the technical contribution. Possible directions include self-supervised or weakly supervised learning; event detection, classification, localisation, and source separation; representation learning for spatiotemporal signals; uncertainty and interpretability; domain adaptation across cables, locations, and environments; efficient high-volume processing; and validation using incomplete ground truth. Applications could include transport, infrastructure, environmental hazards, ocean acoustics, marine activity, or ecological monitoring.

The project builds on capabilities and datasets developed through SOUNDSCALE project. You will work across computer science, engineering, signal processing, environmental research, and responsible innovation, with access to high-performance computing and collaboration with the National Oceanography Centre (NOC) and researchers working across urban and marine sensing applications.

listings.title: Engineering quantum photonic simulators for complex open quantum systems
listings.summary: Can we build a controllable quantum system that reproduces the behaviour of another quantum system that is far harder to access experimentally? This project will develop engineered quantum-photonic environments as analogue simulators of complex open quantum systems, enabling experimentally controlled studies of…
listings.description:
Can we build a controllable quantum system that reproduces the behaviour of another quantum system that is far harder to access experimentally? This project will develop engineered quantum-photonic environments as analogue simulators of complex open quantum systems, enabling experimentally controlled studies of decoherence, quantum transport, memory effects and coherence preservation.

Many quantum systems interact strongly with structured environments, making their dynamics difficult to calculate and even harder to probe experimentally. This project takes a different approach: rather than modelling a complex target system only through direct computation, you will engineer a simpler quantum-photonic platform whose interactions and environmental spectral properties reproduce selected features of the target system.

You will develop theoretical and computational frameworks for quantum emitters coupled to structured photonic reservoirs. Photonic crystals, hyperuniform and correlated disordered structures, coupled resonators and other engineered electromagnetic environments will be used to control the photonic density of states, spectral correlations, localisation and emitter-reservoir coupling. The aim is to establish mappings between target quantum dynamics and experimentally controllable photonic architectures.

Particular emphasis will be placed on open quantum systems beyond conventional Markovian descriptions, where memory effects and information backflow can qualitatively change quantum evolution. Target systems will include excitation transport and long-lived coherence in complex molecular and quantum-biological systems, many-body quantum systems with structured dissipation, and system-environment dynamics relevant to decoherence and quantum measurement. The goal is to reproduce selected spectral densities, correlations and coupling mechanisms in a controllable photonic platform.

Large-scale electromagnetic simulations will be combined with open quantum-system theory to connect realistic nanophotonic structures directly to quantum dynamics. Selected simulator architectures will be developed in collaboration with experimental researchers working on quantum emitters and integrated photonic platforms, providing a route from theoretical design to experimentally accessible tabletop quantum simulators.

listings.title: Freeform light routing in photonic circuits
listings.summary: Integrated photonic circuits need compact interconnects that can route light around bends and between components without being constrained by a periodic layout. This project will develop freeform photonic routing based on nearly hyperuniform disordered structures, creating pathway-first design rules for low-loss,…
listings.description:
Integrated photonic circuits need compact interconnects that can route light around bends and between components without being constrained by a periodic layout. This project will develop freeform photonic routing based on nearly hyperuniform disordered structures, creating pathway-first design rules for low-loss, scalable optical interconnects with arbitrary geometries.

Conventional photonic-crystal waveguides are strongly constrained by the symmetry directions of the underlying lattice. Recent work has demonstrated a different strategy: prescribe the desired optical path first, then construct a nearly hyperuniform photonic environment around it to provide bandgap-assisted confinement. This pathway-first approach has already enabled curved and right-angle interconnects with low transmission loss in simulations and experiments.

The project will develop this proof of concept into a more general design platform for integrated photonic routing. You will investigate how local structural order, photonic pseudo-bandgaps, light-line constraints, modal evolution, slow-light effects and disorder-induced scattering determine the transmission and robustness of freeform interconnects. Large-scale finite-difference time-domain simulations and band-structure calculations will be combined with geometry-based optimisation. Artificial intelligence will be used to accelerate the exploration of complex routing geometries, learn transferable design rules and identify low-loss architectures beyond what can be efficiently searched by conventional parameter sweeps.

The longer-term goal is to move from individual bends to scalable families of interconnects and routing networks that can connect photonic components at arbitrary positions and orientations. Selected designs will be realised and characterised in close collaboration with experimental partners, providing direct feedback between modelling, fabrication and measurement. The project will also explore applications in compact high-density photonic circuitry, including photonic implementations of neuromorphic computing, where flexible and scalable optical connectivity is a key enabling requirement.

listings.title: Impact of Fluids of Different Densities
listings.summary: The impact of two bodies of liquid, such as droplets, is a phenomenon that occurs widely in nature and in engineering applications, from waves breaking onto layers of marine biological matter to streams of different inks in additive manufacturing.
listings.description:
The impact of two bodies of liquid, such as droplets, is a phenomenon that occurs widely in nature and in engineering applications, from waves breaking onto layers of marine biological matter to streams of different inks in additive manufacturing.

Impacts are notoriously complicated problems to study, with rapid topological changes occurring over disparate length scales. For example, in wave impact, the size of the wavefront may be orders of magnitude larger than the spray thrown up post-impact. Impacts may therefore be challenging to capture using direct numerical simulations or in laboratory experiments.

It is here that mathematical modelling can excel. In many applications, it is the early stages of the impact that capture the critical physical phenomena, such as the formation of splash or spray and the subsequent breakup of the splash into smaller satellite droplets.

In this project, we will seek to extend existing models of liquid–liquid impact to scenarios in which the density of the fluids is allowed to change. We will build upon inviscid Wagner theory for impact dynamics by accounting for such density differences and including the effects of viscosity and surface tension in the fluids where necessary.

The successful applicant will need to have experience in fluid dynamics and mathematical modelling, while knowledge of asymptotic methods and complex variable methods will be highly beneficial.

listings.title: A study of rolling contact fatigue in electric vehicles (EVs)
listings.summary: This PhD project investigates how electrical currents damage rolling-element bearings in electric vehicles (EVs), reducing fatigue life and EV reliability. Using twin-roller tribological tests, metallography and picoscope capturing high frequency charging-discharging signals, it will identify failure mechanisms and…
listings.description:
This PhD project investigates how electrical currents damage rolling-element bearings in electric vehicles (EVs), reducing fatigue life and EV reliability. Using twin-roller tribological tests, metallography and picoscope capturing high frequency charging-discharging signals, it will identify failure mechanisms and evaluate material and lubricant solutions, supporting longer-lasting, sustainable electrified transport systems and machinery.

This PhD will address a critical reliability challenge in electric vehicles (EVs): how electrical currents passing through rolling-element bearings accelerate surface damage and shorten rolling contact fatigue life. The problem also affects electrified trains, aircraft and other high-speed rotating machinery.

Electrification exposes bearings to higher rotational speeds and stray currents not normally encountered in conventional internal-combustion-engine drivetrains. Even relatively low currents can produce electrical pitting, disrupt lubrication and initiate premature fatigue. These failures threaten vehicle durability, increase maintenance and material demand, and could hinder progress towards reliable, sustainable, zero-emission transport.

The project will determine how current amplitude and frequency influence bearing damage and fatigue life, identify the underlying charging, discharging and microstructural failure mechanisms, and establish how electrical effects interact with contact mechanics and lubrication. The intended outcome is a mechanistic evidence base for designing more durable bearings and predictive monitoring strategies.

You will conduct controlled rolling-contact experiments on bearing steels using a twin-roller tribometer, with electrical currents applied across a range of amplitudes and frequencies. Post-test metallography will reveal surface and subsurface damage, while electrostatic sensing offers a standout capability for monitoring charge–discharge events in real time. Candidate materials and lubricants with different electrical properties will be evaluated to mitigate damage and extend component life.

You will join the University of Southampton’s national Centre for Advanced Tribology at Southampton (nCATS) and Energy Technology research group, with access to specialist tribology, materials-characterisation and sensing facilities. listings.title: Ammonia-fuelled internal combustion engines: how does ammonia affect wear and friction of their tribological contacts?
listings.summary: The transition to carbon-neutral transport has accelerated interest in alternative fuels that cut greenhouse-gas emissions while remaining compatible with current engines. Although combustion and emissions performance have progressed, ammonia’s effects on tribological contacts in internal combustion engines are poorly…
listings.description:
The transition to carbon-neutral transport has accelerated interest in alternative fuels that cut greenhouse-gas emissions while remaining compatible with current engines. Although combustion and emissions performance have progressed, ammonia’s effects on tribological contacts in internal combustion engines are poorly understood. This PhD will investigate those effects under realistic operating conditions.

Ammonia is transforming marine propulsion, heavy-duty transport and distributed power by providing a carbon-free alternative to conventional fuels. However, a major challenge remains: ammonia, hydrogen, water and nitrogen-containing combustion products in ammonia-fulled engines may degrade lubricants, disrupt protective tribofilms and accelerate corrosion, wear and scuffing in highly loaded engine components. Without a clear understanding of these interactions, unexpected component failure could delay the adoption of ammonia-powered machinery.

This project offers the opportunity to tackle that challenge at the forefront of sustainable engineering. You will investigate ammonia–lubricant–surface interactions under representative engine conditions, exploring how lubricant formulations, engineering materials, coatings and operating parameters influence friction, wear and durability.

The research will deliver a validated ammonia-compatible tribology platform, including unique linked datasets, mechanistic reaction–wear models, and/or physics-informed predictive tools, to help develop practical guidance for selecting robust lubricant–surface combinations.

The project combines hands-on experimentation, advanced materials characterisation and data-driven modelling. You will gain interdisciplinary expertise in tribology, lubricant chemistry, surface engineering and physics-informed machine learning, with access to techniques including FTIR, SEM/EDS, Raman, XPS, ToF-SIMS, profilometry and/or FIB cross-sectioning.

You will also engage with engine, lubricant and coating specialists through an industrial advisory group, stakeholder workshops and specialist facility visits, with opportunities to present at international conferences. This is an opportunity to develop sought-after technical and transferable skills while contributing directly to reliable net-zero propulsion and the next generation of sustainable machinery.

This PhD project will develop novel composite anti-resonant hollow-core fibres integrating atomically thin 2D materials for advanced photonic and optoelectronic applications. The successful candidate will gain multidisciplinary expertise in cleanroom fabrication, materials integration, device characterisation, and numerical modelling while contributing to next-generation light management and photon processing technologies.

Hollow core optical fibre waveguide geometries are becoming increasingly relevant to modern telecommunications systems, an exemplar of which is the anti-resonant fibre (ARF) structure, which can guide light in the air core using a variety of cladding architectures. Intriguingly, the high internal surface area presented by this waveguide geometry offers an ideal material deposition template for strong light-matter interaction and to this end, we have developed world leading knowledge and expertise in deposition technologies that allow a wide variety of functional materials such as semiconductors and metals to be embedded within these air-silica structures.

More recently, we have explored the extraordinary properties of atomically thin two-dimensional (2D) materials within ARF structures, opening up exciting opportunities for next-generation photonic and optoelectronic devices and applications at the monolayer limit. In this PhD studentship, the candidate will further develop this novel composite material ARF (CM-ARF) technology, spanning the multidisciplinary remit between cleanroom based, 2D materials fibre integration technology for the highly innovative CM-ARF platform, with applications in active photon management and light processing functions.

Analysis of device properties will be performed in our fully equipped characterization laboratories, complemented by numerical simulation studies to complete the development cycle.

This photonic device technology and materials science driven project would thus be suitable for a highly motivated candidate with a strong physics, materials or engineering related background and programming abilities to develop highly transferable skills in cleanroom sample fabrication and electronic or photonic device characterisation, numerical simulations working with leading academic experts.

listings.description:
Are you interested in fabricating the future of optical fibre technology? In this project you will help to create a new generation of polarisation maintaining optical fibres that rely on revolutionary hollow-core fibre technology. These fibres will enable new applications in many areas including quantum computing and laser power delivery.

Hollow-core fibres are a revolutionary technology where light is guided in air rather than glass, creating the opportunity for next level performance. However, until recently these fibres have not been able to control the polarisation of the light they are transmitting. In this project you will work with our highly experienced team (and industrial collaborators) to address this short coming.

The fibres realised in your project will support a broad range of applications in areas as diverse as quantum communication, sensing, manufacture, and laser light delivery, making them highly relevant to industry. And as such, your work will offer the opportunity to make a significant impact beyond the research lab.

This project will combine theoretical simulation, hands-on fibre fabrication, and experimental fibre characterisation to achieve its goals, and will be suited to students with a more experimental STEM background. Previous experience of photonics or optical fibre is an advantage, but not essential, as full training will be given.

Your project will be based at the world-recognised Optoelectronics Research Centre (ORC), home to a broad and diverse PhD student community and >150 academic researchers. This community will support you and provide the guidance needed to achieve your goals.

If you are enthusiastic, engaged, and interested in helping to develop an exciting new technology, then this is the project for you!

listings.title: More data, less energy: multicore fibre amplifiers and components for future submarine networks
listings.summary: The internet’s next big leap could happen beneath the oceans. Meta’s planned petabit-scale cable signals a new era for multicore fibres. At Southampton’s Optoelectronics Research Centre (ORC), where researchers pioneered the first practical erbium-doped fibre amplifier, you’ll design and test next-generation multicore…
listings.description:
The internet’s next big leap could happen beneath the oceans. Meta’s planned petabit-scale cable signals a new era for multicore fibres. At Southampton’s Optoelectronics Research Centre (ORC), where researchers pioneered the first practical erbium-doped fibre amplifier, you’ll design and test next-generation multicore amplifiers and components, helping global networks carry more data with less electrical power.

Every video call, streamed film and online game relies on a hidden network. Deep beneath the oceans, optical fibre cables link continents and carry almost all intercontinental internet traffic. As demand for data grows, a major question emerges: how can we send more information without using more energy?

The industry is already taking the next step. In 2026, Meta announced Petal, a planned transatlantic cable designed to carry one petabit of data per second using multicore fibres, with service expected in 2029. These fibres contain several paths for light within a single strand, allowing more data to travel through each fibre. However, signals fade over long distances and must be boosted by optical amplifiers, which operate under strict power limits at sea.

You'll explore new ways to amplify multiple light signals using less electrical power. Combining modelling with hands-on experiments, you'll design, build and test multicore fibre amplifiers and optical components to help future submarine networks increase capacity while reducing energy use and cost. At Southampton’s Optoelectronics Research Centre (ORC), Sir David Payne and colleagues pioneered the world’s first practical erbium-doped fibre amplifier (EDFA), transforming long-distance communications. Building on this legacy, you will help develop tomorrow’s optical amplifiers in ORC’s specialist laboratories.

listings.summary: This PhD project explores van der Waals semiconducting ferroelectrics for programmable, energy-efficient optoelectronic devices. Combining nanofabrication, electrical characterisation and optical spectroscopy, you will investigate how switchable polarisation controls light–matter interactions, aiming to enable…
listings.description:
This PhD project explores van der Waals semiconducting ferroelectrics for programmable, energy-efficient optoelectronic devices. Combining nanofabrication, electrical characterisation and optical spectroscopy, you will investigate how switchable polarisation controls light–matter interactions, aiming to enable nonvolatile optical functionality for future computing, sensing and quantum technologies with reduced power.

This PhD project at the University of Southampton will explore van der Waals ferroelectrics for electrically programmable, energy-efficient integrated optoelectronic devices.

Optoelectronic devices can convert electrical signals to photons and vice versa, with applications in communications, sensing and quantum technologies. However, maintaining their optical configuration often requires continuous electrical power. Ferroelectric materials offer an exciting alternative as their electrically switchable polarisation can persist after the applied voltage is removed. The emerging family of semiconducting van der Waals ferroelectrics hosts strong light-matter interactions, potentially enabling optoelectronic devices with reduced standby energy consumption.

You will investigate how polarisation in van der Waals ferroelectrics can control its optical properties, both within these materials and in heterostructures. Key questions include how interfaces, material thickness and ferroelectric domains influence light-matter interactions, switching behaviour and stability.

The research will combine assembly of van der Waals heterostructures, nanofabrication, electrical measurements and optical spectroscopy. You will fabricate devices in the Southampton Nanofabrication Centre and develop skills spanning materials science, nanoelectronics and integrated photonics. Device characterisation will assess optical contrast, photoresponse, luminescence, switching energy, retention and endurance, establishing opportunities and limitations for practical integration.

You will join the vibrant 2DMINDs research lab within the Sustainable Electronic Technologies research group and be affiliated to the ECS Centre for Neuromorphic Technologies, and contribute to emerging technologies connecting electronic memory with light.

Even chemically identical compounds can exhibit subtle spectral differences arising from variations in isotopic composition, providing clues about their origins. In this project, you will combine Nuclear Magnetic Resonance data with…
listings.description:
Can we determine where a chemical came from using its spectroscopic fingerprint? Even chemically identical compounds can exhibit subtle spectral differences arising from variations in isotopic composition, providing clues about their origins. In this project, you will combine Nuclear Magnetic Resonance data with advanced Bayesian methods and machine learning to decode these signatures, for applications in forensic science and chemical security.

Determining the origin of chemical compounds is an important challenge in analytical chemistry, with applications in forensic science, chemical security and environmental monitoring. Although chemically identical compounds share the same molecular structure, subtle variations in isotopic composition can reveal clues about their production history. Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy can detect these differences, but extracting reliable information from complex, noisy data remains challenging.

In collaboration with the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), this project will develop statistical methods that combine physical understanding of NMR spectroscopy with Bayesian inference. Beyond classifying samples, we aim to identify which spectral features distinguish chemical origins, understand how they vary between samples, and quantify the confidence with which unknown compounds can be attributed to particular sources.

You will develop probabilistic models that account for measurement uncertainty, sample-to-sample variability and correlations between spectral features. Using experimental NMR datasets, you will investigate how subtle isotopic signatures can support reliable source attribution. The project will also explore how machine learning could complement Bayesian methods, particularly by making complex analyses more efficient and scalable.

Working at the intersection of chemistry, statistics and data science, you will gain hands-on experience in advanced data analysis, computational modelling and Python programming. You will have opportunities to collaborate with researchers at Dstl and the Interdisciplinary Centre for Magnetic Resonance at the University of Southampton. Training in statistical methods, programming and NMR interpretation will be tailored to your background, providing valuable skills for research and industry.

Training and guidance will be provided in Python programming, statistical modelling and data analysis, depending on your existing experience and background.

listings.summary: Artificial intelligence is transforming society but comes with a growing energy and carbon cost. This project will explore new nanostructured materials and device architectures that can deliver brain-inspired computing with radically improved energy efficiency.
listings.description:
Artificial intelligence is transforming society but comes with a growing energy and carbon cost. This project will explore new nanostructured materials and device architectures that can deliver brain-inspired computing with radically improved energy efficiency.

You will design and fabricate nanoscale neural elements using emerging semiconductors, such as 2D materials, redox-active molecules, perovskites, ferroelectric polymers, and hybrid organic–inorganic systems, exploring their potential for in-memory sensing, learning, and computation. By integrating these materials into scalable device arrays, the project aims to create neuromorphic systems capable of energy-efficient information processing.

Working within a multidisciplinary environment, you will collaborate with researchers across electronics, photonics, device physics and materials science to advance the next generation of green intelligence technologies, bridging materials innovation and sustainable AI architectures.

You will join the multi-disciplinary Flexible Nanoelectronics Lab, work at the world-class labs of the Optoelectronics Research Centre (ORC), while you will have the opportunity to build connections with UK and European research partners by being affiliated also with the UK Multidisciplinary Centre for Neuromorphic Computing – NeuroSYNC and the Centre for Neuromorphic Technologies - CeNT. Additionally, you will be encouraged to attend major conferences, sharing your work and networking with leading experts.

The outcomes of your research can have various applications, such as Internet of Things and edge computing, AI, artificial vision, high density data storage for wearable devices, and many others.

This project is a chance to contribute to emerging technologies with the potential to revolutionise data processing and computing, while gaining skills, recognition, and experience that will position you as a leader in the field of nanoelectronics and brain-inspired memory technology.

The project provides hands-on training in materials deposition in films, device nano-fabrication, optoelectronic device engineering, and photonic system integration, with access to advanced cleanroom facilities and state-of-the-art optical characterisation tools. You will gain interdisciplinary skills spanning materials science, nanotechnology, photonics, and neuromorphic computing, positioning them for careers at the forefront of brain-inspired technologies and AI hardware.

listings.description:
This project pioneers deep learning for turbulence modeling, focusing on wall-bounded flows. By combining convolutional neural networks (CNNs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), and physics-informed methods, it aims to develop dynamic predictive models that overcome current limitations. The research supports scalable, accurate simulations of multi-scale phenomena, advancing computational design across energy, transport, and biomedical applications.

This project explores the cutting edge of artificial intelligence for turbulence modelling in turbulent flows, particularly in wall-turbulent flows. Using advanced deep neural networks, the research aims to create hybrid predictive models that combine theoretical insights with data-driven approaches that reliably simulate turbulent flows. While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and generative adversarial networks (GANs) have shown promise in capturing complex flow structures (e.g., reverse energy cascade), they also come with challenges, including the need for extensive, high-resolution training data and limitations in generalizing to new conditions. The goal is to develop predictive hybrid models

This project will push the boundaries of current methods, addressing specific limitations: CNNs’ difficulty with high-frequency flow features and GANs’ computational demands. The research will pioneer the use of physics-informed loss functions and reinforced learning in a hybrid framework, enhancing model accuracy and applicability. The ultimate goal is to contribute models that can guide the design and development of fluid systems by predicting multi-physics, multi-scale phenomena, critical to advancing technologies in any field such as sustainable energy, transport or medical.

This work will also focus on scaling solutions to Exascale computing, bringing new possibilities to turbulence simulations.

listings.description:
AI for Zero-Carbon Combustion. Develop a dynamic mixed model powered by super-resolution GANs to predict hydrogen and sustainable-fuel flames in large eddy simulation. Combine deep learning, physics and exascale computing to help design future zero-carbon energy systems. Ideal for engineering, physics or maths graduates passionate about AI and fluids.

Hydrogen and carbon-neutral fuels are key to net zero, but their flames are notoriously hard to predict. They switch between combustion regimes, develop intrinsic instabilities and push energy back up the scales. Today’s turbulence-combustion models can’t keep up. Your PhD will change that.

You’ll advance a new hybrid approach: a dynamic mixed model powered by super-resolution GANs. It pairs the robustness of physics-based closures with AI’s ability to reconstruct unresolved small-scale flow features. The goal is large eddy simulation models that generalise beyond their training data, need less high-fidelity data and run on the world’s fastest supercomputers.

Training will be provided on HPC, programming, machine learning, and fluid dynamics will be realized through participation in Summer Schools and European Training events (e.g. Cypher COST)

This PhD will investigate specialty optical fibres and develop components to make quantum networks more reliable and practical. Closely linked to the EPSRC-funded BOUNDLESS and HASC programmes, you will gain hands-on experience in advanced photonics and future communications.

Quantum technologies could change how we communicate, process information and measure the world around us. Optical fibres will play a key role in connecting quantum devices and building future quantum networks. However, these networks need better fibre connections and components to carry very weak quantum signals with minimal loss and disturbance.

This PhD project will investigate specialty optical fibres and develop new fibre components for next-generation quantum networks. You will explore hollow-core and multicore fibres, test their performance and design components that connect different fibre systems and quantum devices. The work will combine optical modelling, hands-on experiments and optical measurements. You may also explore how well these fibres carry single photons and how stable the signals remain under different conditions.

You will join the Optoelectronics Research Centre (ORC) at the University of Southampton, a leading research centre in optical fibres and photonics. The project is closely linked to two major UK EPSRC-funded research programmes: BOUNDLESS (Boundless Light) and HASC (Hubs in All-Spectrum Connectivity), offering opportunities to engage with wider research activities in advanced photonics and future communication networks. You will gain hands-on experience in fibre technology, optical system development and advanced measurement techniques, while working in a collaborative research environment.

listings.description:
Using light to detect gases with extraordinary sensitivity for environmental, industrial and healthcare applications, this PhD combines hollow-core optical fibres, advanced modelling and hands-on experiments. You will join a leading photonics research environment and shape the project around your interests and discoveries from day one.

How can we detect tiny traces of gas quickly, remotely and with exceptional sensitivity? Hollow-core optical fibres offer a powerful answer. Inside the gas-filled core, light and molecules can interact over long distances, creating new possibilities for environmental monitoring, industrial safety, healthcare and fundamental science.

In this PhD, you will investigate how gas composition, pressure and temperature alter light travelling through hollow-core fibres affecting optical loss, phase, dispersion, molecular absorption and nonlinear interactions. You will identify the strongest (or most sensitive) of those interactions and then turn them into innovative sensing technologies.

You will work across theory, simulation and experiment: building numerical models, designing optical systems, testing ideas in the laboratory and analysing real measurements. You will graduate with a distinctive combination of skills in computational modelling, optical measurement, fibre photonics and sensor design. listings.title: High-speed and avalanche photodetectors on silicon photonics
listings.summary: Future Artificial Intelligence (AI) infrastructure and data centres will require highly sensitive, energy-efficient optical interconnects operating at unprecedented data rates. This project will explore novel integration approaches to combine III-V semiconductor heterostructures with silicon photonics to develop…
listings.description:
Future Artificial Intelligence (AI) infrastructure and data centres will require highly sensitive, energy-efficient optical interconnects operating at unprecedented data rates. This project will explore novel integration approaches to combine III-V semiconductor heterostructures with silicon photonics to develop high-speed and avalanche photodetectors, enabling next-generation optical receivers for future communication systems.

The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and hyperscale data centres is driving demand for faster, more energy-efficient optical interconnect technologies. Silicon photonics has emerged as a leading platform for future co-packaged optics, providing scalable integration of optical communication functions. However, significant challenges remain in improving receiver sensitivity, reducing power consumption, and sustaining continued growth in data transmission capacity.

This project will investigate a new generation of high-speed and avalanche photodetectors based on III-V semiconductor heterostructures integrated with silicon photonic circuits. Leveraging emerging epitaxial growth techniques, the research will explore novel device architectures that enable precise control of optical absorption, carrier transport and avalanche multiplication, creating opportunities for highly sensitive and energy-efficient optical receivers.

You'll undertake research spanning semiconductor materials, device physics and photonic integration. A major focus of the project will be the growth and characterisation of advanced III-V heterostructures, together with the design and optimisation of doping profiles and junction architectures for photodetector applications. The project will investigate carrier transport, high-field effects, impact ionisation and avalanche processes in semiconductor devices, providing insights into the physics governing high-speed and high-sensitivity photodetection. This project offers a unique opportunity to work across multiple disciplines, combining materials growth, nanofabrication, device engineering and photonic integrated circuits. There will be opportunities to interact with our academic and industrial partners across the UK and internationally.

listings.title: Design and fabrication of large-area metasurface optics
listings.summary: This project aims to investigate the design and wafer-scale fabrication of large area metaoptics for imaging and sensing. It combines advanced design with fabrication using our state-of-the-art cleanroom and optical experiments in a world-leading research laboratory.
listings.description:
This project aims to investigate the design and wafer-scale fabrication of large area metaoptics for imaging and sensing. It combines advanced design with fabrication using our state-of-the-art cleanroom and optical experiments in a world-leading research laboratory.

Metaoptics, the application of metasurface concepts in optical systems, is a rapidly growing field that has the potential to revolutionise a wide range of applications, such as sensing, imaging, and telecommunications. However, the design and manufacturing of high precision, large-area metaoptic components remains a challenge due to the difficulties in achieving high precision accuracy over a large diameter.

Recently our team has made first steps in producing high quality metalenses using the deep-UV (DUV) scanner lithography tool available in the University of Southampton’s cleanroom.

The scope of this PhD research is to advance the design and fabrication of metaoptics in the near- and mid-infrared range making use of state of the art capabilities in design of metasurfaces and their integration into optical systems.

The project will explore the design of metasurfaces through both commercial and custom-built (e.g. deep learning) software. Experimentally, we will fabricate metasurface optics using advanced full-wafer fabrication tools such as Southampton’s Deep-UV lithography (the only such system available in the UK’s academic research community) and our new 200 kV electron beam lithography system (the only such system currently installed in UK and Europe).

During the PhD research you will receive training and will develop strong expertise in fabrication of devices using one of the leading research cleanroom facilities in the UK.

Applications are invited for a postgraduate researcher to join this new activity taking place in the Quantum, Light and Matter group at the University of Southampton. We are looking for highly motivated applicants with interest in the topic of metasurfaces and an affinity for experimental optics research, involving numerical design, nanofabrication using the University’s cleanroom facilities, and optical studies.

listings.title: Metasurfaces for machine vision and compact photonics
listings.summary: This project will develop and demonstrate advanced bilayer metasurface optical elements addressing performance trade-offs and constraints (field of view vs. numerical aperture and efficiency; off-axis aberrations) that limit the applications potential and real-world deployment of single-layer metalenses.
listings.description:
This project will develop and demonstrate advanced bilayer metasurface optical elements addressing performance trade-offs and constraints (field of view vs. numerical aperture and efficiency; off-axis aberrations) that limit the applications potential and real-world deployment of single-layer metalenses.

Metasurfaces – planar arrays of subwavelength nanostructures – enable precise control of electromagnetic waves within an ultrathin layer of material. As a replacement for bulk glass/crystal optics they can dramatically reduce the size and weight of optical systems.

However, while metasurface lenses are now being deployed in a range of axial focusing, beam steering, and structured light generation applications, single-layer designs are inherently subject to off-axis aberrations, and performance trade-offs that limit their usefulness in applications dependent on high-fidelity imaging and wavefront control, such as micro-endoscopy, optical metrology, and automotive LiDAR. Bilayer architectures can address these issues, and/or add novel optical functionalities not possible in bulk or single-layer metasurface lenses, but present complex design and fabrication challenges.

This project will leverage computational (inverse) design-for-manufacturing methodologies, and Southampton’s unparalleled nanofabrication facilities to demonstrate the applications potential, and a pathway to scalable fabrication, of bilayer metasurface optical elements.

listings.title: Time crystals: a new state of matter for next-generation data processing
listings.summary: Time crystals are an eagerly sought phase of matter with unique functionalities. This project will explore the exciting physics of time crystals and the foundations of ‘timetronics’, an information and data processing paradigm relying on the unique characteristics of this sophisticated yet esoteric state of matter.
listings.description:
Time crystals are an eagerly sought phase of matter with unique functionalities. This project will explore the exciting physics of time crystals and the foundations of ‘timetronics’, an information and data processing paradigm relying on the unique characteristics of this sophisticated yet esoteric state of matter.

The earliest computers, from the abacus to sophisticated clockwork calculators, were mechanical and digital. They dominated computation well into the twentieth century. Why did electronics ultimately prevail? It’s advantage was the transition to the nanoscale, where transistors enabled fast operation, dense integration, scalable manufacturing, and cascaded binary Boolean logic. Can mechanical computers also be scaled to the nanoscale, and if so, could they compete with electronic architectures?

As the central building block for mechanical computation, based on the concept of a time crystal, we examine the ‘timetron’: a nanomechanical element switched by light between two dynamical states of motion – rest and sustained oscillation – encoding logical ‘0’ and ‘1’ states for timetronic data processing. Based on the timetron, key logical and memory elements can be implemented, at femtojoule-level switching energies, and with only a few femtowatts of optical power required to sustain the logical state.

listings.description:
Optical imaging and metrology techniques now routinely break the classical diffraction limit on resolution. This project will reach further still – leveraging recent advances in the subwavelength structure of light fields, metamaterials, information theory and artificial intelligence to achieve sub-nanometric (atomic scale!) optical measurement precision.

Optical imaging and metrology become increasingly challenging at the nanoscale, as objects and the parameters we seek to quantify (dimensions, shapes, positions, displacements) become small compared to the wavelength of light. Existing ‘super-resolution’ microscopy techniques rely on fluorescent tagging and low frame rates – they cannot be employed to probe the structure or sub-millisecond dynamics of metal/semiconductor/dielectric nanomaterials and devices.

We have shown recently that optical measurements with deeply subwavelength (sub-nanometre) resolution are possible via analyses of objects’ light scattering patterns (for further read: 'Picophotonic localization metrology beyond thermal fluctuations'). This project will explore the physics and test the limits of the approach in application, for example, to the study of thermal and optically-driven motion in nanomechanical systems.

listings.title: Enhancing power capture of tidal turbines using novel blade designs
listings.summary: Tidal turbines need to reduce their cost of energy and novel blade designs can be employed to do this taking inspiration from nature, wind energy and the aviation sector.
listings.description:
Tidal turbines need to reduce their cost of energy and novel blade designs can be employed to do this taking inspiration from nature, wind energy and the aviation sector.

The freestream tidal energy industry is still in its infancy with some full-scale commercial demonstrator devices in operation. Costs are still high relative to comparable forms of power generation, but it is thought that there are further advantages of tidal energy in that the flow can be constrained locally around the seabed, water surface and other devices to increase power output.

This PhD will investigate novel blade designs that can be used to enhance power capture. It will initially build upon existing experimental research conducted at Southampton regarding blade winglets whilst also potentially expanding to alternative geometric modifications inspired by nature and related engineering applications. Work will be conducted in collaboration with industrial partner Proteus Marine Renewables.

This is an analytical, numerical and experimental-based research project. For the latter, various experimental facilities will be used. Smaller-scale works will be conducted in our recirculating flumes and water channels whilst larger-scale mechanical turbines will be tested in the largest UK University-operated towing tank at our Boldrewood innovation campus.

listings.description:
Recent developments in quantum materials and topological design principles is transforming how we control the flow of light and charges. This project will develop nanostructured metasurfaces where optical and electronic functionalities are codesigned, fostering the emergence of novel coherent phenomena, leading to new generations of light-emitting and detecting optoelectronic (meta)devices

Metasurfaces are thin planar arrays of subwavelength nanostructures that have transformed the way we can control the flow of light. Recent breakthroughs in quantum materials and topology-led design have extended their capabilities from passive to active manipulation.

This project pursues the dynamic control of light emission and absorption in optoelectronic metasurfaces where the optical and electronic responses intertwine and become crucial for determining their functionalities.

During the project you will research strategies to engineer the short- and long-range interactions of matter with light in these platforms by engaging various degrees of freedom like polarization, spin, and symmetry. You will do it through a blend of experimental activities, theoretical analysis and numerical modelling.

You will join the Optoelectronics Research Centre (ORC), a world-leading photonics research organization, and collaborate closely with students, researchers and academic experts. You will be encouraged to take initiative, develop and test your own ideas. You will have the opportunity to engage in collaborations, research meetings and to present your work at major international conferences. Your research is expected to generate several papers in leading academic journals and contribute to shaping the future of this exciting field.

As the project progresses, you will learn new ideas and concepts and develop highly transferable know-how and skills. These include cleanroom nanofabrication, photonic and electronic materials and devices design, manufacturing and characterisation, numerical simulations. This experience will prepare you for opportunities in academia and industry.

Our extensive PhD training programme provides knowledge and skills through photonics lectures, training for report writing, project management, time management, presentation skills and full safety training for your research area. These are all essential life skills for the next step in your career.

listings.title: Laser-based fabrication of microfluidic devices for clinical diagnostic testing
listings.summary: The project explores the development of microfluidics-based sensors or diagnostic devices that are affordable, user-friendly and provide and effective testing strategy (widely-adopted during COVID-19 for informed decision-making) for rapid testing at the point-of-care which could include a hospital bedside or a…
listings.description:
The project explores the development of microfluidics-based sensors or diagnostic devices that are affordable, user-friendly and provide and effective testing strategy (widely-adopted during COVID-19 for informed decision-making) for rapid testing at the point-of-care which could include a hospital bedside or a care/nursing home, or in an ambulance or at home.

The wider aim of the project is to use a laser-based direct-write technique developed and patented by our group to pattern microfluidic devices in paper for the creation of the diagnostic sensors or tests.

Our innovative laser-based manufacturing technique allows the creation of custom-designed fluid flow paths within porous materials such as paper, and when used in combination with bio-chemical assays provides a route to producing sensors with much desired functionalities, including multiplexing, semi-quantification, and enhanced sensitivity.

This research which will happen in collaboration with clinical researcher is highly multi-disciplinary, which not only draws upon expertise in laser physics/engineering and microfluidics, but also vital knowledge of biochemistry and medicine.

The objective of the PhD is the development of paper-based tests such as lateral flow tests (such as those widely used during the COVID-19 pandemic) for simultaneous detection of multiple disease-specific biomarkers which help early-stage detection of the targeted diseases or conditions – examples of these include tuberculosis, sepsis, cytokine storm and urinary tract infections.

The project is mainly experimentally oriented and will provide opportunities to train across disciplines through working within different laboratories (laser- and bio-labs with different systems and instrumentation and procedures) and locations (universities, central governmental labs or NHS hospitals) within UK and outside.

We are seeking to enrol individuals enthusiastic about learning across the diversely different disciplines and contributing as an effective team player.

listings.title: Boundless light: fibre optic systems unconstrained by glass properties
listings.summary: BOUNDLESS is a six-year Programme Grant that aims at redefining fibre-optic communications and sensing based on the capabilities of hollow-core fibres. A range of PhD opportunities are available covering fibre development, broadband amplification, integrated photonics, communications, multifunctional systems, gas…
listings.description:
BOUNDLESS is a six-year Programme Grant that aims at redefining fibre-optic communications and sensing based on the capabilities of hollow-core fibres. A range of PhD opportunities are available covering fibre development, broadband amplification, integrated photonics, communications, multifunctional systems, gas detection and sensing in harsh environments.

Optical-fibre systems have traditionally been designed around the limitations of glass. BOUNDLESS, an ambitious six-year EPSRC-funded Programme Grant, aims to remove those constraints and explore what fibre technologies could achieve if they were designed around applications instead. BOUNDLESS seeks to unlock the full potential of hollow-core fibre and create a new generation of communication and sensing systems.

Unlike conventional optical fibres, hollow-core fibres can offer broad transmission bandwidths, exceptionally low nonlinearity and dispersion, operation across wavelengths from the ultraviolet to the mid-infrared, and strong resilience in challenging environments. BOUNDLESS will exploit these capabilities by developing an ecosystem of fibres, amplifiers, photonic devices, communication technologies and advanced sensors.

We are seeking talented and highly motivated PhD candidates interested in contributing to a collaborative programme developing new components and systems for applications ranging from future communication networks multifunctional infrastructures to gas detection, sensing in fusion and other harsh environments.

The project will be developed jointly with you, reflecting your interests, expertise and career aspirations. The supervisory team will be chosen from across BOUNDLESS according to the chosen research direction.

The predominantly experimental nature of these projects will provide extensive hands-on training using the ORC’s advanced fibre fabrication, photonic device, characterisation and optical systems facilities. These include the extensive Zepler cleanrooms for fibre and photonic component fabrication, the ‘X-band’ ultrafast measurement facility, and a suite of characterisation and application laboratories. Depending on the selected research area, you'll develop specialist expertise in optical fibres and amplifiers, integrated photonics, communication systems or advanced sensing, alongside transferable skills in experimental design, data analysis and scientific communication.
